News.title: Seedy underbelly of Croatia hotspot where rowdy tourists wee in street as ‘Pitbull police’ clamp down with booze ban
News.content:
A DRUNK tourist held up by two friends is seconds away from being hit with a huge fine for vomiting in the street.

City council workers who issue the penalties — dubbed tourist police by locals — zero in on the three lads and get their machines out, ready to issue the penalty just after midnight.





But just before the wasted Brit throws up, a fourth pal appears with a plastic bag that is opened and primed to catch it.

Thwarted, the “fun police” return to scouring the crowd for the next opportunity to slap a tourist with a draconian fine.

Welcome to Split in Croatia, where party tourists are having to get creative to avoid the city’s €300 (£256) fines for vomiting, urinating or drinking in the street.

The city’s crackdown on drunks is now in its third year.

The gigantic fines were introduced in 2023. Then, the following year, the mayor forced the Old Town’s bars to shut at midnight instead of 2am in a bid to quieten things down.

And now, officials have voted in a temporary ban on the sale of alcohol in shops between 9pm and 6am.

It will remain in force until September 15.

Announcing the restriction plan at the start of summer, Mayor Tomislav Suta told Croatian press the move would “curb drunkenness and disorderly behaviour”.





But business owners have branded it “virtue signalling”.

One, who did not want to be named amid fears of upsetting City Hall, said: “It’s pointless and posturing as most shops close by 9pm.

“Most tourists aren’t drinking from cans on the street anyway.”

Every night, the tourist police — two officials dressed in white — prowl the city streets to catch out anyone breaking the rules.

They are flanked by six security guards in uniform emblazoned with the word “Pitbull”, who will catch anyone who tries to swerve a fine.

The Sun watched as, just after midnight, two men walking along the street drinking beer were stopped and fined for boozing.

Another tourist who was hit with a fine for urinating in a side street said: “It’s ridiculous that they’re issuing fines for weeing in the street when the public toilets are closed.

“I can’t go into a bar after midnight, and the clubs take for ever to get into.”



When The Sun last visited Split three years ago, gigantic signs peppered pedestrian-only Marmontova street, laying out oppressive rules.

The notices warned visitors they were “in the city of a Roman emperor, so act like it”.

Now they are gone, replaced by smaller signs at the entrance to the Old Town, making Split look less like a city with a drunken tourist issue.

But given that a €3.80 (£3.25) beer is the same price as a lemonade in most bars, it is no surprise visitors are choosing the harder stuff.

The crackdown has left some bars struggling, however, as they have been forced to close during their busiest time of night — midnight to 2am.

Leo Males, owner of Mandrill’s pub and Leopold’s Craft Beer Bar, told The Sun: “The streets are louder now than ever before because the drunk tourists are just being let loose on to them at midnight. If a guest in my bar is behaving like an idiot, I’ll tell them and they always calm down.

“But once they’re on the street, they won’t listen.

“There’s a respect for workers, but they won’t listen to random locals.



“The city wants people to be more respectful, but when they’re stuck on the street at midnight there is nowhere for them to go to the loo other than the streets.

“Public toilets shut at 11pm or 12am, and they can’t go into a bar any more. It’s just not very sensible, but we’ll survive. The service industry is very resilient and before long, someone else will be in power with different ideas.”

Leo has had bars in the city for 15 years, and his craft beers keep punters coming back for more — as do his drinking challenges.

Customers can take on the Tequila Dum Dum challenge, where they put on a World War One helmet and get smacked three times with a shot of tequila and tonic water, before downing it for just €5 (£4.27).

Thankfully, the city’s fines are not putting most tourists off coming and having fun.

Phoebe, 22, from South London, is on a girls’ holiday in Split with three pals and they have had no issues.

She said: “We were out until 5am last night. We were in Charlie’s Bar until 4am and then just on the street. We’ve had so much fun. There’s so many different people here.”

Last year 825,000 Brits holidayed in Croatia, with Split being the country’s second most popular destination.



It is a two-and-a-half hour flight from the UK and return tickets cost around £250 during the summer months.

Around 3,000 people live in the city’s Old Town — and it was complaints from some of these locals about “rowdy” tourists that sparked the crackdown.

For Juraj Perisic, who owns Georgy Shooters Bar, having to close early has cost him around 20 per cent of his profits.

“The city has made a mistake,” he said. “They wanted to make it quieter but instead, it’s louder. People make a mess because they’re stuck outside on the streets.

“I’m lucky that my bar is a secondary income.

“But for people who rely on the tourism sector, it’s been hard on them the past few years.

“They want elite tourism but there are no five-star hotels in the centre, no Michelin-star restaurants, or designer outlets.

“The city doesn’t really cater to five-star guests.

“The only thing Split can be is a party place or it can go back to being a transit town, like it was for decades — a place where people would just board a ferry.

“Young people bring money, but they need to be managed. They can’t be managed if they’re sent on to the streets at midnight.” Juraj’s bar is renowned for offering wild-named shots such as Deep Throat, Morning Wood and Nipple Twister.



And girls can still flash the bartenders — who are both female — to get a free drink.

Seasoned boozers who can down ten shots in ten seconds also win a round for free.

Bartender Nicole Wray, 24, from West Sussex, is in Split for her second season, and loves it.

She said: “I couldn’t ask for a better place to work. People have fun and are polite.

“I understand the bans are for the older generation, but it is having a massive economic impact on the Old Town and pushing people away from the city.” However, one business that is busier than ever is Out To Sea Split, which sails party-loving punters 300m away from the Old Town so they can drink to their hearts’ content.

Day trips cost €50 (£42.73) or €20 (£17.09) at night.

Sam Houghton, founder of Out To Sea Split, said: “I think they see it as us taking the problem away from the city with tourists looking for a night out.

“People are taken out on the boat, and after the night boat, we put them straight on to a bus to a club.

“We are definitely seeing a younger crowd, but it’s been our biggest year yet.”

Boiler Club, a nightclub which charges €30 (£25.63) to get in, is in favour of the city’s restrictions to reduce antisocial behaviour.



A spokesman said: “We believe that the discussion about Split’s future should be grounded in proven European practices, that have delivered results in destinations that have faced the same challenges for many years.

“At the same time, we believe any new measure should be assessed in terms of its effectiveness, proportionality and application, while ensuring a balance between the interests of local residents, the sustainable development of tourism and the interests of responsible hospitality businesses.”

Whatever side you support, it is safe to say the party in Split is still very much in full swing.

The mayor and city council were contacted for comment.

News.title: Ex-gang boss and Kray twins rival Eddie Richardson dies aged 90 after ruling London underworld with brother
News.content:
EX-gangster and Kray twins rival Eddie Richardson has died at 90.

The London mobland boss, who led the fearsome Richardson gang with late brother Charlie, is understood to have passed away peacefully surrounded by family.



Eddie, an enforcer in the 1950s and 1960s, developed a career as an after-dinner speaker and artist in later life.

Born in Camberwell, South London, in 1936, Eddie started off working in the scrap metal industry.



He and older brother Charlie went on to build an empire of clubs and businesses across South London.

They expanded into Soho and made a fortune through blue movie cinemas and providing fruit machines and bouncers for other venues.



The Richardson crew, also including “Mad” Frankie Fraser, were dubbed the Torture Gang with a reputation for sadistic punishments.

They fought a deadly turf war with late East London villains Ronnie and Reggie Kray in the 1960s.



The Krays got life for murder and Eddie and Charlie, who died aged 78 in 2012, also served long jail terms.

He also worked with charities and boxing clubs.



Eddie dismissed the Krays in an interview with The Sun last year, saying: “They were f***ing mugs. Very thick.”



An underworld source said: “When people think of old-school gangsters, they think of the Krays.

“But the Richardson gang were arguably more heavy-duty.

“With Eddie passing, it’s the end of an era.”

News.title: Chancellor raises hopes fuel duty will remain frozen at autumn Budget in boost for motorists
News.content:
MILLIONS of motorists have had their hopes raised by the Chancellor that fuel duty will remain frozen at his autumn Budget.

John Healey is under pressure amid a living costs’ squeeze to abandon a planned 5p fuel duty hike that kicks in from January.



His intervention comes as he weighs up the cost of living crisis for both households and giving business more breathing space amid the Middle East conflict and rising pump prices.

The Chancellor was pushed on whether drivers and hauliers would be at the forefront of his mind when he takes the decision at the end of October.



When asked, he told The Sun: “Yes, and just as we, as a government, have done for the last two years, we’ve already said there’ll be no increase in fuel duty this year.

“I know the cost of fuel is still high. I’m very aware of the Middle East, as many people are, and the way that that’s putting pressure on prices at the pumps, prices in the supermarket, just prices on stalls. So we take that into account.”

The Sun’s Keep It Down campaign has successfully kept fuel duty frozen since 2011.

The Chancellor also has to decide on his intentions for the 5p temporary cut by the end of October. It was brought in by the Tories in 2022 amid the Ukraine war energy price shock.

The Iran war saw energy prices rocket with disruption through the vital Strait of Hormuz trading route.

The Chancellor added: “I’m very conscious of The Sun’s championing of fuel duty, fuel prices, and this isn’t just a cost of living.



“This is a cost of business for many. When five million people are self-employed, for many of them, the the cost of living is also the cost of business, and fuels are the heart of that.”

He has received a letter from the Petrol Retailers Association to help motorists at the start of next year when personal finances are strained.

Mr Healey was speaking at the Chantry Brewery in his Rawmarsh and Conisbrough constituency, in South Yorkshire.

The new Andy Burnham introduced a 20 per cent cut to business rates for pubs and music venues in his first few days in office.

He added that the move will help with the PM’s pledge to have growth in every postcode.



It comes after figures showed conomy slowed to 0.4 per cent for April to June.

It was down from 0.6 per cent for the first three months of the year.

An upbeat Mr Healey said: “But you know, we can see businesses beginning to invest, beginning to grow, beginning to believe that there is hope, and that’s part of our mission in government.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Now we want to drive some of that activity, that growth into every postcode.

“It’s things like this 20% cut in business rates for for pubs, clubs, for live music venues, the sort of places that make a town not just the place we live, but place we love.”

News.title: Brazen gang of thieves steal masterpiece paintings worth £7.7m in under three minutes as shock footage shows break-in
News.content:
THIS is the astonishing moment a gang of masked thieves stormed an Italian museum and painting worth £7.7 million in under three minutes.

CCTV shows the brazen raiders creeping into the Magnani Rocca Foundation museum near Parma in the dead of night on March 22.



Two masked men can be seen slipping through a window with headlamps blazing as another accomplice waits outside.

In a breathtakingly swift sweep, the gang ripped three paintings from the museum’s “French Room” before passing them through the window.



Within minutes, the gang had vanished with works by Paul Cezanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse.

But their spectacular haul has now been recovered after police swooped on the Parma home of one of the suspects.



The three masterpieces were found during searches carried out by the Carabinieri of the Parma Provincial Command and Cultural Heritage Protection Unit.

Investigators believe the paintings had remained at the suspect‘s home ever since the dramatic raid.

Nine people, including women, are now under investigation over the audacious theft and alleged criminal conspiracy.

The suspects are reportedly of Moldovan origin and are believed to be an experienced gang of thieves, although not specialists in art theft.



Police say the spectacular public outcry surrounding the robbery may have made it almost impossible for the gang to offload the highly recognisable masterpieces.

Investigators believe the thieves first sawed through the bars of a perimeter gate before breaking into the museum.

The gang then made their escape with the three works, completing the entire operation in less than three minutes.



A fourth painting was abandoned inside the museum, apparently after the alarm system was triggered.

Forensic investigators later combed the scene for fingerprints and biological traces, paying particular attention to the abandoned artwork.

The stolen haul was worth more than €9million (£7.8million), with Cezanne’s Still Life with Cherries accounting for a staggering €6million (£5.2million).

The rare pencil and watercolour on paper, measuring 38 by 49cm, was painted around 1890 and depicts a table with a cup and a plate piled with red cherries.

Renoir’s Les Poissons, an Impressionist oil on canvas from 1917, was valued at around €3million (£2.6million).



Matisse’s Odalisque on the Terrace, a colourful aquatint on vellum measuring 63 by 91cm, was valued at around €20,000 (£17,000).

The theft, which took place between March 22 and 23, was only made public a week later, sending shockwaves through Italy’s art world.

Stefano Roffi, scientific director of the Magnani Rocca Foundation, said the recovery had finally brought the collection back together.



He told ANSA.“I was at the Carabinieri until a few minutes ago; I had to identify the works, draw up reports, and do many other things.

“It’s truly a happy day because the Magnani Rocca collection is finally being reunited. This theft had truly left us shocked.”

He said the return of the Cezanne was particularly poignant because the artist had been one of Luigi Magnani’s favourites.

“Our thoughts go to Luigi Magnani , the founder of the Magnani Rocca Foundation, who created this pantheon of art of all time, and Cézanne in particular was his favourite artist along with Giorgio Morandi, so the return of this wonderful watercolour with cherries, which he loved so much, would have made him especially happy,” Roffi added.

The director described the raid as a devastating blow to the collection.



He said: “The Magnani Rocca Foundation houses the largest collection of Impressionist works in Italy, so it was a particularly serious wound.

“Now we hope to be able to celebrate together with the mayor and the community of Traversetolo, because an event like this deserves appropriate celebration.”

Roffi also suggested the gang may have struggled to find a buyer for such conspicuous masterpieces.

He added: “I imagine it may have been difficult to ‘place’ them, as always happens with masterpieces.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They are certainly not works that can enter a commercial circuit with impunity.”



The investigation remains ongoing.

News.title: Why didn’t I get the emergency Government alert on my phone?
News.content:
MILLIONS of people across the UK received an emergency alert on their phone today.

The alert was to warn people again the high risk of wildfires. however, some people didn’t receive the message, here’s why.

The alarm has been used on five real occasions, and was first tested in 2023, to warn UK citizens about emergencies such as storms or flooding.



The government issued the alert warning people “not to light anything that could spark a fire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks” with the country in the middle of another heatwave.



The blaring alert pinged the phones of millions across the nation around 7pm today.

The alert has gone through even if a phone is set to silent, with the sound and vibration lasting about 10 seconds.

Accompanied by a siren sound, it warned that “even a small flame can rapidly develop into a major wildfire placing lives, homes, businesses and emergency responders at risk”.

The alert added: “Recipients will also be urged to report any fire immediately by calling 999.”

Andy Burnham said that the alert was sent out after a request by fire and rescue services.

The Labour PM said: “This evening, an Emergency Alert has been sent to people across England and Wales as the wildfire risk remains very high.

“I was in Stourbridge today and saw first-hand the devastating impact these fires have had on people’s homes and lives.



“Our priority now is to keep everyone safe and prevent more fires from starting. During this period of extreme heat, I’m asking everyone to take extra care.”

Why didn’t I receive the UK emergency alert test on my phone?

Every device connected to 4G and 5G networks across the UK would have received the emergency alert.

This means older phones and any phone still connected to 2G or 3G networks did not receive the message.

Phones on silent were still expected to sound the siren but mobiles that have been switched off or put on airplane mode will not have got the alert.



The alarm system works by using phone masts to signal all mobiles within their range.

This means anyone outside the country at 7pm also did not receive the emergency message.

News.title: Jason Arday dead after being found unresponsive at home following Cambridge plagiarism scandal
News.content:
FORMER Cambridge University professor Jason Arday has been found dead at an address in south London.

Dr Arday, 41, was discovered “unresponsive” at a property in Battersea on Friday afternoon.



Shortly after the married father-of-two was pronounced dead at the scene, as reported first by The Telegraph.

The Metropolitan Police said officers were called by the London Ambulance Service at 3.12pm.



A spokesperson for the force said: “Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene.

“His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.

“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

“The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit.

“A file will be prepared for the coroner.”

It comes after a turbulent few weeks for Dr Arday, who was at the centre of a high-profile dispute having been accused of plagiarising from other students for his PhD thesis.



On August 5, Dr Arday resigned as professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge.

Last week, Cambridge launched an investigation into Dr Arday’s appointment and tenure at the university.

Dr Arday, who became the university’s youngest black professor in 2023, also came under fire after critics accused him of stealing research.

An initial investigation into the professor’s “appointment and tenure” was launched last week.

Dr Arday resigned just a few hours after the university announced the investigation, citing the “unrelenting level of public scrutiny”.



Last week, he admitted to a series of errors in his work and quit his role as professor, though denied the claims against him.

Dr Arday went on to insist he is not a “liar and fantasist” after a remarkable list of personal achievements were also called into question.

These include running 600 miles in six days and raising millions of pounds for charity.

He also claimed to have appeared in the TV series Seven Up, despite it broadcasting two decades before he was born.

He told The Times: “I am accountable for the mistakes I’ve made. I hold myself accountable and other people should hold me accountable.



“I think the cruelty that I’ve experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable.”

Analysis of Dr Arday’s PhD thesis reportedly showed 180 passages were a match or near-match for another student.

Since the allegations were made, Dr Arday has said this was a result of his autism, meaning he absorbs information through mimicry.

He admitted that his outstanding feat of running 600 miles in six days was also wrong and it had taken 12 days.

Dr Arday also said the £5.5million he has raised for charity was not done alone but instead as part of a syndicate of around 100 others.



Jesus College said previously that it was launching its own process in relation to the allegation.

An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Prof Arday of wrongdoing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Dr Arday said in his open resignation letter that the “only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away”.

For help and support, call the Samaritans for free from a UK phone, completely anonymously, on 116 123 or go to samaritans.org.

News.title: Why did I get an alert on my phone? The Government emergency wildfire warning explained
News.content:
MILLIONS of Brits have been sent an emergency alert warning them of the high risk of wildfires.

The blaring signal raised eyebrows as it pinged to the phones of millions across the nation at around 7pm today.

But why was it sent, who gets the alerts and what should you do if one does not appear on your phone?

Why was the emergency alert sent?

The Government issued the warning as the wildfire risk remains very high during another spell of extreme heat.





The alert urged people not to light anything that could spark a fire, including barbecues, campfires and fireworks.

It warned that even a small flame can quickly become a major wildfire, putting lives, homes, businesses and emergency responders at risk.

Recipients were also told to report any fire immediately by calling 999.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the request for the alert “came directly from Fire and Rescue Services”.

He said: “This evening, an Emergency Alert has been sent to people across England and Wales as the wildfire risk remains very high.

“I was in Stourbridge today and saw first-hand the devastating impact these fires have had on people’s homes and lives.”

Who sends the alert and who gets it?

Emergency alerts are sent by the Government and emergency services using mobile phone masts in the affected area.

Every compatible mobile phone or tablet within range of a mast can receive the warning.



The system works across all 4G and 5G mobile networks in the UK.

You do not need mobile data or Wi-Fi switched on to receive an alert.

The alert can sound even if your phone is set to silent.

When has the alert been sent before?

The siren sound was part of a test in September last year.

The last real use was on January 8, when a threat to life from high winds prompted an alert in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly.



In January 2025, alerts were sent to people in Scotland and Northern Ireland during Storm Eowyn.

Around 3.5 million people across Wales and south-west England received a warning during Storm Darragh in December 2024.

A 500kg unexploded Second World War bomb found in a Plymouth back garden also triggered an alert in February 2024 – around 50,000 phones received that warning.

The system can also target much smaller areas.

Some 15,000 phones were alerted during flooding in Cumbria in May 2024.



And 10,000 received a warning during flooding in Leicestershire in January this year.

What can I do if I didn’t receive the alert?

There are several reasons why you may not have received the warning.

Your phone will not get an alert if it is switched off, connected to a 2G or 3G network, Wi-Fi only or not compatible with the system.

You may also miss one if your phone is in airplane mode.

Emergency alerts work on iPhones running iOS 14.5 or later and Android phones and tablets running Android 11 or later.



Older Android devices may still be able to receive them, so check your phone’s settings for “emergency alerts”.

The Government advises keeping your device updated with the latest software.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

If you need to see an alert again, you can find current or past alerts in your phone’s settings.

Android users may also receive more than one reminder about the same alert, which can be switched off through the emergency alert settings.

News.title: Fury after millions of phones ring out with wildfire emergency alert leaving Brits fume alarm was ‘absolute abuse’
News.content:
BRITS have been left fuming after a blaring emergency alert suddenly ripped through millions of phones tonight, warning of the soaring risk of wildfires.

The government urged people to “not light anything that could spark a fire”, including barbecues, campfires and fireworks, as Britain battles another spell of scorching heat.



But the deafening siren accompanying the alert immediately sparked a backlash, with some questioning whether such an ear-splitting warning was necessary.

One furious Brit said: “@GOVUK absolute abuse of the Severe Alert system, which is now being turned off on my phone.



“You’ve totally undermined the purpose of the system. Send a text, for sure, but don’t abuse emergency broadcast systems to tell us about not using BBQs.

Another fumed: “The noise accompanying that emergency alert feels overkill.



“Lot of older people or those hiding phones for their safety possibly put at risk. Does it have to come with a loud noise?”

A third blasted the siren saying it sounded more like a warning to flee for your life than a reminder to put away the barbecue.

They wrote: “It’s for emergencies, so the noise seems reasonable. Whether it should have been used on this occasion is a different matter

One more commented: “The noise was giving ‘you have 10 minutes to evacuate your home’ not ‘put the BBQ away’.”



The blaring alert pinged phones across the country at around 7pm today, accompanied by a piercing siren designed to grab attention.

Brits were alerted even if their phone was put on silent, with the vibration lasting around ten seconds.

It warned: “Even a small flame can rapidly develop into a major wildfire placing lives, homes, businesses and emergency responders at risk.”



The alert added: “Recipients will also be urged to report any fire immediately by calling 999.”

It comes as wildfires and blazes have rattled the country in recent weeks.

Just yesterday, a total of 11 major fire incidents were reported in the past 24 hours in the West Midlands alone.

A total of 19 homes were completely destroyed and 18 others damaged as families forced to evacuate as the fire spread across Stourbridge, West Midlands, yesterday afternoon.

But residents of the UK were left almost hysterical at the lack of severity of the alert.



Another Briton raged online: “What a misuse of the system. You hear the emergency alert klaxon and you think Putin’s finally launched the missiles, and then you check your phone and it’s the government asking you to not have a barbecue.”

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the request “came directly from Fire and Rescue Services”.

The Labour PM said: “This evening, an Emergency Alert has been sent to people across England and Wales as the wildfire risk remains very high.



“I was in Stourbridge today and saw first-hand the devastating impact these fires have had on people’s homes and lives.

“Our priority now is to keep everyone safe and prevent more fires from starting. During this period of extreme heat, I’m asking everyone to take extra care.

“Please do not light any fires in gardens, the countryside or other open spaces, including parks, moorland and wooded areas.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Our firefighters and emergency responders are working around the clock in incredibly difficult conditions.

“We can all help them. Please take the Emergency Alert seriously and follow the guidance in place.”

News.title: Ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row found dead
News.content:
The former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row has been found dead.

Jason Arday was found "unresponsive" at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon, emergency services said.

Metropolitan Police officers were called by the London Ambulance Service. A 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene and his next of kin have been informed, the force said.

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

In a statement, the Met Police said: "At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious."

The 41-year-old academic had denied any plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and last week said the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in Prof Arday's work and questioned some of his stated achievements.

Arday's appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment.

Some critics said the treatment of him has been motivated by racism, but others said the claims of plagiarism were legitimate.

Announcing his resignation last week, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny had become "too great".

He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.

"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

News.title: Temporary ban on sale of disposable BBQs over wildfire risk
News.content:
"We have a fire and rescue service across the country that isn't properly set up to deal with these incidents," Burnham said.

"We don't have the capability in the way that we should have to fight these fires.

"There's thousands of firefighters out there today doing back-breaking work, in full kit, in the most difficult conditions", he added.

He said the UK must face up to the "changing climate" and transition to "more clean energy".

His comments came ahead of the appointment of Baroness Blake of Leeds as fire minister.

Friends of the Earth urged the prime minister to tackle the "root cause" of the "climate emergency" that is fuelling this summer's extreme weather events.

"Without urgent action to curb the carbon emissions driving this crisis, future heatwaves, droughts and wildfires will only get worse and the ability for future generations to adapt will disappear" the environmental group warned.

Burnham was speaking during a visit to Stourbridge to see the impact of a devastating blaze.

As the UK experienced its hottest day of the year on Thursday, residents fled their homes when fires spread through dry grass and tore through houses.

West Midlands Ambulance Service said it treated 54 casualties at eight different fires across the region. Nineteen people were taken to hospital for treatment.

In 2025, fire and rescue services in England and Wales broke a new record when they responded to nearly 1,000 wildfire incidents, with the NFCC warning at the time that climate change is increasing their risk and severity.

The conditions the UK is experiencing so far this summer also mirror the warnings given by climate scientists that human-induced climate change would lead to more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as potential summer droughts.

In England, the Rugby Football Union has delayed the start of the community rugby season because of concerns about player welfare and pitch conditions because of the drought conditions.

News.title: Mangione admits killing healthcare CEO and pleads guilty to federal charges
News.content:
Mangione had initially pleaded not guilty in both the federal and state cases against him for the shooting death of Thompson.

At a hearing in Manhattan federal court on Friday, Mangione's lawyers announced that he intended to plead guilty to the two federal charges against him.

Wearing a beige prison outfit, Mangione appeared solemn and serious throughout the hearing.

Reading a statement aloud to the court, he admitted to planning the attack ahead of time, crossing state lines with the intent to kill and using a gun he printed on a 3-D-printer and equipped with a silencer and magazine.

He told the court he was driven to kill Thompson because of his experience with the healthcare system "after years of enduring severe pains from a broken back".

Mangione stated that he had learned UnitedHealthcare would hold an annual investor conference in Manhattan in December 2024.

He then travelled to New York for the event, he told the court.

He also said he emailed UnitedHealthcare prior to the conference "posing as an investor" and asking questions about the event.

"I emailed UnitedHealthcare with the intent to shoot Brian Thompson," Mangione said in his statement. "On the morning of Dec. 4, 2024 I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan in his back."

The sentencing for the federal charges is scheduled for 18 December.

Brian Thompson's family said in a statement that they will continue to seek justice in both New York state and Pennsylvania, where Mangione was arrested.

"While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable.

"Now we look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime," the family added.

News.title: Derailed Essex to London train leads to travel chaos
News.content:
Martin Frobisher, of Network Rail, said the summer's hot weather had "presented exceptional challenges to the railway".

In an interview with the BBC Transport Correspondent Katy Austin, Frobisher also confirmed speed restrictions were not in place in either Wickford or Lewes.

On the possible impact of the hot weather, he said "yes, that's one of the things that we're looking at.

"We've got our investigations underway. We've got technical engineers on site, our best experts who are on site with the Rail Accident Investigation Branch.

"They're looking very thoroughly at what's happened. And based on that, we will act on what we learn."

However, he added it was "too early to speculate on the full findings".

The investigation would specifically assess "whether or not this was weather-related", said Mark Francois, the Conservative MP for Rayleigh and Wickford.

The Department for Transport stressed Britain's railways were "among the safest in the world" as it reacted to the incident.

It said derailments were "incredibly rare" events.

An East of England Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "Our crews assessed 62 patients who were on board the train.

"Following assessment, all patients were discharged at the scene.

"We also assisted with the evacuation of a second train that was unable to continue its journey due to the derailment.

"There were no casualties among those on board."

A spokesperson for BTP also confirmed there were no reported injuries.

News.title: Chris Mason: Where does this unorthodox by-election victory leave Nigel Farage?
News.content:
It is a question prompting at least some debate within the party.

"When he goes down this angry route he doesn't help himself," the prominent Reform activist Tim Montgomerie told Radio 4's The World At One.

Montgomerie, the founder of the ConservativeHome website, defected to Reform two years ago. He praised Farage's political ability but added: "It's very frustrating how he's behaved today. He needs to get a grip of this problem."

Montgomerie argued Farage and Reform were at their best when they were more positive rather than "inward looking" and focused on "grievances."

The "grievances," as Montgomerie puts it, are real and legitimate, say Farage's friends.

In the short term at least and from a point of weakness I have previously written about, the by-election allowed Farage to get on the front foot and to frame an argument, as he saw it, as the people versus those out to get him.

Rubbish, say his critics, the rules apply to all MPs and the undeclared Â£5m gift from the billionaire businessman Christopher Harborne, in the months before Farage became an MP, should have been registered, they insist.

Talking to GB News in the early hours of this morning, before the result, Farage repeated a concession, of sorts, about this: "If I made one sin, it's that I haven't filled in a piece of paper.

"I've broken no law, I've broken no tax law, I've taken no public money. I don't even own a motor home. Maybe I haven't filled in a piece of paper. I'm confident I'm right - we'll see where we go."

He has long maintained he sought legal advice about whether he needed to declare the money and had been told he didn't.

The wider question is where Nigel Farage and Reform find themselves in the big picture politically and whether their current approach is a wise one.

There is early evidence of something of a Burnham bounce for Labour, which has disrupted Reform's long standing lead in the opinion polls.

And the Conservatives appear more chipper and competitive than a year ago too.

Then there is the rise of Restore Britain, run by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

Let's be clear: none of the political parties are wildly popular at the moment, but Reform's support has shrivelled a bit and their rivals are more upbeat.

The landscape for the new political season at Westminster is taking shape, ahead of MPs returning to the Commons in a few weeks.

Labour with a spring in its step, for now at least. Reform punchy but feeling under the cosh and plenty of the others scrapping for attention too.

It will be a fascinating few months ahead.

News.title: Britain's Finlay Tarling dies in Volta a Portugal accident
News.content:
British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died aged 19 after an accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.

In a statement provided to local media, Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said there had been "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle" and that an investigation was under way.

The Welshman was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe.

In a statement, NSN said: "We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

"Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

In a post on X, the race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation expressed their "most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones".

It added that the racing was stopped and the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of "respect and mourning".

Portuguese president Antonio Jose Seguro added that Tarling's death had "plunged the peloton, the tournament and the host nation into mourning".

British Cycling's performance director Stephen Park, added: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.

"Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh at this tragic time."

World governing body the UCI added on X: "The UCI is deeply saddened by the tragic death of British rider Finlay Tarling, who passed away following a serious accident during today's eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

"The UCI extends its deepest condolences to Finlay's family, friends, and team-mates."

Meanwhile, Welsh Cycling added: "We at Beicio Cymru are absolutely devastated to hear the news of Fin Tarling's passing today while competing at the Volta in Portugal.

"Fin was an incredible athlete, role model, friend, brother and son. We send our love and deepest condolences to Mike, Dawn and Josh at this incredibly difficult time.

"Rest in peace, Fin. You were incredible, and we will always remember you."

The Volta a Portugal got under way in Lisbon on 5 August and is raced over 10 stages, concluding in Porto on 16 August.

Tarling looked to be following in the footsteps of his older brother Josh as a time trial specialist.

He finished in third in the under-23 men's individual time trial at the British Championships in June and competed in the Tour of Britain just under 12 months ago.

News.title: Bezos-backed consortium buys a third of Liverpool FC
News.content:
Liverpool's owners have agreed to sell about a third of the club to a consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

In a statement, Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed it had entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale of a "strategic minority investment" to 1892 Holdings.

The group is led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia and also includes billionaire Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

Bhatia is set to become Liverpool's vice-chairman, and will join an expanded board pending regulatory approval.

The son-in-law of Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal, he had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before relinquishing his stake in the club last month.

American businessman Bezos, founder of e-commerce giant Amazon, is the fourth-richest person in the world, with an estimated net worth of $256bn (Â£192bn). This marks his first foray into sports ownership, although he will not join Liverpool's board.

However, Bryan Baum, founder of venture capital firm K5 Sports - through which Bezos is investing - will join the Anfield board, alongside Saverin's wife Elaine. Bezos is the biggest investor in K5 Sports.

BBC Sport has been told that the transaction will have no impact on the club's approach to the transfer window, and that there is no new or separate transfer budget associated with the investment.

The agreement includes an option for the consortium to increase its investment in the future. That suggests the group will be in pole position to become majority shareholders if Fenway wants to sell up, but according to one source, no commitments have been made to do so.

The deal is said to value the club between Â£5bn and Â£6bn.

News.title: Stephen Bear jailed over sex offender breaches
News.content:
Reality TV contestant Stephen Bear taunted police by "bragging" he was on a beach in Brazil while he breached his requirements as a sex offender, a court has heard.

He was not on the run during the trip last year, but under the rules of his registration requirements he was ordered to tell authorities about foreign travel.

Bear, 36, admitted five counts of failing to comply with the register notification requirements at Thames Magistrates' Court and was sentenced to 24 weeks in prison.

He is already in prison having been jailed on Thursday after admitting breaching a restraining order that banned him from posting online about his ex-partner Georgia Harrison.

News.title: Prisoners charged over attack on Sara Sharif's father
News.content:
Two prisoners have been charged with the attempted murder of fellow inmate Urfan Sharif who was jailed for killing his daughter Sara Sharif.

Steven Sansom, 47, and Adam Watson, 39, have also been charged with other offences relating to the incident in Belmarsh Prison on 1 January 2025, the Crown Prosecution Service said.

The men will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court for a first hearing on 26 August.

Sharif, 43, and Sara's stepmother Beinash Batool were sentenced to life imprisonment after being convicted at the Old Bailey for murdering 10-year-old Sara at their home in Woking, Surrey.

Sharif reportedly suffered cuts to his face during the attack, and received medical treatment at the prison.

Daren Streeter, deputy chief crown prosecutor at CPS London, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with the Metropolitan Police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and pursue criminal proceedings."

Sara was hooded, burned and beaten during a "campaign of torture" that lasted two years before her body was found at the family home in August 2023.

During the trial, Justice Cavanagh told the court "the degree of cruelty involved is almost inconceivable".

Urfan Sharif was sentenced to a minimum of 40 years in prison for murder, while his wife Beinash Batool, 30, received a minimum of 33 years.

Sara's uncle, Faisal Malik, 29, was sentenced to 16 years' imprisonment for causing or allowing her death.

The three fled to Islamabad, Pakistan, with Sara's five siblings, the day before her body was found, prompting an international manhunt.

They hid out there for four weeks before returning to the UK, where they were arrested.

News.title: Two dead after light aircraft crash
News.content:
Two people have died following a light aircraft crash in north Wales.

The aircraft was found in a remote location close to Trawsfynydd, near Blaenau Ffestiniog, Gwynedd, with the two people on board pronounced dead at the scene, North Wales Police said.

The force received reports shortly after 12:00 BST that a light aircraft travelling from an airfield in England had not arrived at Caernarfon Airport as scheduled.

Multi-agency air and ground searches were carried out until the aircraft was found.

A team of investigators have since been deployed by the Air Accidents Investigations Branch (AAIB).

News.title: Weekend cancellations after East Sussex train derailment
News.content:
Rail services on a busy line in the South East are being cancelled this weekend after a train carrying 150 people derailed in East Sussex.

Two passengers suffered serious injuries and 18 others were also hurt when three carriages of the train came off the tracks near Lewes on Thursday. Police have since said none of the casualties had life-threatening injuries.

Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) inspectors are at the scene gathering evidence, examining infrastructure and reviewing CCTV, signalling and train data.

The derailment was followed by another incident in Essex on Friday, when a Greater Anglia train came off the tracks near Wickford.

Train operator Southern Rail said trains between London Victoria and Eastbourne will be cancelled this weekend as the line between Haywards Heath and Lewes has been closed indefinitely in both directions.

Southern says Cooksbridge and Plumpton will also not be served all weekend, with rail replacement buses operating.

Eastbourne is expected to get a bumper number of visitors this weekend when the seaside town hosts its popular Airbourne air show.

The rail company has advised people to travel to Eastbourne along the coast via Brighton.

It has also urged commuters planning to travel on Monday to check for updates on its website, external on Sunday evening.

News.title: UK diplomats no longer get hardship bonus for being posted to Buenos Aires
News.content:
British diplomats in six locations around the world, including Buenos Aires and Santiago in South America, will no longer get hardship payments for working in dangerous cities.

Bonuses and respite breaks are granted to those working in cities considered risky, like Beirut in Lebanon, or with high crime, such as Pretoria in South Africa, or high air pollution in cities including New Delhi and Beijing.

The UK government has removed Santiago, in Chile, Panama City in Panama, Pyongyang in North Korea, Bamako in Mali, and Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in addition to the two south American cities, according to the latest list published last week, external.

The 144 locations still on the list include many trouble spots but also popular holiday destinations such as Bali and Rio De Janeiro, prompting criticism from the Conservatives.

Tory chairmanÂ­ Kevin HollinÂ­rake said civil servants receiving extra pay for working in such areas is unfair on the taxpayer.

The Foreign Office has given civil servants extra payments for working in areas where there is a high level of danger, or high risks to health, for the past 30 years.

They are meant to compensate staff and families for the additional costs and challenges of living overseas in difficult locations and are reviewed regularly.

Factors and risks covered by the allowance include security measures, climate, natural disaster, isolation and other impacts on quality of life.

Amounts are not routinely published but in 2009, the last time a breakdown was released, the highest payments for civil servants and their spouses were for postings to Karachi, Pakistan, which was worth an extra Â£26,647, or Â£14,804 in Abuja, the capital of Nigeria.

The hardship payment for being posted as part of a couple to Buenos Aires was Â£1,517 and Santiago was Â£777, according to the 2009 Diplomatic Services Allowances, external.

Answering a parliamentary question from Tory peer Lord Moylan, external, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield said assessments of hardship take into account factors that mean members of staff are required to take additional breaks for the benefit of their physical or mental health.

He added: "These arrangements are not new, and indeed have applied consistently under successive governments for a number of decades."

Bangkok, Cape Town, and Kuala Lumpur are still among the cities that qualify for hardship payments, alongside Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Muscat.

Hollinrake said it was unfair that taxpayers were "footing the bill" for these destinations and pledged to cut the size of the civil service if Conservatives were returned to power.

"Whilst businesses and families are paying higher taxes to fund this government's policies, civil servants are being sent on taxpayer-funded jollies to places like Bali, Cape Town and the Maldives," he said.

"This kind of nonsense has no place in government."

But the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office defended the scheme, with a spokesperson saying: "British diplomats serve their country around the globe, including in some of the toughest and most challenging physical and political environments in the world.

"We have a duty of care to ensure our staff are properly supported, and compensation and other provisions reflect the circumstances of the posting, as it would be in any private sector job."

News.title: Woman cleared of owning XL bully which fatally bit man
News.content:
A woman has been cleared of owning an XL bully dog that bit her partner's father, causing him to bleed to death.

Chanel Fong, 33, was accused of owning the dog, Cookie, which was dangerously out of control and of an alternative charge of being the person in charge of the animal at the time of the attack.

She was found not guilty of both by the jury at Caernarfon Crown Court.

Her partner's father, Keven Jones, 62, from Chester, died from severe blood loss after being bitten on the leg.

The attack took place before XL Bullies were added to the banned dog list.

The court heard Keven Jones had been in poor health and had been taking methadone and blood thinning medication, and had been staying at Fong's Wrexham home in May 2022.

Fong said the dog belonged to her partner Joshua Jones, who was not present when his father was bitten, although the prosecution claimed she was Cookie's joint owner.

The court was told there had been a number of dogs at the home on Holt Road in Wrexham, including two XL Bullies, called Fire and Rogue.

Rogue was Cookie's mother and in season at the time, so had to be kept separate from other dogs.

At about 11:30 BST on 23 May, Jones told Fong he would get Cookie and another dog in from the garden, but he was then heard shouting at Cookie to "get off" him.

The court heard Fong also called into the garden for Cookie to get down, which is when Jones came towards her "wobbly".

He pointed to his leg, which was pumping blood, and he said to Fong, "he's got me there".

Fong called the emergency services and attempted first aid, including applying pressure to the wound, but Jones could not be saved.

A post-mortem examination said he had died from extreme blood loss caused by dog bites.

Cookie was later humanely euthanised.

News.title: Sign of life as bright orange 'fire fungus' grows at park ravaged by wildfire
News.content:
A fungus that grows in places damaged by fire has been found at the site of a major wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park.

Forestry and Land Scotland (FLS) said the bright orange, pyrophilous (fire-loving) fungus could be the first sign of nature's recovery at Glenmore near Aviemore.

A wildfire started in the area on 15 July and the incident, which has burned through thousands of acres of woodland and moor, continues to be monitored for hotspots.

FLS said the fungus was among the "first colonisers" of burned ground and played a role in breaking down carbon and preventing soil erosion.

News.title: Mother jailed for killing baby by burning her with a hairdryer
News.content:
A mother who killed her baby daughter by burning her with a hairdryer has been jailed for six years.

Courtney Gartshore, 28, used the appliance to subject three-month-old Dahlia-Rose to "significant and sustained heat" on her head and body.

Emergency services were called to the scene at a property in Peterhead, Aberdeenshire, in September 2023, but the child had died.

Gartshore was convicted of culpable homicide - the closest equivalent to manslaughter in Scots Law - following a trial at the High Court in Aberdeen in July.

Warning: This article contains details readers may find upsetting

Sentencing Gartshore at the High Court in Edinburgh, judge Simon Collins KC told her, external she had inflicted "severe and disfiguring" burns on her daughter.

He said: "Given Dahlia-Rose's very young age, and the horrifying way that she died, this is a uniquely disturbing and distressing case.

"But it is tragic as well as terrible. And that is because the evidence suggested that the accused loved Dahlia-Rose, yet will have to live the rest of her life with the knowledge that she was responsible for her death."

News.title: One million sign petition to keep PC Harper's killers in jail
News.content:
A petition to block the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers has been signed by more than one million people.

The police officer, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died in 2019 when he was dragged by a car as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were sentenced to 13 years for his manslaughter in 2020 but could be released next year under plans to tackle prison overcrowding. The prime minister is looking at ways to keep them in jail.

Thames Valley Police (TVP) Federation acknowledged the important milestone the petition had reached "without fanfare" due to the seventh anniversary of the officer's death on Saturday.

The petition was started by TVP federation chair Aileen O'Connor who said the decision to consider the killers for early release "pours salt into wounds that have never healed".

She added it was an "insult to Andrew's family, his friends, his colleagues and the entire policing family".

The federation thanked all those who have signed in support.

President Donald Trump on Friday suggested ‘beautiful, young girls” are approaching him to gush about the effect his federal takeover of law enforcement has had on the District of Columbia as he addressed a crowd of police officers in support of a GOP candidate for governor of his former home state.

Trump was speaking at a de facto political rally in Nassau County in New York when he began boasting about the crime rate in Washington, which was falling for years before he took office and has continued to fall even as he has attempted to take credit for the years-long trend.

He claimed his administration’s extended use of the National Guard to have soldiers wandering about the capital with guns but without any police powers has made Washington “one of the safest cities in the country” with “very little crime” before pivoting to a bizarre anecdote about random women demanding to thank him for it.

“Every day I come to the White House, people are thanking me: ‘Thank you, sir. Thank you, thank you, sir,’” he said.

“ You know these young, beautiful girls. These young, beautiful girls. These young, beautiful girls in the White House. You know they come in. Now I'm not supposed to say beautiful, but what the hell? These young, these gorgeous, beautiful girls-they-they want to be safe, and they come,” he continued before feigning an alleged conversation with one of them.

‘”Mr. President, may I speak to you? Thank you, sir. Thank you’ — I said, "Why are you thanking me?” he said.

He then returned to the alleged girl’s part and replied: “’Because a year and a half ago, I was afraid to leave. I was afraid to open the door of my apartment, and now I walk to the White House every morning, and I have absolutely no fear.’”

More follows...

News.content:

The mother of an Arkansas teen is suing Elon Musk’s X Corporation and its artificial intelligence arm, xAI, developer of the Grok chatbot, after the technology was used to turn innocent photos of the boy into sexually explicit imagery that was widely shared, according to a federal complaint reviewed by The Independent.

Plaintiff “Jane Roe” filed the complaint August 13 on behalf of son “John Doe,” a 16-year-old who enjoys football, golf, fishing and “loves to ride his bike.” The complaint says he is part of his church’s youth group, and, like “many minors of that age, he is blissfully ignorant to the harsh realities of the world in which we live in.”

In June, Roe was contacted by local police, who told her they had received a tip that pictures of Doe were being transformed into CSAM – Child Sexual Abuse Material – via Grok, according to the complaint. An unnamed perpetrator had harnessed the technology to create “thousands” of hardcore images and videos of other local children, as well, the complaint states.

It describes the material as CSAM because, as the complaint explains, “‘pornography’ implies a consensual act between adults, whereas this material includes minors who cannot legally consent.”

Attorney Derek Potts, who is representing Roe and Doe, said on Friday that the case, now pending in Fayetteville federal court, is among the first of many additional ones to come.

“This is the fourth such lawsuit of what appears to be countless more coming in the future as we learn more about the true scope and size of these tragic events for the children and their families,” Potts told The Independent. “The creation of CSAM by artificial intelligence should not be happening under any circumstances and we are honored to be on the legal frontline to seek not only justice for the families we represent but to hopefully facilitate much needed change of how artificial intelligence is designed and allowed to operate going forward.”

open image in gallery Grok, Elon Musk's generative AI chatbot, is the focus of another lawsuit involving child porn and a teenage victim in Arkansas ( Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images )

Grok “generated and disseminated CSAM images and videos of… Doe over the course of several weeks,” the complaint states. It says they showed Doe’s “entire 16-year-old body, nude, including his genitals, and without any clothes,” and “portrayed… Doe engaged in various sex acts.”

“Although the images and videos were synthetically generated, the harm inflicted upon [Doe] and his family is real, profound and enduring,” according to the complaint.

“They can’t sleep, they can’t eat, and this has caused Jane Roe extreme stress and uncertainty,” it says.

While Doe “currently remains in the dark about much of this,” his mother has developed “overwhelming anxiety,” “depression” and lives in “constant fear that these CSAM images and videos will persist and exist through John Doe’s lifetime – there is no way to be certain that they are fully eliminated, ever.”

“These CSAM images and videos could be trafficked, traded and maintained by pedophiles for eternity,” the complaint states.

It emphasizes that the case is “not about unforeseen technological malfunctions,” but rather “about [xAI’s]’ corporate choices, including [its] choice to monetize a system that they could have reasonably foreseen would be used to create child sexual abuse material, nonconsensual intimate imagery, and sexually explicit deepfakes depicting identifiable individuals, including minors like John Doe.”

An xAI spokesperson did not respond Friday to a request for comment.

open image in gallery The latest complaint against Grok says xAI must be held accountable for what happened to John Doe, an Arkansas teen, 'to make clear that no company gets to treat [the exploitation of] a child's body and identity as an acceptable cost of doing business' ( Getty Images )

Musk, the world’s wealthiest person, founded xAI in 2023. He said the company’s generative AI output would be “rebellious,” rather than “safe, cautious or filtered,” the complaint notes.

It says Grok, xAI’s public-facing chatbot, was then incorporated directly into the X platform, formerly known as Twitter, and soon offered a “Spicy” version of the product, for a fee, “even after regulators, journalists and victims around the world began documenting the predictable result.”

While other AI companies included numerous safeguards to prevent their products from generating child pornography, xAI “ignored all warnings” and touted Grok as “honest” and “largely uncensored,” according to the complaint. xAI “chose not to build in the protections,” according to the complaint, and “not because doing so was impossible.”

By January 2026, the concern over Grok CSAM deepfakes had become so acute, attorneys general in 35 states signed onto a letter to xAI, demanding action, and governments around the world launched investigations.

In January, X announced new restrictions on Grok’s output of nonconsensual imagery. However, the chatbot continued to generate sexualized deepfakes even after being warned in prompts that the subjects of the images had not given their permission, Reuters reported. Musk, for his part, has called the backlash an “excuse for censorship.”

Yet, as Doe’s complaint says, he “did not choose to become sexually explicit content.”

“He is [a] 16-year-old child,” it states. “Defendants' technology made that choice for him, and Defendants' business made money from it. Photographs of a real child were turned, by a machine Defendants built, trained, priced and shipped, into an image of him being sexually abused.”

open image in gallery Grok and xAI have prompted pushback around the world, with advocacy groups calling for people to delete their X accounts. A new lawsuit out of Arkansas highlights the potential harms to children brought on by the unrestrained technology ( AFP via Getty Images )

The offending images and videos “cannot be recalled, they can be copied infinitely, and [Doe] will have to live with the existence [of] this CSAM for the rest of his life. That is not a glitch,” the complaint goes on. “... Of tantamount concern is that Defendants knew of the exact type of harm that occurred in this case well before these injuries and this harm ever happened, and they did absolutely nothing about it.”

The harm to Doe is “severe and continuing,” and the consequences surrounding this experience “will never cease,” the complaint argues, claiming Doe will live “the rest of his life knowing that CSAM images and videos exist of him in the ether.”

“No verdict can undo what was done to [Doe],” it asserts. “... The unauthorized sexualization of a child through artificial intelligence invades the child’s dignity, autonomy, privacy, emotional well-being and fundamental right to control his own identity. The source of the exploitation does not diminish the resulting harm.”

Roe, on behalf of Doe, is now demanding, among other things, compensatory and actual damages, in an amount to be proven at trial, for severe emotional distress, psychological injury, reputational harm, invasion of privacy, humiliation, loss of enjoyment of life, and “all other damages caused by Defendants' conduct,” as well as statutory damages, actual damages, punitive damages, and legal costs.

Additionally, they are seeking permanent injunctive relief requiring xAI to permanently delete all unlawful depictions on its platform of Doe, and for the company to “implement reasonable technical safeguards sufficient to prevent the generation of non-consensual sexually explicit depictions of identifiable real individuals, including minors.”

xAI must be held accountable for what happened to Doe, the complaint says, “to make clear that no company gets to treat [the exploitation of] a child's body and identity as an acceptable cost of doing business.”

Former University of Cambridge professor Jason Arday has been found dead at a property in London, police have said.

The academic was pronounced dead after being found “unresponsive” at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday.

A spokesman for the Metropolitan Police has said officers were alerted on the death by the London Ambulance Service at 3.12pm on Friday.

A force spokesman said: “Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.

open image in gallery ( St Mary's University Twickenham )

“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.”

A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said: “We were called at 3.06pm on Friday 14 August to reports of an incident on Daley Thompson Way, SW8.

“We sent a number of resources to the scene, including an ambulance crew, an advanced paramedic in a fast response car and members of our Hazardous Area Response Team.

“Sadly, a person was pronounced dead at the scene.”

Prof Arday, a professor of sociology of education who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, quit following a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.

Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million for charity.

An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Prof Arday of wrongdoing.

Durham and Glasgow universities are investigating the circumstances around Prof Arday’s appointment to academic posts there .

open image in gallery ( Supplied )

Prof Arday said in his open resignation letter that the “only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away”.

He said: “This decision should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge.

“Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me.

“It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.”

Four more belugas have arrived at a Chicago aquarium as part of a plan to move Canada's last remaining captive whales from a shuttered theme park to aquariums in the United States and Spain.

The four whales, named Caspian, Peekachu, Rain and Secord, were the second group of belugas sent to Chicago's Shedd Aquarium from Marineland, in Ontario near Niagara Falls, after an initial four arrived in July.

They are among a total of 30 whales and four dolphins that will be transported from Marineland after the Canadian government approved of the rescue plan, which might have saved them from mass euthanasia.

Marineland announced in early 2023 that it was for sale and closed to the public in late summer 2024. Twenty whales — 19 belugas and one killer whale — have died at Marineland since 2019, according to provincial government data obtained through freedom-of-information laws and official statements.

As part of the rescue efforts, the whales have been making their international trips in custom-built slings and temperature-controlled transport containers. A team of experts flew to Canada to meet the whales’ previous caretakers months prior and pored over years of their health records in preparation for the trip.

“This is a very complex and unprecedented rescue effort. This has never been done before,” said Charlie Jacobsma, the director of animal behavior and training at the Shedd Aquarium.

The new arrivals first interacted with other whales already at the aquarium through gates to find the best aquatic roommates, he said. The whales for now live in the same space as three other belugas, and they trade “signs of affiliation” and sounds with each other.

“Belugas are very social animals,” he said. “It was really special to be able to see some of our animals pairing up with these new animals.”

Dr. Karisa Tang, Shedd’s lead veterinarian, said all the belugas are taking the adjustment to their new home “day by day.”

Tang said the whales are monitored “hour by hour, minute by minute,” including their food intake, interactions with other animals and signs of their mood, like “relaxed swimming.” Caretakers look for signs of soreness or bruises on their bodies.

Belugas have “great personalities” and expressive faces, she said.

“Every single day it is an absolute joy to work with belugas,” she added. “There’s something about them that seems magical.”

Under the plan, the belugas and dolphins are being relocated to five marine parks: Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, SeaWorld locations in San Antonio and San Diego, and Oceanografic Valencia.

___

Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

With eight restaurants and bars, a spectacular spa and a prime location by Hoan Kiem Lake, Fairmont’s latest outpost brings polished charm to Hanoi’s French Quarter

Location

Nestled between the Old Quarter and French Quarter, Fairmont Hanoi is the luxury hotel group’s first property in Vietnam. The grand building with its colonial-style facade is a stone’s throw from the city’s government and diplomatic offices, many of which date back to the French era. Walk left, and you land in Hanoi’s bustling food markets and famous street food spots. Seek out Bún Cá Sâm Cây Si for its fried fish noodle soup.

Hoan Kiem Lake is a five-minute walk, where the Ngoc Son Temple sits on Jade Island, accessible by a bright-red wooden footbridge. It’s a spiritual and historic hub in the city, where locals participate in dance aerobics and Tai Chi each morning. Hanoi is pleasingly walkable, though I’d suggest soaking up the sights and sounds further afield by ordering a scooter from the ride-hailing app Grab.

The vibe

The hotel’s imposing architecture is designed to blend into the French colonial neighbourhood, but Fairmont Hanoi celebrates Southeast Asian heritage in its thoughtful interiors. The Tran Dynasty restaurant nods to Vietnam’s ancient 13th-century monarchy, resplendent with a temple-shaped bar, dragon relic, and cultural motifs. Royal influences feature throughout the hotel, from gold-leaf ceilings to phoenix sculptures and mosaic tile flooring. A spectacular crystal chandelier steals the show in the lobby.

open image in gallery The lobby features a floral display that changes with the seasons ( Fairmont )

The building’s curved structure centres a shaded, serene open courtyard, while the rooftop enjoys panoramic views across Hanoi. Like Fairmont’s other properties, the hotel attracts business travellers, families and older couples with its reliably luxurious offering.

Service

Service is warm and welcoming throughout the hotel. Staff look smart in red silk blazers and navy bottoms, offering informative and attentive service in the restaurants and lounges. Everyone from the bartenders to the reception staff are readily available for local dining recommendations, wine suggestions, and to help with ordering bikes and taxis or booking tours.

Bed and bath

There are 260 rooms at Fairmont Hanoi, spanning King Rooms, Junior Suites, Suites, Gold Suites, Signature Gold Suites and the vast Presidential Suite.

The King Rooms and Junior Suites are generously sized, with freestanding bathtubs, a Japanese smart toilet in a separate cubicle, a marbled shower room, and a living area. The rooms are pared-back, luxurious and uncluttered. All feature large balconies, though there is no outdoor furniture.

open image in gallery The Gold suites come with Gold Club lounge access, where all-day canapés and drinks are served ( Fairmont )

Some rooms facing the inner courtyard also look into a conference room, which doesn’t offer much privacy (request a room with a different view when booking), while outward-facing rooms look out onto a derelict building – though demolition plans mean these rooms will eventually have a lake view.

As with all Fairmont hotels, a stay in the Gold Suites includes Gold Club Lounge access, where breakfast and all-day canapés, drinks, and buffets are served. These rooms also come with Le Labo Santal 33 toiletries, Dyson hairdryers, and more picturesque views across the city.

Food and drink

There are eight restaurants at Fairmont Hanoi, including Hiyru, a Japanese omakase counter experience, and Bacco, an all-day Italian spot. Others, including 10 Central Cafe in the lobby and the spa cafe, are more casual, offering light bites and afternoon tea.

Tran Dynasty is undoubtedly the jewel in the hotel’s crown. Guided by Vietnamese-Australian Chef Luke Nguyen, as much attention has been paid to the opulent interiors as to the theme and menu. Get the seared wagyu crispy rice noodles, followed by the scallops in fish sauce and chargrilled pork tomahawk.

open image in gallery Vietnamese-Australian Chef Luke Nguyen – and Master Chef Australia judge – heads up the Tran Dynasty restaurant ( Fairmont )

Breakfast is served at Bacco, and is a casual buffet affair with bread, cured meats, fresh fruit, granola and hot continental food, while the a la carte menu offers Vietnamese, Korean and Japanese twists on breakfast classics. The Pho station must be tried (when in Rome).

Considering Hanoi is one of the top food destinations in the world, there’s almost too much choice for dining and cuisines within the hotel (families seeking ease will appreciate the variety). Once you’ve had a meal at Tran Dynasty, I’d encourage looking beyond the hotel and exploring what the city’s incredible culinary scene has to offer.

The rooftop pool bar is a sun-drenched spot for pre-dinner cocktails: though a stylish space, it feels too tucked away on the other side of the rooftop to have a buzzy atmosphere. Meanwhile, the candle-lit YY Bar serves signature cocktails for a nightcap (try the Ha Noi and Ha Long).

Facilities

The hotel’s spa is spectacular and stylish. Spread across 3,500 square metres, the wellness facilities take inspiration from Japanese and Korean onsens. With multiple saunas, steam rooms, three thermal pools at different temperatures and a Vichy shower room – a luxurious spa hydrotherapy treatment – you could easily spend an entire day drifting through the serene space. The male and female bathing areas are separate, and nudity is optional.

There are also meditation pods and salt rooms, alongside 10 beautiful treatment rooms and an indoor lap pool. Except Sundays, the facilities are adult-only. Striped sun beds and cabanas line the rooftop swimming pool (open to families), which is more for lounging than lengths.

open image in gallery The indoor lap pool is flanked by loungers and thermal pools ( Fairmont )

The gym is equally impressive, with a dedicated studio, daily fitness classes for guests, and complimentary personal training available to book. TechnoGym machines offer guided workouts, with the layout designed for privacy.

Concierge experiences include an enriching day out to the ancient village of Duong Lam (with a homestead lunch), a walking tour through the bustling Hang Be Market, and fun, educational Vespa tours through the city's historic sights or surrounding countryside.

Accessibility

There are seven spacious accessible rooms available, equipped with roll-in showers, grab bars and emergency buttons. There are wheelchair-friendly entrances, lifts and step-free navigation throughout the public areas, including all restaurants and bars.

Family friendly?

Fairmont Hanoi caters to families with interconnecting suites and twin rooms and children’s menus. Children are allowed in the rooftop pool, but the indoor pool and spa facilities are age-restricted and only available to families on Sundays. Infant beds are available at request, and babysitting services can be arranged by the hotel concierge.

Pet policy

Pets are not allowed at Fairmont Hanoi.

Check-in/check-out

Check-in from 3pm, check-out is 12pm.

At a glance

Best thing: The spectacular spa facilities and location.

Perfect for: First-time visitors to Hanoi and families.

Not right for: Design-lovers and those wanting a more intimate, boutique stay.

Instagram from: The rooftop pool with sweeping views across the city.

Address: 10 P. Trần Nguyên Hãn, French Quarter, Hoàn Kiếm, Hà Nội 100000, Vietnam

Phone: +84 24 3228 8888

Website: fairmont.com

Daisy was a guest of Fairmont Hanoi.
