British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died at the age of 19 following a serious accident at the Volta a Portugal.

Tarling, the younger brother of Ineos Grenadiers cyclist Josh, was riding for the NSN Development Team and taking part in the eighth stage in the north of the country when the accident occurred.

A statement on the team’s website read: “We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

“Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

“Our deepest condolences go out to Fin’s parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend. Rest in peace, Fin.”

The eighth of 10 stages was a 166km race from Melgaco to Fafe on Friday.

Race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation posted on X their “most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones.

“In light of this tragic event, the race will be neutralised until reaching Fafe and, as a sign of respect and mourning, the podium ceremony scheduled for today will not take place.”

British Cycling paid tribute on Facebook, saying: “All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

“Fin was a hugely talented rider with a bright future ahead, a loyal team-mate, and a brilliant young man.

“Our thoughts are with his parents and brother Josh at this devastating time. Rest in peace, Fin.”

World governing body the UCI added on X: “The UCI is deeply saddened by the tragic death of British rider Finlay Tarling, who passed away following a serious accident during today’s 8th stage of the Volta a Portugal.

“The UCI extends its deepest condolences to Finlay’s family, friends, and team-mates.”

A San Diego man pleaded guilty to a federal charge after he was caught on video kicking and chasing a protected sea lion at a local beach.

Tyler Muehl, an 18-year-old from the upscale neighborhood of La Jolla, pleaded guilty Thursday to violating the Marine Mammal Protection Act when he repeatedly kicked the animal as it tried to get away on July 22 at La Jolla Cove beach, U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon said in a statement.

The video, which went viral, shows Muehl throwing kicks at the sea lion that was sitting on a sea wall as at least one other person can be heard laughing in the background. Muehl follows the sea lion, throwing more kicks at it as it tries to scoot away before the video ends.

Muehl admitted that he kicked at the sea lion four times and landed at least two kicks on the animal, federal prosecutors said.

As part of his plea agreement, Muehl also acknowledged that a video capturing the attack was a fair and accurate recording of what occurred, they said.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s guidelines say people should stay at least 50 feet (15 meters) away from sea lions, seals and other species protected by the Marine Mammal Protection Act.

“Intentionally striking or kicking a marine mammal is not only illegal — it is dangerous for the well-being of the animal,” said Eric Morgan, an official with the NOAA-Fisheries Office of Law Enforcement West Coast Division, which investigated the case.

Muehl faces up to a year in prison and a fine of $100,000 when he's sentenced Oct. 20.

News.title: How to have the perfect slow-paced holiday in Zakynthos
News.content:
Zakynthos, also known as Zante, is renowned for raucous nightlife, but there’s a far more authentic side to the Venetians “Fiore di Levante” (Flower of the East). For such a small island, scenery is extremely varied: the southern coastline – home to Laganas’ notorious nightlife strip – also encompasses the pristine beaches of Zakynthos Marine Park, where loggerhead sea turtles come to nest, while some of the island’s best-known attractions, including Navagio Beach on the cliff-lined northerly coast, can only be reached by boat.

Birthplace of the man who penned Greece’s national anthem, Zakynthos was also a magnet for literary greats: Byron lay in state here and philhellene Edgar Allan Poe wrote a sonnet to the island’s “verdant slopes”.

Last but not least, food is a powerful lure here: sit in a rustic sea view tavern sipping local Verdea white wine with a plate full of traditional kouneli stifado – a garlic and tomato-soaked rabbit stew – and you’ll be hooked.

News.title: Ebola doctors ‘step back’ from WHO in drug trial ethics row
News.content:
Two leading doctors have “stepped back” from long-held positions with the World Health Organization amid a row over the ethics of an Ebola drug trial underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The randomised control trial, called Ebo-Pep, is testing whether an experimental antiviral is an effective post-exposure treatment.

But experts believe the study’s design puts healthcare workers on the frontline of the epidemic at risk, because it means medics exposed to Ebola might receive a placebo treatment.

“We owe them [healthcare workers] a duty of care to do the best possible thing, and a 50 per cent chance of getting a placebo tablet is not that,” said Prof Tom Fletcher, director of the Global Health Trials Unit at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. The WHO’s health emergencies clinical unit has also deployed him to Ebola ‘Red Zones’ for more than a decade.

This week, Prof Fletcher and eight other experts based in the UK, US, Uganda, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Canada published their concerns in Nature Africa, calling for a “careful reconsideration” of the trial protocol.

They said they are not against Ebo-Pep or randomised trials, but warned there are “additional ethical obligations” when including healthcare workers in studies like this, given the case fatality rate currently stands at 40 per cent.

Prof Fletcher said: “Ebo-Pep is a really good trial, it’s the trial we’ve talked about doing for years. But we’re talking about [protecting] the ‘one-per-centers’, the people who willingly step into one of the most dangerous environments in the world.”

News.title: Wildfire watch: Inside London’s fire control centre on the hottest day of the year
News.content:
“It’s been relentless, an immense number of calls,” says Yvonne Woodhams, control room commander at the London Fire Brigade’s headquarters on the morning of what turned out to be the hottest day of the year so far.

Inside a nondescript building in South-west London, dozens of fire brigade dispatchers field calls from the public and direct the city’s 5,000 or so firefighters across 102 stations to where they are most needed.

In the middle of another heatwave and on a day when temperatures rose to just above 38 degrees, the control room was busy – the scale and frequency of wildfires in London’s parks and grasslands are now considered unprecedented.

Above the dispatchers there is a live map, with red dots representing each active fire, sprawling from Enfield in the north to Purley in the south.

Wildfires nearly always have a human origin like dropped cigarette butts, glass bottles that magnifies the sunlight, or the now-temporarily banned portable barbecues.

But it’s the tinderbox that London has become which is worrying firefighters.

Scorching hot, low-humidity weather, a bit of wind, and tinder-dry vegetation can cause the smallest spark to ignite an inferno. Conditions like this have been described as “fire weather” by the author John Vaillant.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

Treasury officials have predicted UK growth of just 0.3pc in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked for the rest of this year.

That is far lower than the 1.6pc predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March, based on assumptions made before the start of the war. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Iran war threatens to cripple growth, Treasury warns Burnham | Officials predict economic expansion of just 0.3pc in 2027 if Strait of Hormuz stays blocked

2) Britain facing £54bn bill for North Sea shutdown | Costs soar amid shortage of specialised ships needed to clear up abandoned oil rigs

3) Ban on zero-hours contracts to cost companies up to £3bn | Businesses face huge bill to offer workers guaranteed hours under Employment Rights Act

4) Nvidia’s AI push has echoes of Enron, says Big Short investor | Michael Burry claims chip giant is engaging in ‘circular’ financing

5) Shadow bank founder battles to stave off bankruptcy threat | Paresh Raja launches legal claim to prevent administrators from chasing him for repayment

What happened overnight

Asian shares were mostly higher, powered by gains for AI-related stocks including computer chips as regional markets tracked a rally on Wall Street.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 advanced 1.6pc to 68,601.21. In South Korea, the Kospi jumped 4pc, climbing to 6,844.65, as shares in Samsung Electronics surged 5.4pcc. Computer chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 7.1pc.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.3pc to 3,967.28, while the Shanghai Composite index added 0.5pc to 3,967.65.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.4pc to 9,155.80.

Data from the US on Wednesday showed consumer prices had risen in line with analysts’ expectations in July.

Wall Street stocks were boosted on Wednesday by gains made by tech companies CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer, both of which closed up by more than 19pc.

The Nasdaq Composite ended the session up 0.5pc, with the S&P 500 up nearly 0.3pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished the session marginally down.

Oil prices were little changed as investors weighed the deadlock in talks between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was broadly flat at nearly $89 a barrel.

News.title: H5N1 sparks a very Australian epidemic
News.content:
H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia’s shores and is threatening to infect some of the country’s most unique wildlife.

Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1, a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020.

Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly ‘jump’ to other species.

While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia’s most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth.

An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction.

Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes.

Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments.

News.title: Selfie-seekers bring Man Utd vs Leeds match to premature end
News.content:
Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

Sports.title: Enzo Fernandez deadline passes as Chelsea reject transfer amid Man City interest
Sports.content:
Enzo Fernandez deadline passes as Chelsea reject transfer amid Man City interest

Enzo Fernandez is wanted by new Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca and Chelsea set a strict deadline for any club to meet their £120million valuation by 5pm on Friday

View 2 Images Enzo Fernandez's future remains undecided (Image: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Chelsea expect Enzo Fernandez to remain at Stamford Bridge after their deadline for clubs to bid £120million passed without an offer. Fernandez, 25, is a top target for Manchester City with just over two weeks of the summer transfer window left.

‌



Former Chelsea manager Enzo Maresca wants to reunite with the Argentine at City, who were told alongside other interested clubs that they had until 5pm UK time on Friday to meet his valuation. But it's understood that Chelsea have not received a bid.

‌



The Blues now expect Fernandez to be part of Xabi Alonso's squad after deadline day on September 1. City, however, don't believe the saga is over and that Chelsea would still be open to selling their vice-captain, who returned to training this week following the World Cup.

‌



City are looking to sign a replacement for star midfielder Rodri, who's edging closer to a move to Barcelona. Another City midfielder, Tijjani Reijnders, has agreed to join Saudi Arabian side Al-Qadsiah in a £52m deal.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Barca have made two offers for Rodri, the latest of which came in at £51m, after the 30-year-old agreed personal terms. But City held firm and turned down the proposal. Etihad chiefs are demanding £60m for Rodri, who's in the final year of his contract.

Maresca will take charge of his first competitive match as City boss on Sunday, as his side face Arsenal in the Community Shield at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff. During his pre-match press conference, the Italian said that he didn't anticipate any imminent arrivals, but reckons that City will make 'one or two' more signings before the window closes.

"For sure there are things that we need to do. How many, I don't know," Maresca admitted. "Could be one, could be two. Depends also if players leave.

‌



"Now, in this moment 48 hours before a final - my first final in this club - I will try to win the first trophy. First of all, the transfer window is open, we can buy players and we can sell players, anything can happen ... I just saw Rodri now in the building, I gave him a big hug, he looks good so we see what happens."

Is the Enzo Fernandez saga over? Have your say in the comments section.

View 2 Images Enzo Fernandez is back training with Chelsea (Image: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC via Getty Images)

‌



On Reijnders, he added: "It is not done officially, we will see in the next hours. I already spoke with him a few times in pre-season. We will see at the end if he is going to leave or going to stay.

"In the way he was playing in the pre-season games I was quite happy with his performances overall. I know Tij from Italy, from (AC) Milan when he was there, so I know him quite well.

"Probably there he was playing in a different position, he likes to play a little bit more deep than higher on the pitch. But again, in the pre-season he was good and now we see what happens and then we decide."

Sports.title: Liverpool announce £1.4bn investment that sees Jeff Bezos become co-owner at Anfield
Sports.content:
Liverpool announce £1.4bn investment that sees Jeff Bezos become co-owner at Anfield

Liverpool have been in talks with a wealthy consortium that includes Amazon founder Jeff Bezos for a number of weeks over a minority stake in the Premier League club

View 2 Images Jeff Bezos is part of the consortium (Image: Anadolu, Anadolu via Getty Images)

Liverpool's owners, Fenway Sports Group, have agreed to sell a 30 per cent stake in the Premier League club to a consortium including Jeff Bezos, led by former Queens Park Rangers director Amit Bhatia. The deal is understood to be worth £1.4billion.

‌



While Amazon founder Bezos won't have a seat on the board, Bhatia has been given the new title of vice-chairman at Liverpool. Bezos, the third-richest man in the world with an estimated net worth of £204bn, will instead be represented by Bryan Baum, the managing partner of K5 Global which has helped fund the consortium named 1892 Holdings.

‌



The club confirmed: "Fenway Sports Group (FSG), a global sports, media, entertainment, and real estate company, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement for the sale of a minority equity stake in Liverpool F.C. to 1892 Holdings, a consortium led and managed by Amit Bhatia, with investments from Amit Bhatia and the Mittal Family Trusts, K5 Sports (a K5 Global Fund), with Jeff Bezos as the lead investor in the K5 Sports fund, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.

‌



"The strategic investment supports Liverpool F.C.'s long-term growth ambitions by bringing together experts from across global business, technology, and investment. The consortium partners will work with FSG and the club's leadership team to evaluate opportunities that enhance the club's objectives on and off the pitch. FSG continues to retain majority ownership and operational control of Liverpool F.C."

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



FSG President Mike Gordon commented: "Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club's long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.

"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together."

Where will Liverpool finish this season? Give us your prediction in the comments section.

‌



View 2 Images Amit Bhatia is Liverpool's new vice-chairman (Image: Andrew Fosker/REX/Shutterstock)

In addition to Bezos and Bhatia, the wife of Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, Elaine, will also join the expanded Liverpool board. The Saverin family are in the consortium as part of EE Capital.

Bhatia said: "We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.

"To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come."

Sports.title: Championship 1-24 predictions: Every club's finishing place this season decided
Sports.content:
The most unpredictable, chaotic league in the world is officially back tonight, with Wolves and Blackburn kicking us off at Molineux.

Between now and May, 24 teams will battle it out over 46 gameweeks for a chance to land a golden ticket to the Premier League. Two will succeed with another joining them following an extended play-off campaign (don't forget it's now the top eight!). Three other teams will also exit the Championship, albeit through the trapdoor.

We all know from experience how gruelling and unpredictable the Championship is. So it's only logical that, for the second year running, I take a stab at calling where every team will finish.

Check out our 1-24 predictions below ahead of the big kick-off...

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

24 - Bolton Wanderers

I'm backing two of the promoted teams to stay up this year, or at the very least make a good fist of doing so. I'm less optimistic on Bolton, largely because in Amario Cozier-Duberry and Mason Burstow, they will have to make do without two of their most influential attackers from last season. It also feels like a lack of business has been done, particularly in those forward areas.

Ryan Hardie was signed on loan earlier this week and has double figure pedigree at this level but goals may still be hard to come by with loanees Cozier-Duberry and Burstow (their top scorer last term with 12 league goals) not returning. Sam Dalby was next best in the scoring charts with 10 goals but is an unknown quantity at this level. It feels like more firepower is essential before the transfer deadline. David Watson, Ben Davies, Akin Famewo, Luca Stephenson, Kyliane Dong and Gaizka Larrazabal have all come through the door but none really jump out at you. If any team needs a big final few weeks in the window, it's Bolton.

23 - Charlton Athletic

Charlton got over the line last year after a bit of a slog to give themselves an opportunity to kick on under Nathan Jones. The issue is that they will have to try and do so in a division which feels significantly stronger this time around - and I'm not totally sold on the business they've done being enough to keep their heads above water.

Jones has spoken about Charlton wanting to evolve but it's hard to see where the goals are coming from for them to do so. The Addicks were the third lowest scorers in the division last year; other than Charlie Kelman (7) and Sonny Carey (8) no other Charlton player registered more than three goals in the league. Millenic Alli and Karlan Grant have been brought in to add to Charlton's wide attacking options but the former has a dearth of Championship experience and Grant last hit double figures in the league back in the 2021-22 campaign. Their midfield options don't inspire confidence either; it's one thing questioning whether the strikers can get more goals but the service into them also needs to be better. I'm not seeing that correlation right now.

Charlton will be solid and diligent but I don't think that will be enough. It feels like Jones recognises that with his desire for Charlton to be less limited this year. Have they done the business to do so? It doesn't feel like it.

22 - Lincoln City

View 7 Images Lincoln City went 29 games unbeaten to romp League One last season (Image: PA)

Momentum can be a force of nature in football and it half feels like Lincoln have forgotten how to lose games after going 29 unbeaten to absolutely romp their way to the League One title. But even for one of the most sensible and well-run clubs in the pyramid, take away your manager and star player from that formula and it's a pretty devastating one-two.

The reason I have them in the final relegation spot is that I fancy them to at least give a good fist of upsetting the odds again. However, Jack Moylan was their talisman and his loss is significant, maybe more so than Michael Skubala. On the incoming front, it feels like Tanto Olaofe has the tools to make a nuisance of himself at this level even if he may not be prolific. Mason Melia, the promising young Tottenham striker, is a wildcard in attack after signing on loan. There's not been loads of business done but Lincoln do still have the nucleus of the team that absolutely demolished League One last season.

The step up will be significant and they will undoubtedly become reacquainted with the feeling that comes after losing games. But Lincoln can hold their own and will bloody some noses.

21 - Blackburn Rovers

Blackburn have arguably had the weakest transfer window of any side in the division, adding just Moussa Baradji, Jayden Fevrier and Sam Morsy to a squad that flirted with relegation for most of last season. Already, we're in alarm bell territory.

Tony Mowbray returning to Ewood Park has probably been Blackburn's most significant capture of the summer but the squad he will start the season with is threadbare. Rovers will play on the front foot more under Mowbray and have players who can outscore teams; that will be what sets them apart from others down the bottom. The fact they have attacking players who you would genuinely back to deliver over the course of a season, like Ryoya Morishita, Andri Gudjohnsen and Yuki Ohashi, is encouraging. But they lack depth in other areas and that will prove problematic as the season goes in.

20 - Portsmouth

After two consecutive survival battles, it feels like Portsmouth are trying to kick on this summer by opening up the purse strings, operating at a different level in the transfer market compared to what we have seen previously. Big striker Marko Milovanovic and the all-action midfielder Rocco Shein after intriguing pick ups and the onus will be on the former to hit the ground running to ease some of the goal-scoring burden on Adrian Segecic, who is a right player. A fit and firing Josh Murphy will also go some way to helping on the goal front; plagued by injuries last year, he racked up 22 goal contributions in 45 league games during the 2024-25 campaign.

I think Portsmouth will be okay but I don't see them having the depth to climb the table significantly compared to last year. A lot will hinge on how their new signings adapt. We've seen lots of clubs, Millwall most recently, enjoy success from overseas signings and effective player trading. This year could be Portsmouth's first step in emulating that model, which would serve them well.

19 - Stoke City

It almost feels like Stoke are stuck in some weird sort of Narnia whereby they do business I like each summer but don't tend to go anywhere. Therefore I just can't bring myself to back them for any sort of decent finish.

It's now been nine years since Stoke dropped out of the Premier League and they still haven't recorded a top-half finish in the Championship. Ethan Galbraith quickly established himself as one of the Championship's best playmakers at Swansea after making the step up from Leyton Orient last summer and landing him for big money felt like a real statement of intent at the time. But beyond that I'm not sold on any of their other incoming business. Viktor Johanssen and Million Manhoef are quality and Mark Robins should, theoretically, be the perfect manager to finally get Stoke out of their 14th-18th malaise. Maybe this will be the year. But it'll be a braver man than me who backs it.

18 - Preston North End

A Championship without Preston North End just doesn't feel right. I did initially have fears that could change, but late transfer business has convinced me to nudge them up this list.

Ambition wise, PNE smashed their transfer record to retain the services of star man Alfie Devine after his stellar loan last year earlier this summer. But beyond that, it all felt a bit underwhelming for a while. Delano Burgzorg managed just three Championship goals last season and five the year before, while Jusef Erabi, also joining in attack, is an unknown quantity at this level. Captain Ben Whiteman chucking the towel in a fortnight before the season starts following interest from Wrexham is hardly a resounding vote of confidence for where PNE were at, either.

But they have replaced him swiftly with Leo Leroy from Basel, who looks a good signing. And it was confirmed on Friday that a deal for Stan Mills to join the club in January has been agreed due to Oxford United's current transfer embargo. More could follow before the window shuts. So although the vibes at Deepdale haven't been great throughout the summer, I don't see them in a relegation fight.

17 - Cardiff City

View 7 Images Cardiff City are back in the Championship after winning promotion last season (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA)

Cardiff look by far the best equipped of the promoted sides to cope with life in the Championship and I debated placing the Bluebirds a fair bit higher on the list here. I always think this pool of teams, the ones who won't be troubled by relegation but are perhaps unlikely to mount a realistic play-off push, are the hardest ones to place.

Brian Barry-Murphy's total football should translate well to a higher level and in Yousef Salech they boast a striker whose game will suit the league. Moylan is another player I fancy to replicate his stunning League One form in the Championship, while signing Nathan Trott permanently is huge after his excellent loan last season. Maybe Cardiff can maintain their momentum from last season and push for a higher finish than this. There has also been talk of significant further spending in the transfer market, which could skew these predictions. One thing I am certain of is they won't be looking anxiously over their shoulder.

16 - Watford

Individually, Watford have some proper talent in their squad. But they are another team that you just wouldn't feel comfortable backing to achieve something based on a lots of factors. One big one is the manager: Alessio Dionisi starts the season, but will he end it? Who knows. Probably not even Watford.

Giorgi Chakvetadze and Nestory Irankunda (who is finalising a move to Sporting Lisbon as I finish these predictions) are big losses. Imran Louza would be another with intense speculation over his future. That would be three big losses and probably kill off any outside chance of a play-off push. That being said, who really knows what any season holds for Watford. The only thing I'll stick my neck out and say is that, like Cardiff above, they won't be looking over their shoulder at any point.

15 - Birmingham City

Birmingham will have grand ambitions this season and will be all the better for last year's campaign, where they consolidated themselves in steady if not spectacular fashion. The problem I think they'll find is that there are just too many teams who are better than them currently for them to really kick on this year.

Maybe that sounds harsh. Or lazy. Or both! But I just don't see the significant upturn in points they will require to break into the top eight, although they do have the scope to do something completely bonkers in the final weeks of the transfer window to make me look foolish.

14 - Derby County

Derby came close to the play-offs under John Eustace last year and the nucleus of that squad is still intact. But I think they will be one of the teams who find themselves finishing lower this term simply due to the strength of others.

The unexpected collapse of a takeover by the Saudi Arabian boxing kingpin Turki Alalshikh is likely to have an impact on the club's incoming transfer activity, though they have managed to secure the permanent signings of popular loanees Sammy Szmodics and Bobby Clark. Derby are a strong, powerful team who nobody will fancy playing. And on their day, they are a match for any team in the division. Across the course of a season is another matter, though I wouldn't be too shocked if any of the teams placed between 10 and 14 here end up in slightly different spots.

13 - Bristol City

It felt like Bristol City needed a big summer after falling away bigtime last year and, on paper, they've delivered. They've spent the best part of £9million on League One's two top strikers in Dom Ballard and Lorent Tolaj. Plus they've brought in the highly-rated Sam Tickle as their new No 1 keeper, the industrious Sam Greenwood to further strengthen in the attacking areas and Championship stalwart Jed Wallace. On paper, not bad, right?

Does all that equate to a play-off finish under the guidance of new head coach, Michael Skubala? Maybe. I still reckon Bristol City fall just short, mainly due to the strength of the division. There are just too many good teams ahead of them and, let's not forget, they are effectively ripping things up and starting again with Skubala at the helm. A top eight finish at the first time of asking is probably a stretch, but a good season here should set them up nicely for next year.

12 - West Brom

View 7 Images James Morrison will lead West Brom permanently after keeping them up last season (Image: Adam Fradgley/West Bromwich Albion FC)

James Morrison is one of the big unknown quantities ahead of the new season. His arrival as caretaker boss was the catalyst for West Brom retaining their Championship status after a truly chastening campaign He rightly landed the job on a full-time basis off the back of that, but can he now oversee a promotion challenge?

The Baggies went back to basics under Morrison in a bid to accumulate the points necessary to stay afloat and it remains to be seen if they will stick with the same approach given the former midfielder has now effectively been given a blank canvas to work with. Squad-wise, West Brom have good players and better depth than some others. Does that translate into a top eight finish? I'm unsure, so I'll hedge my bets.

11 - Swansea City

Swansea start the season with perhaps the best striker in the division in Zan Vipotnik. But will they end the window with last season's Championship top scorer still in tow with Hull City circling? That remains to be seen and plays a factor here.

Keeping Vipotnik would be a major transfer win and they've done smart business too: Elijah Just looked a right player at the World Cup and will bolster their attack and if they can keep Ross Stewart fit after snapping the striker up from Sunderland, then it could be the signing of the summer. Unfortunately, it's at the other end Swansea look less convincing. The news on the eve of the new season that Cameron Burgess has suffered an ACL injury isn't particularly helpful for Vitor Matos.

10 - Wrexham

Wrexham came agonisingly close to landing a play-off spot last season and will be in the mix to go one better this season. But again, the quality of the other teams pushing for those top eight positions could just nudge Phil Parkinson's team aside.

After hitting their stride in the second half of last term, Wrexham have opted for continuity and strengthened smartly rather than opting for full-scale surgery. Danny Imray is an excellent pick-up at right-back and will enhance their attacking threat from that area. Anthony Patterson will come in as first-choice keeper and is an upgrade on last season. Josh Windass will lead from the front again after bagging an impressive 17 goals last season with only Vipotnik, Ollie McBurnie and Haji Wright netting more. Kieffer Moore and Sam Smith will provide support but I reckon a marquee addition in attack is needed for them to gatecrash the top eight this time.

9 - QPR

View 7 Images QPR could be dark horses for a top eight finish (Image: MI News/NurPhoto)

In terms of transfer window wins, QPR are right up there. Looking at their business, there is a lot to like: Pierce Charles on loan feels shrewd, albeit the youngster dropped a clanger in the cup game with Millwall. Picking up Dennis Cirkin on a free transfer is just tremendous business and Tariq Lamptey could still be a game-changer if he can rediscover his fitness and hit top form again. Glenn Kamara also adds some steel in midfield.

The bonus QPR have despite their form absolutely falling off a cliff at the end of last season (and largely why I'm choosing to ignore that) is that they already have an adequate attacking arsenal to compliment their new signings. Richard Kone and Rumarn Burrell should both be in the goals after acclimatising to Championship level last term and are backed up by the likes of Karomoko Dembele, Kwame Poku and Koki Saito. And Illias Chair. What does that all up to? My prediction is QPR will be a good watch and dark horses for a top eight finish.

8 - Sheffield United

Sheffield United were an absolute calamity last season and probably ruined many an ante-post bet. They were steady if unspectacular following Chris Wilder's return and feel safer to back this time around, albeit with the caveat that troubling the top two feels beyond them.

The incoming business so far doesn't feel like much to crow about, while the sale of Andre Brooks to Norwich was a painful one. But the team that finished the season is far superior than their final league standing of 13th. This time around, Wilder and Co won't be playing catch up after the sort of nightmare start even a depressed supercomputer would struggle to realistically muster up. They've lost Gustavo Hamer, but the squad still boasts plenty of firepower and players who have experience of doing the business at this level. Defensively they have some of the division's top performers in their respective positions in keeper Michael Cooper, Japhet Tanganga and Femi Seriki. That's a nice mix and I reckon they return to the pack challenging for promotion.

7 - Burnley

Of all the relegated sides, Burnley feel like the hardest to predict. They are not the only club to head into the season with a manager who is untested on these shores but it feels like Nicky Hayen has a bigger job on his hands than Cesar Peixoto. If they retain the services of Zian Flemming, then Burnley could finish higher. They absolutely haemorrhaged goals last season - almost two a game - but I like the loan signing of Max Alleyne from Manchester City.

Cards on the table time: I really don't know what to expect from Burnley and they were by far the hardest to place on this list. My gut and head says they will not be the force they usually are in this division after dropping down. I had a couple of absolute shockers last year and Burnley could very well be the shout I try to avoid looking at for the next 12 months.

6 - Millwall

Millwall enjoyed their best campaign in a generation last time out as they defied all the odds to finish third, missing out on automatic promotion on the final day. Emulating that feat will take some doing, even though the nucleus of the squad that won more games than any other team in the division bar champions Coventry City largely remains.

Talisman Femi Azeez is likely to depart and losing his ability to conjure up something from nothing in the final third will hurt a team who were the lowest scorers in the top eight. On paper, Millwall's incoming business looks positive and you can tell from their recent track record in the transfer market that they generally know what they're doing on that front. They also boast one of the division's top managers in Alex Neil, who underlined his credentials with last year's showing. The squad does feel imbalanced, though, with just two out and out senior wingers in Azeez and Kyrell Lisbie. And with Azeez likely to depart and Tristan Crama recently undergoing ankle surgery, Millwall will be without the dynamic right hand pairing that was so influential last term.

The Lions may not finish as high as last year, but another play-off finish feels within reach and would represent another strong season.

5 - Southampton

View 7 Images Tonda Eckert remains in charge of Southampton but he could face a ban over 'Spygate' (Image: Matt Watson/Southampton FC via Getty Images)

Southampton were absolutely motoring at the end of last season and probably have the squad to finish better than the fifth place I've got them down for. But the uncertainty over Tonda Eckert plays a big role in that; if the German is handed a ban for the Spygate scandal that marred last year's play-offs, then that could skew Southampton's season massively. The shadow of that possibility even hanging over them might even do the trick.

Regardless of who is at the helm, Southampton won't be on minus points for long and will be among the teams slugging it out for promotion. It's hard to pinpoint a weakness in the squad: Daniel Peretz is back permanently and we already know his quality, while Cyle Larin, Lewis Dobbin and Divin Mubama give the Saints even more firepower. The squad is just a joke all around, really. Leo Scienza and Tom Fellows on either flank...forget the spying, are we sure that's allowed? Really, it's a poor season for Southampton if they are in the play-off eliminators. If the Eckert situation had been resolved and there was clarity on that front, I've have them well clear of them.

4 - Norwich City

Under Philippe Clement, Norwich feel like proper promotion contenders. The former Rangers boss inherited a team in turmoil with Norwich second from bottom after failing to win a staggering seven straight home games in the Championship. He would oversee 17 wins from 31 games, which is promotion form.

I feel like a broken record banging on about strikers and firepower, but goals win prizes and Norwich have some seriously heavy artillery up top. Jovon Mokoma is the business and should be a decent shout for top scorer, while Mo Toure has adapted to the Championship seamlessly. Norwich are less convincing at the other end and will ship goals. But for every goal they concede they could go and score three. I can see them troubling the top, top dogs but having to settle for a play-off spot, eventually. Again, think they will be a really good watch for any neutrals who find themselves flicking through Sky Sports + via the red button on midweeks.

3 - West Ham

I know, I know: West Ham was the banker. This was the no-brainer, the one that couldn't fail etc etc. If we're speaking about absolute jokes of a squad then West Ham are bang up there in terms of invidual players (Jarrod Bowen in the Champ? Come on). And yet I think that's also part of the reason why a top two finish could elude them. They have the tools to succeed but does it all work together?

Nuno Espirito Santo has been there, done that, got that t-shirt when it comes to promotion from the Championship, so he's not walking into the unknown. But the landscape has changed drastically since then. West Ham in the Championship now feels far more significant than it did when they were last in here more than a decade ago and the dynamics have shifted; if they attempt to continue with the same pragmatic style Nuno has typically deployed throughout his career, then I don't see them doing enough to crack the top two. And that's before we even touch on the weight of expectation that will be on them and their manager. With respect, Wolves in the Championship at the time was a big job. But this feels like another level for him and a group of players who went down last year.

I don't mean to go into full-on cliche mode, but how will this star-studded squad cope with being the scalp of the division? Can they, in fact, do it on a cold Tuesday night away at Stoke? Maybe I'm wrong and West Ham will absolutely romp it. But coming off the back of a bruising relegation and with off-field drama still prevalent in the background, I'm not sure it'll be as straightforward as some are expecting.

2 - Middlesbrough

You've got to give it to Boro - they have had the sort of transfer window that wouldn't look out of place in Football Manager (the good ones, not 2026). They've scooped major windfalls from sell-on clauses, banked a tidy sum from the sale of their talisman Hayden Hackney (bittersweet but necessary as his deal was up next year) and they've used it to level up in the two positions that cost them automatic promotion last year in goalkeeper and striker.

Radek Vitek is a huge upgrade on Sol Brynn and will be one of the division's top keepers, while Will Lankshear should absolutely feast if he is served up the same number of quality chances that Boro's forward's spurned last season. Just the impact from those two alone will serve Boro incredibly well. We know the squad is strong, even though the loss of Hackney is a huge blow.

Backing Boro to finish second ahead of some of the other quality teams in this league might feel bold, but the team and manager Kim Hellberg are impressive. And while others, like the teams coming down, may have to find their feet back at the level, Middlesbrough should get motoring far quicker.

1 - Wolves

View 7 Images Wolves are likely to be in the frame for an instant return to the Premier League (Image: David Rogers)

Wolves needed a huge revamp after one of the worst Premier League seasons in history…that hasn’t happened. Wolves needed to shift the deadwood and high earners out of the club…that hasn’t happened either. So why - I hear you ask - are we tipping Cesar Peixoto’s side to finish at the top of the Championship pile?

Simply put, Wolves have an embarrassment of riches for the second tier. In midfield, they have a Brazilian international in Andre, the exciting Fer Lopez and potentially Jordan James. Signing Kieran Trippier was an impressive coup, bringing Raul Jimenez back to Molineux was potentially even more eye-catching. Adam Armstrong, who was on course to be the league’s top scorer before moving to Molineux in the 2025/26 campaign, may have to settle for a place on the bench this time around.

Pre-season has shown Wolves will play on the front foot and press high, a method which has worked for previous title winners. They will need to start well to ease the toxicity and could still do with a new keeper and centre back, but Wolves will fancy their chances of lifting the trophy next May.

Sports.title: Ex-Liverpool star Jarell Quansah emerges as shock Arsenal target amid William Saliba fears
Sports.content:
Ex-Liverpool star Jarell Quansah emerges as shock Arsenal target amid William Saliba fears

Arsenal are in the market for a new central defender this summer with William Saliba currently injured, and Jarell Quansah is the latest name to be linked with the Premier League champions

View 2 Images Jarell Quansah could join Arsenal before the transfer window closes (Image: Jose Breton/Pics Action/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Arsenal have opened talks with Bayer Leverkusen over a deal to bring former Liverpool defender Jarell Quansah back to the Premier League in a bid to strengthen their defence.

‌



The Gunners are in the market for another central defender amid fears that William Saliba faces months on the sidelines in order to recover from the back injury that plagued him during the World Cup. Arsenal have already been linked with a host of players this summer including Ezri Konsa. However, they and Aston Villa are said to be some way apart when it comes to their respective valuations of the 28-year-old.

‌



With the new Premier League season now just one week away, it seems Arsenal are considering other options in the market - including one of Konsa's England team-mates.

‌



According to The Sun, Quansah has emerged as a surprise target for the champions, just 12 months after quitting Anfield to move to Germany.

It's claimed the 23-year-old is keen on the idea of returning to the Premier League, though Leverkusen will not sell Quansah unless they receive a significant increase on the £30million sum they parted with to sign him last summer. Such a deal could still come in cheaper than meeting Villa's demands for Konsa, who they are understood to value at around £60m.

‌



Quansah's versatility is an added bonus for Arsenal and their manager, Mikel Arteta, with the Liverpool academy graduate also able to deputise to right-back. He was picked to fill in for the injured Reece James during the World Cup, although his tournament was marred by the red card he received during the round-of-16 triumph over Mexico.

View 2 Images William Saliba is likely to miss a significant period of action due to a back injury (Image: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista, Getty Images)

Arsenal are also in the market for an elite left winger, as they bid to level up the team that can within a whisker of clinching a Premier League and Champions League double last season.

‌



Morgan Rogers and Vinicius Junior were touted as ambitious targets earlier in the summer, but the former joined Chelsea in a blockbuster transfer worth £117m, while Vinicius put pen to paper on a new contract with Real Madrid last week.

Rogers is one of four players to have moved for a fee in excess of £100m this summer, with Arteta admitting that the amount of nine-figure transfers had taken him by surprise on Friday. He said: "Yes it has, yeah. I wouldn't bet on that to be fair. But that's the market, that means that there are clubs that are happy to invest or they believe the valuations of players are that and that's fair.

"At the end, the value of the player is what somebody can pay for you. They've done it so that's the value and it is the right one because someone is happy to sell and someone is happy to buy. In the middle a player is happy to move from one club to the other so I think that's fair."

Sports.title: Eva Carneiro's life now after Jose Mourinho Chelsea row and net worth as football club owner
Sports.content:
Eva Carneiro's life now after Jose Mourinho Chelsea row and net worth as football club owner

Eva Carneiro was once a key part of Chelsea's medical department, but her Stamford Bridge career came to an abrupt halt after an infamous row with Jose Mourinho in 2015

View 4 Images It's been over a decade since Eva Carneiro's infamous bust-up with Jose Mourinho (Image: Getty Images)

It was the moment that shattered the illusion of harmony at Stamford Bridge - and 11 years later, the echoes of one of the Premier League's most notorious touchline bust-ups are ringing loud once again.

‌



Thanks to a newly released 'Mourinho' Netflix documentary, centred around the career of managerial titan Jose Mourinho, the infamous 2015 clash between the former Chelsea manager and the club's then-team doctor, Eva Carneiro, has been thrust back into the spotlight.

‌



In the programme, Mourinho doubles down on his actions, backed by former Chelsea captain John Terry. But Carneiro, who has spent the last decade rebuilding her life and career away from the harsh glare of the media, isn't taking the comments sitting down.

‌



Here is a look at what actually happened, how Carneiro responded to the new documentary, and what her life - and bank balance - looks like today.

FOLLOW OUR CHELSEA FB PAGE! Latest Blues news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Cristiano Ronaldo married in front of just FOUR witnesses and signed pre-nup READ MORE :

Eva Carneiro slams Jose Mourinho and John Terry after Netflix dredge up Chelsea controversy READ MORE :

The infamous 2015 bust-up

The incident that derailed Chelsea's 2015/16 season occurred on its very first day. The defending champions were drawing with Swansea City and were already down to 10 men after goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois was sent off. When Eden Hazard went down injured, Carneiro and physio Jon Fearn rushed onto the pitch to treat him.

‌



Mourinho was incandescent. By receiving treatment on the pitch, Hazard temporarily had to step to the sidelines, leaving Chelsea to defend a counter-attack with just nine men. After the match, the Portuguese manager publicly threw his medical staff under the bus, branding them "impulsive and naive."

Carneiro was subsequently stripped of her first-team matchday duties. A month later, she resigned, sparking a bitter and high-profile legal battle.

View 4 Images Jose Mourinho and Eva Carneiro infamously fell out in 2015 (Image: BPI)

‌



The £5m last laugh

While Chelsea's season spiralled out of control - culminating in Mourinho's sacking just months later - Carneiro took her fight to an employment tribunal. She filed a claim for constructive dismissal against Chelsea and a separate personal claim against Mourinho for sex discrimination and harassment.

Court documents revealed she rejected a £1.2million settlement offer, demanding a formal apology and proper compensation for the distress caused. Just moments before she was due to testify in 2016, a confidential settlement was agreed upon. Reports widely indicated the payout was in the region of £5m.

Crucially, Chelsea issued an unreserved public apology, stating unequivocally that Carneiro was simply following the rules of the game and fulfilling her duty of care as a doctor by putting the player's safety first.

‌



View 4 Images Carneiro was ultimately awarded a £5m pay out (Image: Getty Images)

Life now: net worth and football club ownership

Since leaving the Premier League, Carneiro, now 52, has thrived. She established her own private practice, the Sports Medical Group, located on London's prestigious Harley Street. She also acted as a private consultant for the Aspetar Orthopaedic and Sports Medicine Hospital in Qatar ahead of the 2022 World Cup.

She hasn't completely turned her back on English football, either. In 2024, Carneiro transitioned from club employee to club owner, becoming an investor in semi-pro side Lewes FC. The Isthmian League club is famous for its pioneering stance on equal pay for its men's and women's teams. Carneiro shares the boardroom with other high-profile investors, including Andy Murray's mother, Judy, and British musician Kate Nash.

‌



Thanks to her lucrative private practice, successful business investments, and her substantial Chelsea settlement, Carneiro's net worth is currently estimated to be around £3.8m.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Firing back at the Netflix doc

Mourinho's recent Netflix feature saw the 'Special One' refuse to apologise, claiming his "eyes know when a player is injured" and suggesting his anger was entirely justified. The Real Madrid boss said it was "very, very simple" to understand that Hazard wasn't really injured and didn't require treatment.

‌



Terry added that there was an unwritten "understanding" among players and staff that medics wouldn't enter the pitch unless an injury was obviously severe.

Carneiro, however, immediately took to social media platform X to set the record straight, quoting the General Medical Council (GMC) guidelines on a doctor's absolute duty of care.

View 4 Images Mourinho defended his actions in the new Netflix documentary about his career (Image: Courtesy of Netflix)

‌



"11 years on and here we are reliving the worst. Hope they made some money," Carneiro wrote, alongside a photo of her time at Chelsea. Targeting Terry's comments, she added: "We are bound by a medico-legal code of conduct. Genuinely it would be healthy for John Terry to learn the rules of the game. It's been long enough mate."

Breaking down the reality of the incident, Carneiro explained that her hands were tied the moment the referee requested her presence.
