If you are wondering what is on in Puebla this weekend, you are in luck: Saturday 15 and Sunday 16 August 2026 are packed with things to do. And the two biggest draws will not cost you a peso.

French megastar DJ Snake plays a free open-air show on the Plaza de la Victoria on Saturday. While the city’s international book fair takes over the historic center for the full weekend.

Add a warm evening, some of Mexico’s best food a short walk away, and it is an easy weekend to fill.

Puebla This Weekend at a Glance

The headline event is a free concert. As part of Festival Frecuencias, a national circuit of free festivals, DJ Snake performs on the Plaza de la Victoria on Saturday 15 August.

With his set billed for around 16:00 and no ticket required. Running alongside it, the Feria Internacional del Libro Puebla, known locally as FILIP.

Is open every day from Friday 14 to Sunday 23 August. As a result, both Saturday and Sunday are full of free readings, talks and staged performances across the Centro Historico.

So whether you want a big crowd and a bass drop or a quiet browse among book stalls. This weekend has you covered.

Below you will find the details for each event, plus practical notes on getting around. Eating well and planning ahead for the festivals still to come.

DJ Snake’s Free Show at Plaza de la Victoria

DJ Snake, the French producer behind global hits like ‘Turn Down for What’ and ‘Lean On’. Headlines Festival Frecuencias on Saturday 15 August.

The show takes place on the Plaza de la Victoria, a central Puebla plaza. And organizers have confirmed free, open access rather than ticketed entry.

Because a free set from an artist of this size draws huge numbers. Plan to arrive well before the 16:00 start if you want to be anywhere near the front.

Meanwhile, wear comfortable shoes, carry water, and agree a meeting point with your group in case the crowd swallows the phone signal. We have already published a full guide to this concert, so if DJ Snake is your main reason for heading out.

Read our dedicated write-up for the finer details before you go.

The FILIP Book Fair, Free All Weekend

The second edition of the Feria Internacional del Libro Puebla runs from Friday 14 to Sunday 23 August. Which means it is in full swing throughout the weekend.

Admission is free, and the city says the program includes more than 300 activities. The fair spreads across three main venues in the Centro Historico: the Zocalo.

The Teatro de la Ciudad and the Capilla del Arte UDLAP, with additional forums nearby. Because everything sits within a compact, walkable area, you can drift between book stalls, author talks and staged shows without needing transport.

For families and casual readers alike, this is one of the easiest free days out in the city. In addition, the Zocalo setting means you are steps from cafes, ice-cream stands and the cathedral.

So it is simple to make an afternoon of it.

What to Catch at FILIP on Saturday and Sunday

On Saturday 15 August, a standout is the staged ‘Requiem por Juana Ines de la Cruz’ at the Teatro de la Ciudad at 16:00. A fitting nod to Puebla’s deep literary history.

Since seating at the theatre venues can fill up, arrive early even though entry is free. On Sunday 16 August, the pick of the day is ‘Don Quijote de la Mancha’ featuring Omar Ruiz at 18:00.

It is a family-friendly way to close the weekend, and again there is no charge to attend. Beyond these two highlights, the daily program shifts constantly, so it is worth checking the official FILIP agenda on the day.

That way you can catch any author signings, children’s workshops or concerts that suit your schedule.

Looking Ahead: Tecate Comuna Tickets Go On Sale

If you want a bigger night out with a ticket in hand. The region’s marquee rock festival opens its sale just after this weekend.

Tecate Comuna 2026 lands on Saturday 28 November at Foro Cholula, on the western edge of the Puebla metro area. With Caifanes, The Flaming Lips and The Mars Volta headlining.

Tickets sell exclusively through eTicket. A Banamex cardholder presale opens on Tuesday 18 August, and general sale follows on Wednesday 19 August.

Prices start at MXN 1,590 (about US$93) for a Fase 1 General pass. With a Comfort Pass at MXN 2,130 (around US$125) and VIP at MXN 3,030 (around US$177), each plus service fees.

In short, this is not a this-weekend event. But the timing means you can lock in the best-value passes while you are already in festival mode.

For the full lineup and buying tips, see our separate Tecate Comuna guide.

Getting Around the Centro Historico

The good news is that this weekend’s free events cluster around central Puebla, so you can do most of it on foot. The Zocalo, the Teatro de la Ciudad and the Capilla del Arte UDLAP are all within an easy stroll of one another.

For the DJ Snake show on the Plaza de la Victoria. A ride-hailing app is the simplest option on a busy night, because parking near the plaza fills up fast.

If you are coming from Cholula or the outskirts, budget extra travel time both ways. From Mexico City, Puebla is roughly two hours by highway or by frequent ADO buses to the CAPU terminal.

From where a short local ride brings you to the center. Despite the crowds, the compact layout makes the weekend easy to navigate.

Where to Eat Between Events

You will not go hungry in central Puebla. The streets around the Zocalo are lined with taquerias, cafes and traditional restaurants.

So it is simple to grab a bite between a book talk and the concert. This is the home of mole poblano and, in season, chiles en nogada, the patriotic dish served through late summer.

For a quick, portable classic, hunt down a cemita, the city’s overstuffed sesame-seed sandwich, from a market stall. For a fuller list of where to eat across every budget and craving.

Our Puebla dining guide breaks the city down neighborhood by neighborhood.

Where to Stay for the Weekend

If you are visiting rather than living locally, the Centro Historico is the obvious base. Its UNESCO-listed streets are dotted with boutique hotels, hostels and guesthouses, many within walking distance of the fair and the concert plaza.

Because a free superstar concert can tighten availability, book early if you can. Still, midweek arrivals and stays just outside the core tend to be easier on the wallet.

Staying central also means you can drop your bags and rejoin the action quickly. Which matters when the day runs from an afternoon book reading straight into an evening dance set.

Practical Tips for the Weekend

Carry some cash for market stalls and tips, even though many venues take cards. A small power bank is worth its weight when you are coordinating with friends across a crowded plaza all day.

August in Puebla can bring afternoon rain, so a light layer or a compact umbrella is a smart pack. As a result, you can move from an outdoor stall to an indoor theatre without missing a beat.

Finally, plan your exit from the DJ Snake show before you need it. Line up a ride or note a pickup spot in advance.

And you will end the night on a high rather than stuck in a scramble for a taxi.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best free thing to do in Puebla this weekend?

Two stand out. DJ Snake plays a free concert on the Plaza de la Victoria on Saturday 15 August as part of Festival Frecuencias.

When and where is the DJ Snake concert?

It is on Saturday 15 August 2026 at the Plaza de la Victoria in central Puebla. With the set billed for around 16:00.

How much does the book fair cost?

Nothing. All activities at the Feria Internacional del Libro Puebla (FILIP) are free and open to the public.

How do I get Tecate Comuna tickets?

Tickets sell only through eTicket. A Banamex presale opens Tuesday 18 August and general sale opens Wednesday 19 August.

Sources: Sources: Puebla city government (FILIP 2026); Festival Frecuencias organizers and Mexican cultural press; Tecate Comuna official site and eTicket; Banxico reference exchange rate (mid-August 2026).

World.title: Costa Rica’s Wild Capuchin Monkeys Are Using AI Touchscreens
World.content:
Wild white-faced capuchin monkeys in Costa Rica are learning to use a touchscreen in the middle of the forest, giving researchers a new way to study animal intelligence without taking the monkeys out of their natural environment. The system, called CapuchinAI, combines artificial intelligence, cameras, a touchscreen and an automatic food dispenser at the Taboga Forest Reserve in Guanacaste.

When a capuchin approaches the station, the technology can detect the animal, record its interaction and present a task on the screen. Successful interactions can trigger a food reward, typically a slice of dried banana. During a two-week field test involving two groups of wild capuchins, 16 monkeys voluntarily interacted with the device. Ten learned how to trigger food rewards, while eight developed and retained a clear association between touching the screen and receiving food.



Some figured it out faster than others. The first monkey to seriously investigate the device was a large male named Trompudo. After initially hitting different parts of the apparatus, he touched the screen and received a piece of banana. He quickly repeated the action.

Other monkeys eventually began using the station as well, with some discovering that the touchscreen responded not only to their hands but also to their mouths. A few learned to effectively “kiss” the screen to get a reward. The research, published in the American Journal of Primatology, is intended to solve a longstanding problem in animal cognition studies: scientists can tightly control experiments in laboratories, but captive conditions do not fully reproduce the social pressures, competition and environmental challenges that animals face in the wild.

CapuchinAI is designed to bring some of that experimental control into the forest. An early facial-recognition model trained on images of six known capuchins was able to identify individual monkeys with more than 97% performance across still images, video and live field footage. During the latest field deployment, the system was adapted to recognize when a capuchin approached the station, allowing researchers to automatically collect more video and build a larger database for identifying individual animals.

That distinction is important as the pilot study primarily tested whether wild monkeys would approach the technology, interact with the touchscreen and learn the connection between touching it and receiving a reward. The next stage is intended to recognize individual monkeys automatically and give each one cognitive tests suited to its progress.

Researchers are developing experiments covering learning, impulse control, cognitive flexibility and short- and long-term memory. Once an individual is recognized, the system could eventually determine which test that particular monkey should receive and track its performance over time.

The portable unit is built around a Raspberry Pi computer and includes a webcam, touchscreen, motorized food dispenser and battery. It can operate for about eight hours on a lightweight battery pack, making it practical for field conditions where normal laboratory equipment would be difficult to use.

The work is particularly well suited to Taboga since the reserve contains about 2.97 square kilometers (1.15 square miles) of protected tropical dry forest and supports one of Costa Rica’s larger concentrations of white-faced capuchins. More than 14 groups have been identified in the area, while long-term researchers concentrate on four groups.

Years of observations also mean scientists already know the histories, social relationships and behavior of many individual monkeys. Combining those records with controlled cognitive tests could help researchers examine why some capuchins learn faster than others, whether social experiences influence problem-solving and how different environments shape intelligence.

The technology is not intended to replace researchers following monkeys through the forest. Instead, it gives them another way to collect standardized information while the animals continue moving freely through their normal habitat. If the approach proves successful, similar systems could eventually be adapted for other wild primates, allowing scientists to compare cognition across animals and environments without relying as heavily on captive populations.

For Costa Rica, the experiment puts one of our most familiar wild animals at the center of an unusual meeting between conservation research, artificial intelligence and behavioral science.

World.title: Nicaragua Bishop Abelardo Mata Says He Is Well After Detention
World.content:
Catholic Bishop Abelardo Mata, a critic of Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, said he is in good condition in an interview broadcast Wednesday by the government, which released him days earlier following his arrest over alleged corruption. Mata, 80, was detained on June 29 for questioning about the origin of his properties, which Nicaragua’s Interior Ministry said did not correspond “with his status as a priest.” Authorities officially announced his release on July 4.

“Thank you, I’m fine,” Mata said in an interview at his home with state-run Channel 6 that was circulated by pro-government media. The interview made no mention of the bishop’s detention. Mata appeared to be in good health, while the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights had previously requested information about his whereabouts.

“Prayer helps a lot,” Mata said after the journalist repeatedly remarked that he appeared to have “a lot of vitality.” The United States denounced what it called “religious repression by the dictatorship” of Ortega and his wife and co-president, Rosario Murillo, over the case. Opposition groups accuse the two leaders of persecuting the Catholic Church, which the government blames for supporting the 2018 protests that left more than 300 people dead and for promoting what authorities describe as a Washington-backed coup attempt.

Mata was one of the most influential figures in Nicaraguan Catholicism over the past three decades and was known for criticizing the government, according to Nicaraguan media outlets operating in exile. In the interview, Mata also said that a brother and a niece visit him at his residence, although he prefers “silence, study and prayer.”

In recent years, the Ortega-Murillo government has intensified its crackdown on critics, stripping some of their nationality and expelling them from the country. Those affected have included politicians, business leaders, journalists, intellectuals, human rights activists and members of the clergy. In some cases, the government has also confiscated their property.

The government’s campaign against its opponents has been accompanied by a constitutional reform that is expected to be put to a vote in early September and would exclude opposition parties from elections.

World.title: Costa Rica Seals Security Contracts as “Operation Pegasus” Remark Goes Unexplained
World.content:
A decree set since August 10 has sealed a wide range of Costa Rican security information from public view, including records of which companies win government security contracts. The dispute over it sharpened Wednesday when a governing-party lawmaker referred to an “Operation Pegasus” during floor debate in the Legislative Assembly, then declined to say what she meant.

President Laura Fernández Delgado and Public Security Minister Gerald Campos Valverde signed Executive Decree 45870-MSP on July 27. It was published in Alcance No. 104 to the official gazette La Gaceta on August 10 and took effect immediately, without prior public consultation, because the text classifies itself as confidential and restricted. The government declared the records a state secret covering its principal intelligence and security bodies.

The declaration reaches the National Public Security Council, the National Intelligence and Security Directorate known as the DIS, and a high-level working group called Fuerza Élite, along with any other security and defense coordination directed by the presidency. It covers documents, files, budgets, operational plans and meeting recordings.

Fuerza Élite brings Fernández together on Mondays with the ministers of security and justice, DIS leadership and police chiefs to coordinate the response to organized crime. It is the same group at whose first session she ordered polygraph examinations for senior police and government officials.

The reach that has drawn the sharpest objections is financial. The decree seals command structures, technological resources, reliability-vetting protocols and their results, budget line items and spending categories. It also covers public procurement files, supplier identities, technical requirements, bids, contract awards, financing arrangements and records of how those contracts are carried out.

The government justified the measure on grounds of public interest and national security, citing the threat posed by criminal structures tied to drug trafficking, contract killing and money laundering. Disclosure, the text argues, would expose institutional vulnerabilities and endanger officials and their families.

That rationale follows a period of sustained concern about criminal penetration of the security forces themselves, including a confidential police intelligence report that flagged 116 officers along the southern border over alleged links to trafficking networks. The decree invokes articles 27, 30, 130 and 140 of the Constitution, several provisions of the General Police Law and the General Public Administration Law, along with Constitutional Chamber rulings and opinions from the Attorney General’s Office.

Wednesday’s exchange began when Frente Amplio deputy Sigrid Segura Artavia challenged the scope of the decree and asked what the government was concealing, raising the possibility that authorities might be acquiring or using technology to monitor citizens who oppose them.

She named Pegasus, the surveillance program developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group, as the cautionary example. The software can extract messages, emails, photographs and location data from a compromised phone, and can switch on its microphone and camera. NSO Group has said it sells the tool only to governments and state agencies for use against serious crime and terrorism.

Pueblo Soberano deputy Kattia Calvo Cruz replied by referring to “the Pegasus operation” and denying it had anything to do with surveillance. “The Pegasus operation is not that. It has absolutely nothing to do with that,” she said, adding that Costa Rica faces a critical security situation and that classifying sensitive security information is a power the executive branch holds and is exercising.

Calvo did not say what the phrase referred to. Segura pressed her on whether the mention amounted to confirmation that the government uses the technology, and said such a program would be worse than the presidential data-analysis unit that triggered a privacy scandal under an earlier administration.

Asked afterward by reporters to explain what she had meant, Calvo declined to give a direct answer, saying she would respond if the question were put to her in the plenary chamber. She later referred the matter to her press officer. No evidence has been presented publicly that Costa Rica has acquired or deployed Pegasus, and Calvo explicitly rejected that reading of her own words. What remains unresolved is what operation she was describing.

Legal opinion on the decree has divided sharply. Of five attorneys who reviewed the text, four concluded it is plainly unconstitutional. Constitutional scholar Rubén Hernández estimated that slightly more than 90 percent of it would fail a constitutional review, and said only the portion concerning the DIS might survive, though not as currently drafted because it is written too broadly.

David Delgado argued that a state secret cannot be created by decree at all and requires a law passed by the Assembly, pointing to Constitutional Chamber rulings 13236-2003 and 00320-2005, which held that limiting access to administrative information through state secrecy is a matter reserved to legislation. Manrique Jiménez said a regulation cannot impose such a restriction on its own, and that any secret must be defined precisely and narrowly rather than leaving broad discretion to the executive.

Marvin Carvajal accepted that a declaration could in principle come by executive decree but said this one contravenes constitutional law, arguing the executive cannot declare state secrets wholesale. Fabián Volio was the lone defender, holding that the decree satisfies constitutional requirements because it governs a matter tied to national security, and that the reserve may properly cover documents, analyses, statistics and evidence gathered by such bodies.

The University of Costa Rica’s Freedom of Expression and Right to Information Program issued its own objection late Wednesday, saying a restriction of that breadth runs against the principles of publicity, transparency, maximum disclosure and accountability. It acknowledged that article 30 of the Constitution recognizes state secrets as a limit on access to information of public interest, but argued the provision grants no unlimited power to decide what citizens may know.

Information held by public administrations is presumed public, the program said, and may be withheld only where there is sufficient justification and express legal authorization. It noted that Costa Rica has no comprehensive law regulating state secrecy. The Inter American Press Association warned separately from Miami on August 11 that a measure of such breadth could obstruct journalism and restrict access to information of public interest, and recommended that journalists and citizens ask the Constitutional Chamber to rule on whether the decree conforms to the Constitution.

There is precedent for that route. Roughly three decades ago, a state secrecy decree covering arms purchases was challenged before the Constitutional Chamber, which never ruled because the government repealed the measure itself 78 days later. In the repealing decree, the executive of the day wrote that alongside protecting national defense it considered it equally essential to guarantee public confidence in institutions and full transparency in administrative contracting.

Opposition lawmakers have signaled they intend to test the current decree. Claudia Dobles of Coalición Agenda Ciudadana questioned why the declaration reaches contracting and the handling of public funds. Álvaro Ramírez, who leads the Liberación Nacional bench, said his party will examine the measure’s legality, singling out the confidentiality applied to DIS purchases.

The decree remains in force while those objections gather. Any challenge alleging violation of a fundamental right, such as access to public information, would go to the Constitutional Chamber, a body already at odds with the president over her claims about criminal infiltration of the judiciary. A claim that the decree conflicts with existing legislation could instead be brought in administrative court.

World.title: International News: World Health Organization warns 2026 Ebola outbreak could become deadliest on record
World.content:
International News: World Health Organization warns 2026 Ebola outbreak could become deadliest on record

By Zoila Palma: The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is on track to become the deadliest outbreak of the disease ever recorded, according to World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

Tedros warned that, at its current pace, the outbreak could surpass the 2014-2016 Ebola epidemic, which killed at least 11,000 people.

The 2026 outbreak was officially declared on May 15 and has so far recorded at least 4,300 cases and more than 2,000 deaths.

However, health officials believe transmission began months earlier, with evidence suggesting the virus started spreading in February and was initially mistaken for illnesses such as malaria and typhoid, BBC reports.

WHO officials say they hope to bring transmission under control within three months, although that would not necessarily mean the outbreak has ended.

WHO Africa Director Dr. Mohamed Janabi said health workers are currently reaching only about 30% of cases, with ongoing instability in eastern DRC making surveillance, treatment and containment efforts more difficult.

The outbreak is being caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which has previously been responsible for only two known outbreaks, in 2007 and 2012.

World.title: Belize assumes regional Environmental Presidency, sets 8 priorities for CCAD
World.content:
Belize assumes regional Environmental Presidency, sets 8 priorities for CCAD

By Zoila Palma: Belize has officially assumed the Pro Tempore Presidency (PPT) of the Central American Commission on Environment and Development (CCAD), the regional environmental institution of the Central American Integration System (SICA), with a call for stronger regional cooperation to address environmental challenges that cross national borders. Belize took over the presidency on July 1, 2026.

At the LXXV Ordinary Meeting of the Council of Ministers of Environment of Central America and the Dominican Republic, being held at the Best Western Biltmore Plaza in Belize City, Minister of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management Orlando Habet outlined Belize’s eight environmental priorities for its term.

The meeting brings together environment ministers and senior technical representatives from eight CCAD member countries to coordinate policies and advance regional responses to environmental and climate challenges.

Belize’s agenda will focus on integrated water resource management, biodiversity management, aligning the Mesoamerican Environmental Sustainability Strategy with the Regional Environmental Framework, climate change and integrated risk management with emphasis on loss and damage, sargassum management, solid waste management, chemical and pesticide management, and wildlife protection.

The priorities recognize the interconnected nature of issues such as water scarcity, food security, climate-related hazards, sargassum impacts on tourism and fisheries, and the protection of coastal communities.

The meeting also addressed major regional initiatives, including the Regional Environmental Framework (ERAM) 2026-2035, which establishes joint priorities across environmental quality, forests, seas and biodiversity, integrated water resources management, and climate change, as well as the launch of operations for the Ridge to Reef/Cuenca al Mar project.

World.title: Belize, El Salvador strengthen bilateral ties through third binational commission
World.content:
Belize, El Salvador strengthen bilateral ties through third binational commission

By Zoila Palma: Belize and El Salvador have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations following a series of high-level engagements in San Salvador focused on regional integration and practical cooperation.

On Tuesday, August 11, Chief Executive Officer for Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Oscar Arnold, joined representatives from across the Central American Integration System (SICA) to welcome Ambassador Lina Ajoy as she assumed the post of SICA Secretary-General.

Belize’s Ambassador to El Salvador, Lou-Anne Burns Martinez, and Belize’s Ambassador to Mexico and Coordinator of Belize’s Presidency Pro Tempore, Amalia Mai, also participated in the engagement.

The meeting highlighted Belize’s continued commitment to regional integration and to advancing initiatives that produce tangible benefits for people across Central America.

On Wednesday, August 12, Belize and El Salvador convened the Third Belize-El Salvador Binational Commission in San Salvador. Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs of El Salvador, Adriana Mira, led the Salvadoran delegation, while Ambassador Arnold headed Belize’s delegation.

The commission provided an opportunity for both countries to strengthen their bilateral relationship and identify new areas for cooperation.

Discussions covered trade, regional integration, defence and security, migration, health, agriculture, education and tourism, with officials from several Belizean ministries participating both in person and virtually.

Belize lands new nonstop routes from Boston to Tampa Bay starting at US$164

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize’s tourism gateway is about to widen considerably. BermudAir has announced new seasonal nonstop flights to Belize City from five US airports, Boston, Raleigh-Durham, Fort Lauderdale, Orlando-Sanford and St. Petersburg-Clearwater near Tampa, with service beginning this winter and one-way fares starting at US$164.

World.title: Sarteneja fisherman Mauri Gomez charged with stabbing murder of Jose Arteaga
World.content:
Sarteneja fisherman Mauri Gomez charged with stabbing murder of Jose Arteaga

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged 33-year-old fisherman Mauri Julian Gomez with murder in connection with the stabbing death of 35-year-old Jose Luis Arteaga.

Gomez was also charged with wounding in relation to injuries allegedly inflicted on 34-year-old Marvin Alexander Arteaga, who survived the incident.

The deadly confrontation occurred on Wednesday, August 12, during a fishing trip near Ranguana Caye, approximately 18 to 20 miles off the coast of Placencia. Reports indicate that police received information shortly after 4:30 p.m. that two fishermen had been stabbed aboard a vessel.

Initial police investigations indicate that an altercation broke out among fishermen at the caye, during which Jose Luis Arteaga and Marvin Arteaga were allegedly stabbed. Other fishermen reportedly managed to subdue the suspect. Because the group was travelling by sailboat, it took some time to transport the injured men toward Placencia, where police met the vessel.

Jose Luis Arteaga was transported to the Placencia Polyclinic but later died from his injuries. Marvin Arteaga received medical treatment for his injuries.

Arteaga, a Belize City fisherman, was the father of five children. His wife told Channel 7 that their youngest child had been born only four days before his death and that Arteaga never got the opportunity to meet or hold the newborn. She described him as a hardworking fisherman and devoted father who regularly spent eight or nine days at sea providing for his family.

Gomez, who has been identified in local reports as a fisherman from Sarteneja Village, Corozal District, was formally charged on Thursday, August 13, with murder and wounding in connection with the incident.
