American rapper Cardi B

Multi-platinum selling rapper Cardi B is set to headline a concert in Jamaica on Sunday, October 18 at the National Stadium.

The event, billed Cardi B and Friends, forms part of the BZR WKND (pronounced Bizarre Weekend) which runs from October 16-18.

According to a release from the organisers, the performance marks Cardi B’s first-ever headlining stadium concert in the Caribbean, bringing her celebrated love for dancehall culture and connection to her Caribbean roots to the island.

Cardi B, who is of Dominican and Trinidadian roots, has been credited for elevating the relevance of female rappers in popular music. Among her Billboard Hot 100 hits are Bodak Yellow, I Like It, Girls Like You with Maroon 5, Outside, WAP and Up.

The Grammy-winning artiste is the female rapper with the most number one singles (5) on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. She also has the most diamond-certified songs (4) among female rappers.

BZR WKND’s three-day celebration of music, culture, tourism, fashion, and entertainment will kick off with the BZR WKND Welcome Party on Friday, October 16, followed by the TIDAL RAVE Beach Party: WYFL Edition on Saturday, October 17, before culminating with Cardi B & Friends on Sunday, October 18.

“Following the incredible success of our inaugural event, we knew BZR WKND had to return even bigger,” shared Ryan Burke, organiser of BZR WKND Jamaica.

“Cardi B is one of the biggest artistes in the world, and her first-ever headlining stadium concert in the Caribbean represents a defining moment not only for BZR WKND but for Jamaica’s live entertainment industry. We’re proud to welcome fans from around the world for what promises to be an unforgettable weekend,” noted Roy “Gramps” Morgan, organiser of BZR WND.

BZR WKND Jamaica 2026 will once again bring together music lovers, travellers, and culture enthusiasts from around the globe while generating significant tourism, economic impact, and international media attention for Jamaica.

More than a music festival, BZR WKND Jamaica is a celebration of Caribbean culture, blending world-class entertainment with fashion, food, nightlife, tourism, and immersive brand experiences.

Throughout the weekend, attendees can expect VIP hospitality, curated events, interactive activations, and an exciting lineup of internationally acclaimed and Caribbean artistes joining Cardi B for what promises to be one of the biggest entertainment weekends in the region. Additional performers, ticket information, travel packages, and festival experiences will be announced in the coming weeks.

World.title: CCJ image at stake
World.content:
DESCRIBING the current discord within the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) as deeply troubling, former Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding has recommended an urgent probe and speedy resolution, warning that delay could irreparably tarnish the institution’s reputation.

“Disagreements are normal and healthy in a panel of judges who may offer different interpretations of the facts and points of law. That is why a panel exists. One expects that such disagreements are expressed respectfully, unlike another jurisdiction where they are sometimes punctuated with personal abuse,” Golding said in a column sent to the Jamaica Observer on Thursday.

Golding weighed in on the turmoil which became public at the start of the week when the Sunday Express newspaper in Trinidad and Tobago published a series of e-mail involving CCJ President Justice Winston Anderson and colleague judges.

In the e-mail exchanges, a majority of the judges accused Justice Anderson of governing the regional court in an “authoritarian” and “dictatorial” manner.

The complaints, as reported by the Sunday Express, range from accusations of Justice Anderson unilaterally imposing a judicial dress code to allegations of “panel fixing” and attempts to influence the outcome of cases.

The newspaper reported that the internal correspondence showed that five of the CCJ’s six sitting judges challenged Justice Anderson’s leadership, with one warning of “creeping patterns of anti-democratic approaches” and another calling for an urgent meeting to address “a level of disenchantment that may well be approaching a crisis point if left unaddressed”.

In one of the e-mail correspondence, presiding CCJ judge Justice Chile Eboe-Osuji told his colleagues: “I have never seen before the level of dictatorship in the administration of a judiciary that I have witnessed at the CCJ in recent months. There is a serious concern, not that the new trend would include an attempt to use a body like the RJLSC (Regional Judicial and Legal Services Commission) as an unwitting instrument of dictatorship. The RJLSC performs important functions within the mandate properly conferred upon it in the CCJ agreement. It would be wrong of any CCJ president — who is also the chairperson of the RJLSC — to try and misuse that important body in that way.”

Explaining his use of the world “dictatorship”, Justice Eboe-Osuji said it was “because Winston himself told us early on in a judges’ meeting — soon after his assumption of office of president (July 2025) — that he did not see himself as ‘running a democracy’ and that he would run the court in any way that he deems fit”.

In his column on Thursday, Golding said, “What is alarming is that the disclosure involves accusations of autocratic behaviour by the president and his manipulation of panel selection aimed at influencing judicial outcomes.”

Added Golding: “More alarming is the fact that these accusations are made not by one or two judges, but all the other five. It is hard to believe that they could have all taken that position without due consideration.”

He said that without appropriate resolution, “this episode will tarnish the reputation of the court, perhaps irreparably. Even if it is resolved, it will have suffered a serious setback in its hopes of gaining acceptance as the final court for all Caricom member states”.

Golding said that responsibility for fixing this débâcle lies firstly with the RJLSC and called on the commission to “move swiftly to investigate the reports and assess the facts”.

Pointing out that removal of the president, if that is deemed necessary, can only be done on the recommendation of the RJLSC and with a 75 per cent majority vote of the Caricom heads of government, Golding said: “God forbid that that becomes another imbroglio similar to that regarding the reappointment of the Caricom secretary general.”

The former head of Government also said he was most surprised by the focus of some legal luminaries as well as The Gleaner newspaper editorial on the circumstances by which the information became public — through a leak of confidential e-mail.

“Without that leak we would most likely never have become aware of this dysfunction and the court could descend into unexplained chaos. The leak may have breached ethical rules for which remedies exist, but are we not entitled to know? Is that not what whistle-blowing is all about?”

Read the full text of Golding’s column on Page 12 of today’s Jamaica Observer.

World.title: Mystery development irks Kingston 8 residents
World.content:
A drone shot of the location where the proposed development is to be built on Broadway Close in Kingston 8. The grassy area to the left in the photo is where the multi-family development is expected to be erected.

RESIDENTS of sections of Manor Park in upper St Andrew are up in arms over what they regard as secrecy surrounding a planned development in the area.

The residents say they have tried, without success, to get information on the development slated for 2 Broadway Close, Kingston 8.

According to the residents, unofficial sources have indicated that a five-storey building is planned for the area but efforts to get the authorities to either conform or deny this have so far failed.

In a letter, which they shared with the Jamaica Observer, the residents claim that people who live on Broadway Close, Broadway Road, Harrow Drive, and Waterworks Road are worried about the proposed development.

“The developers posted a notice of intention to build at 2 Broadway Close on July 6, 2026. Within 48 hours, the Broadway Mews Association formally requested the plans. The developer responded that the plans were in progress and would be provided once completed. Since then, there has been no further correspondence,” the residents said in the letter.

“Despite multiple requests, the community has been left in the dark. The developers were aware of the community’s interest within 48 hours of the notice going up. Yet, they have chosen to ignore all subsequent requests for information,” the residents added.

They claimed that when the community submitted a formal request for plans under the Access to Information Act, they were told it could take up to 60 days to receive them.

“The Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) informed residents they had only 35 days to file an objection. This creates an impossible situation where residents are being asked to object to a developer whose plans they have not seen, may not receive before the deadline, and which the developer has refused to share,” the residents claimed in the letter.

Repeated attempts by the Observer sine last week to get a comment from the KSAMC have so far been unsuccessful.

The residents pointed to comments made recently by Dr Patricia Green, a registered architect and former head of the Caribbean School of Architecture at the University of Technology, Jamaica.

“Dr Green has highlighted this exact issue. When citizens contact the KSAMC, they are denied access to the development proposals. Without the drawings, how are we to object?” the residents charged in the letter.

They pointed out that under Section 18 of the Building Act 2018, once a notice of intention is posted people can object to the development even without seeing the plan.

“The law does not require you to have seen the plans. Under Section 7 of the Kingston and St Andrew Building (Notices and Objections) Regulations, the KSAMC must take into consideration all objections which may be made before making a decision.

“The Supreme Court has confirmed this right. In Wint v KSAMC [2022], the court held that residents have a legitimate expectation that their objections will be considered, and that failing to do so is a breach of natural justice. You can object based on what you already know — the restrictive covenants, the cul-de-sac, the gully course, the road problems, the inadequate notice. You do not need to wait for the plans. But the developer’s refusal to share them speaks volumes,” the residents said.

They told the Observer that they have also contacted the National Environment and Planning Agency for answers and the agency confirmed the area is zoned for residential purposes and that the half-acre lot is permitted for 25 habitable rooms.

But the greatest fear of the residents is that the developers could be allowed to go as high as five storeys. The tallest building in the area is currently two storeys.

“Legal experts have noted that developments on plots smaller than half an acre are a key warning sign of a bad development. Under the 2017 Provisional Development Order, multi-family developments are only permitted if the land exceeds 0.5 acres, unless compelling reasons are shown. The 2 Broadway Close site is exactly 0.5 acres, a fact that should have triggered additional scrutiny,” the residents claimed.

They further argued that with Broadway Close being a dead-end street, a five-storey, multi-family development will generate significant vehicular traffic that must enter and exit through a single point.

“The KSAMC is required to assess access and traffic flow as mandatory planning criteria. Emergency vehicles — fire trucks and ambulances — require adequate turning radius and access. The Jamaica Fire Brigade is a mandatory referral agency that must approve such developments. Residents are demanding that a traffic impact assessment be conducted and made public before any permit is granted,” argued the residents.

They added: “The certificate of title for 2 Broadway Close contains restrictive covenants that are binding on the land and its owners. No building other than that used for the purposes of a private dwelling house with appropriate outbuildings appurtenant thereto shall be erected on the said land or any part thereof. Restrictive covenants are contractual obligations imposed on purchasers by the original vendor, intended to limit the purchaser’s use of the land for the benefit of all land owners in the subdivision.

“They run with the land, meaning successive owners are bound by the same covenants. A covenant that precludes subdivision would limit the owner’s ability to legally construct an apartment complex.”

World.title: It’s an event scene!
World.content:
DJ Zacky (left) and his MC, Flex Supreme.

In recent years, a new generation of event promoters have emerged on the party scene, adding to night-time entertainment offerings.

But even though some of these promoters have been hosting successful events, there are some challenges that come with the territory.

Kyle Chin said securing dates and identifying an appropriate venue remain challenges.

“I got into event promotion as a youth, just by helping my older cousins promote their event in St Elizabeth about ten years ago. Officially, I have been doing my own events for the past three years,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

Known for Socaverse and B43, he added: “The cost of getting the permits to actually keep the event is also of concern as well as the high taxes that promoters face.”

Chin’s events target the 18 and older demographic. Socaverse is a soca/EDM music event and is held twice annually while B43 is held monthly.

“What sets us apart and what we are bringing to nightlife is the experience. We cater to individuals with the different genres that are played and the type of setup we use,” said Chin who works as a corporate broker.

Popular teenage disc jock DJ Zacky, who hosts the bi-weekly SATDEHZ, which is held at Oceano, says he would like to see more support from corporate Jamaica for promoters.

“…I’d like to see more support for young promoters through sponsorship opportunities, easier access to venues, and stronger partnerships… I believe that there can be more collaboration within the entertainment industry. Better regulation and security support would also help events operate more efficiently,” said DJ Zacky.

“[P]eople don’t always take you seriously until you’ve built a name for yourself. But as our events continue to prove themselves, and our attendance keeps growing, you can see people starting to view us differently and put more respect on our name. That journey has motivated us to keep raising the standard with every event,” DJ Zacky shared.

He revealed that his passion for entertainment and creating memorable experiences were what drew him to event promotion.

“I saw an opportunity to bring people together through well-organised events… Event promotion allows me to combine creativity, business, and networking into something I genuinely enjoy,” DJ Zacky, who has been involved in event promotion for over a year, said.

SATDEHZ, a drink-inclusive event that offers patrons a premium nightlife experience, targets the 18-35 age demographic.

“We cater to university students, young professionals, and anyone looking for a quality entertainment experience. We’re focused on creating a premium yet accessible experience. Through strong branding, creative marketing, quality DJs, and engaging social media campaigns, we want every event to feel unique and memorable,” the business Administration student at the University of Technology, Jamaica shared.

On his way to The University of the West Indies (UWI), Mona, where he will be pursuing a degree in management studies, DJ Kovert, a popular disc jock, is the co-promoter for FWD, a bi-weekly event held at Dulce Lounge in Barbican.

Dominic Bartley is his business partner in this series which wrapped up on July 29.

“I decided to get involved in event promotion because I’ve always had a passion for music and creating experiences where people can take a break from their everyday lives and truly enjoy themselves. As a DJ, I realised there was an opportunity to create events that reflected the energy and atmosphere that I wanted to experience in Kingston, especially for my generation,” says DJ Kovert.

“While I’ve been promoting public events for a little over a month, my experience actually started before that. During my time at Ardenne High School, I helped curate and organise several school socials and events, which gave me valuable hands-on experience in planning, marketing, and understanding what it takes to have a successful party. Those experiences built the foundation and confidence that encouraged me to step into the entertainment industry and begin promoting my own events.”

FWD primarily caters to the 18-30 demographic.

“Each FWD staging is designed to have its own identity, with different themes, concepts, and elements that keep the experience fresh for patrons… As a younger promoter, we also bring a fresh perspective on how events are marketed and how audiences connect with entertainment,” DJ Kovert shared.

He spoke with Splash on the improvements he would like to see in the sector.

“I would like to have more support and opportunities created for promoters, especially young promoters who are trying to build sustainable events. This includes stronger partnerships with sponsors, more collaboration between promoters, venues, artists, and other stakeholders, as well as more accessible resources to help events grow. The entertainment industry is a major part of Jamaica’s culture and economy, and creating a better support system for promoters would allow more creativity, innovation, and quality experiences to thrive.”

Lemar Smith, who is from Trelawny, is the new kid on the block as far as event promotion is concerned. His weekly Saturday night event is called Sapphire Saturdays and is held at Vuebar in Liguanea.

“I started promoting Sapphire Saturdays in May this year… Although I’m still relatively new to the industry, the experience has taught me a lot,” said The UWI student, adding, “Whether you’re a university student, young professional, entrepreneur, or simply someone looking for a great Saturday night out, Sapphire is designed to bring people together in a fun and vibrant environment… We also place a strong emphasis on high-quality photography, videography, and social media content so people don’t just attend the event they become part of the Sapphire experience. It’s about creating a lifestyle and a community, not just another party.”

Smith would like the entertainment sector to become more diverse.

“I’d like to see more promoters take chances on concepts that feature house music, Afro House, Amapiano, R&B, throwback nights, and other unique experiences. Giving people more variety not only benefits patrons but also creates opportunities for DJs, artistes, promoters, and creatives to showcase different styles. I believe diversity will help Jamaica continue growing as one of the Caribbean’s top entertainment destinations.”

World.title: TWIN PEAKS: YEARS AWAY
World.content:
JAMAICA’S planned overhaul of financial regulation is likely to take years more to complete, outgoing Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) Governor Richard Byles has said, putting the Twin Peaks reform beyond both its original 18-to-24-month timetable and the Government’s subsequent 2026 target.

Byles, who is scheduled to demit office on August 18, said the BOJ and Financial Services Commission (FSC) were close to submitting the proposed architecture to Cabinet.

“Having brought it to Cabinet, remember now, really still we are at the beginning of the process,” Byles told the Jamaica Observer in an exit interview.

“The laws now have to be drafted… and the two Houses [of Parliament] have to debate it before it becomes law, so we do still have years of discussion and work to do on Twin Peaks, even when it goes to Cabinet and even if Cabinet says yes.”

Twin Peaks was announced in January 2023, shortly after disclosures of an alleged fraud at investment firm Stocks and Securities Limited intensified scrutiny of Jamaica’s regulatory system. The Government said the new structure would be implemented within 18 to 24 months, pointing to a transition between approximately July 2024 and January 2025.

That deadline passed.

In June 2024, then Finance Minister Dr Nigel Clarke told Parliament that implementation was expected in 2026. He said a concept paper prepared by the BOJ-FSC Twin Peaks Steering Committee had been approved and the Cabinet submission was in its “final stages”, after which drafting instructions would be issued.

More than two years later, Cabinet approval has not been publicly announced. BOJ said in June that the architecture would “soon” be ready for Cabinet; its latest Financial Policy Committee statement said only that progress continued.

It remains unclear how the concept paper approved by the then finance minister differs from the architecture Byles said was still being readied for Cabinet in 2026.

Byles hoped the submission could reach Cabinet before its August break. He said much of the time had been spent obtaining comments from the agencies involved.

“Any institution, not just the Bank of Jamaica, who has had to get legislation passed has found that that process is very cumbersome. It is onerous,” he said.

Although Byles described the difficulty broadly as part of the legislative process, Twin Peaks had not yet reached formal drafting or parliamentary debate. Most of the delay so far occurred while the architecture, inter-agency comments and Cabinet submission were being prepared.

MORE THAN MOVING REGULATORS

The significance of the delay extends beyond a missed deadline. Until the laws change, Jamaica must continue regulating institutions largely by sector even though many operate in groups spanning banking, insurance and securities. BOJ supervises deposit-taking institutions, while the FSC oversees securities dealers, insurers and pension funds.

Twin Peaks would divide the work by purpose. BOJ would supervise the financial soundness of institutions across the system. The FSC, or a proposed successor known as the Financial Services Conduct Authority, would oversee how firms treat customers, sell products, disclose fees and risks and handle complaints.

A bank would therefore answer to BOJ for its financial health and to the conduct regulator for its treatment of customers. The same division would apply across the sector.

The challenge is not simply transferring employees. The legislation must determine where one regulator’s authority ends and the other’s begins, what information they must share and how they will handle problems involving both financial safety and customer treatment. Poorly drawn boundaries could replace the gaps in the current system with either new gaps or duplicated regulation.

The public documents reviewed by BusinessWeek identify neither a final list of laws to be changed nor a consolidated schedule assigning responsibility for each stage and setting consultation, parliamentary and legal-cutover targets.

Jamaica is not starting from nothing. BOJ’s 2025 annual report identifies seven work areas covering supervision, consumer protection, legislation, staffing, technology, funding and Twin Peaks Practice. The regulators have trained employees and tested the approach across banking, insurance and securities within their existing powers.

Operational preparation can reduce disruption, but it cannot substitute for law: Only Parliament can transfer the responsibilities and make the new system enforceable.

One concern among non-bank institutions is whether BOJ would apply rules designed for banks. Byles said supervision would instead reflect each institution’s size, complexity and risk.

“It’s not that we will supervise the non-banks in the same way we do banks, because the non-banks are a different animal and we have a concept that says ‘proportionality’,” he said.

Proportionality would not exempt small firms. It would match scrutiny to the risks an institution presents and the wider damage its failure could cause.

THE INTERNATIONAL LESSON

South Africa’s experience shows why Byles’s warning should be taken seriously—and why long transitions still require clear deadlines.

Its regulatory review began in 2007 and widened after the global financial crisis. Twin Peaks was formally proposed in 2011, followed by a draft Bill in 2013. The Bill was tabled in 2015, enacted in 2017 and the regulators opened in April 2018.

The core transition took seven years from the formal proposal, or 11 from the initial review. Even then, the legal overhaul was incomplete. Cabinet approved a unified conduct Bill for submission to Parliament only in 2026-15 years after Twin Peaks was proposed.

That history does not make Jamaica’s delay unavoidable. Its lesson is that South Africa managed a long process through a published roadmap, successive drafts, consultations and phased implementation.

The United Kingdom moved faster, announcing its overhaul in 2010 and launching its regulators in 2013. There is no standard timetable, but reform is more measurable when divided into stages with clear responsibility.

For Byles, Twin Peaks remains his most important unfinished reform. He expects it to continue because it is Government policy rather than a BOJ initiative dependent on his leadership.

The next measurable step is Cabinet approval, which would allow formal drafting instructions to be issued. Legislation, consultation, parliamentary debate and legal commencement would follow.

More than three and a half years after Twin Peaks was announced, Jamaica has begun practising the system but has not legally entered it. Cabinet approval would advance the reform. Byles’s warning is that it would also expose how much of the journey remains.

World.title: Douglas hard on self despite three-medal haul
World.content:
Shanoya Douglas celebrates one of her two silver medals after winning the women’s 100m and 200m at the 21st World Athletics Under-20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, on Sunday. Douglas won three medals — gold in the women’s 4x100m and silver in the 100m and 200m — to take her total to five after winning gold and bronze two years ago in Lima, Peru. (Photo: Paul A Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Shanoya Douglas may have left the 21st staging of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships with three medals, but the highly rated sprinter believes she could have performed much better at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon, on Sunday.

Douglas, who entered the five-day championships as the World Under-20 leader in both the 100m in 10.98 seconds and 200m in 22.11, won gold as the anchor on Jamaica’s women’s 4x100m relay team and silver in both individual events.

The Jamaican women’s relay team won in a World Under-20 leading 42.89 seconds, the fourth-fastest time, ever, but Douglas said she was disappointed with her overall performance.

“I have mixed feelings in this championship. Normally, I always get gold individual medals but I got two silver this time,” she told the Jamaica Observer. “The gold in the relay means a lot for me because I wanted to continue our streak and it means a lot to be able to continue that streak, especially knowing that I’d broken it in the 100 metres.”

The result means Douglas has won five medals at the last two World Under-20 Championships, including another relay gold and a bronze in the 200m at the 2024 championships in Lima, Peru.

The haul puts her among Jamaica’s most successful performers at the championships, a distinction that appears to surprise her.

“You know I never realised that I had that many,” she said, while admitting that she expected more from herself in Eugene.

Douglas won the 100m and 200m doubles at both the Intersecondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA)GraceKennedy Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships and the Carifta Games this year. She is also tied for third all-time with American sprint legend Allyson Felix in the World U-20 200m rankings and is 10th all-time in the 100m, also at the World U-20 level.

Her two silver medals in Eugene, both behind American Mia Maxwell, have given her a different perspective.

“This championship has taught me a lot, knowing that it’s not always things gonna go your way, and I was saying that sometimes it’s good to control the controllable, but this time I was having difficulties controlling the controllables,” she said. “And I’ve been hard on myself this championship, and I was like, ‘Let’s come out here, put everything aside, and deliver for my country.’”

Jamaican women had won the previous four World Under-20 200m titles through Briana Williams in Tampere, Finland, in 2018; Tina Clayton in Nairobi, Kenya, in 2021; Alana Reid in Cali, Colombia, in 2022; and Reid again in Lima, Peru, in 2024.

Douglas was particularly hard on herself when asked to grade her performance on a scale of one to 10.

“A five,” was her instant response.

She said members of the Jamaican coaching staff told her she was being too hard on herself, but she explained that the standards she sets for herself are what drive her.

“When you have a standard for yourself and not been able to reach that standard that you set for yourself, it’s like a different mental struggle,” she said. “And it’s just I’ve not met my standard and the standard that I had for myself going to this championship.”

Despite her disappointment, Douglas believes the experience will benefit her as she begins her professional career. She will forgo another year in high school after signing a professional contract the week before travelling to Eugene.

“I’m still having hope. I have great faith in myself that in the future I will be able to perform way better going into the other championships, and this has taught me a lot,” she said.

Douglas also pointed to the championship format, which required the sprinters to run the first two rounds of their events on the opening day before returning for the final the following day.

“This has set me up for what is to come in the professional setting where facing difficulties will be a reality every day. So yes, it has taught me a lot,” she said.

She said she was able to rebound from what she considered below-par performances in Eugene and resisted the temptation to dwell too long on the moments when she performed well.

Douglas said the experience had reinforced an important lesson about the difference between expectations and performance on the day.

“This championship probably taught me that because you have the fastest time on paper, it’s who show up on the day. And it’s not that I didn’t show up on the day, it’s just that circumstances didn’t make me perform how I wanted to. And regardless of that or not, I’m trying to see the positive in it because I was able to leave the championship with a medal, three medals,” she said.

World.title: 2026 MG ZS: Luxury on a budget
World.content:
The 2026 MG ZS in luxury trim offers premium features at a very competitive price point. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Sports car brands that make SUVs have it tough with the car-buying public. The fact that MG, one of the most-storied British auto makers and a cornerstone of the quintessential English roadster, has given in to the SUV-pocalypse must have the faithful spitting their afternoon tea across their crumpet-laden tables. Still, history has proven them more wrong than right, as these companies with sporting intention are able to infuse the mundane family hauler with their original ethos. MG has done just that with the ZS.

EXTERIOR

SUVs tend to stay on the conservative side of things, whereas the ZS has adopted a previous trend held by the premium brands: Russian Dolling, the act of simply scaling corporate design up or down a specific model. Yes, there is the usual Grilleus Maximus styling across the MG family present on the ZS; however, it has only been possible with the updates made to its larger sibling, the HS, to tell them apart. Otherwise, the ZS is inoffensive, clean, and modern-looking with a bit of sporting purpose due to the standard 18-inch wheels on the luxury trim.

Adding to its visual appeal is its availability in a wider colour palette than many of the sub-compact SUV class rivals. Push past the black, white, silver, and grey to the Brighton Blue Metallic on Auto’s review unit, or the Emerald Green Metallic that instantly brings forth similar tones to the iconic British Racing Green.

INTERIOR

The ZS is feature-rich given its class and price point. Keyless entry gets one into a cabin similar to the exterior. It’s a clear, modern design, highlighted by soft-touch materials across the main contact surfaces. Drop into the 6-way powered driver’s seat for an ergonomic experience.

Button clutter is a thing of the past, as there are hard buttons for the most accessible functions, and the other controls are tucked away in the 12.1-inch infotainment touchscreen. Some functions can even be assigned to steering wheel-mounted buttons. These few physical controls available operate with assuredness.

Luxury trim buyers will enjoy a bit more digital instrumentation via their 7-inch gauge cluster. The system works smoothly, has a logical layout, and all the connectivity modern passengers want.

While the ZS is the smaller MG SUV, the cabin space is more than sufficient for all occupants, and the sense of space is enhanced by the glass-to-body ratio and the sunroof. Even with the large greenhouse, the cabin retains a low-noise quotient for further comfort. Storage, including trunk space, is more than sufficient for family treks.

Combine this with a number of automated or powered convenience features and the ZS is a very nice place to be.

ON THE ROAD

For many class rivals, it would just fall apart right here, falling into either the ‘too soft, I don’t want to drive it fast’ category, or the ‘too stiff, my passengers are going to throw up and complain’ side of the graph. Then there are those soft, yet unable to provide comfort; and hard, yet unable to provide any actual vehicular control. This is where the sports car legacy kicks in.

The real beauty of the ZS is its driving dynamics, clearly inherited from MG’s performance car know-how. The suspension is compliant, but firm enough to be sporty. At the first corner, at speed, there’s magically precious little body roll, instilling confidence to drive with some enthusiasm. Even better, the rest of the car can keep up, as the steering is direct in tracing the given driving line, and the brakes assure constant speed reduction. The 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder is more than willing to respond in unison with the transmission for rapid increases in velocity as demanded by the accelerator pedal. Even on the broken surfaces that make up the Jamaican internal road network, the ZS quickly makes one forget that it’s an SUV, taking on a car-like feel and making as much use of its front-wheels as possible.

For those that are more measured in their pace, the ZS can handle precious human cargo with the abundance of equipped safety systems, passive, and active for urban operations. Things are a breeze in stop-and-go traffic due to the auto hold function on the luxury trim.

Then there is the MG Pilot Driver Assistance suite. Put together, they keep the vehicle in check and the driver alert for potential accidents, while allowing the vehicle to be operated for short periods with minimal driver intervention.

VERDICT

With its size, price, comfort, and feature set, the 2026 ZS Luxury is already a top contender in the cut-throat sub-compact SUV segment. And while the brand faithful may scoff at it, or others mislabel it as another small SUV, MG did take time to work their magic. This is a brand known for driving excellence, and the ZS is a pleasure to be behind the wheel, packed to the gills with the family, or alone on a B-road. If that last part is important, then the 2026 ZS MG Luxury should be at the top of your list.

World.title: Help delivered, but…
World.content:
Tents, provided by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management, erected in the area of Coopers Pen, Trelawny, where 20 houses were demolished on Tuesday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Even as the Government mobilised multi-agency help for about 40 families whose houses were demolished a day earlier, a group of irate residents of Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny staged a peaceful protest Wednesday, demanding more. The residents said they want to be relocated, after their houses were demolished allegedly by the owner of land some of them have occupied for decades.

The protesters insisted that the Government, or the landowner, must provide them with alternative accommodation. They said the temporary tents provided by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), in which some of them spent Tuesday night, are not enough.

“We get tent last night, so we can lay a head for the night. What about today? What is going to happen? We want to know where we are going to relocate to. What is going to happen to the people them that their house push down?” asked demonstrator Jessica Haye.

In a Wednesday afternoon release, while emphasising that the demolition arose from a long-standing private matter, and that the Government of Jamaica was not a party to the underlying private dispute, the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) said a number of State agencies had been deployed “to address the immediate humanitarian and social welfare needs of affected families”. The Ministry of Labour and Social Security, ODPEM, Child Protection and Family Services Agency, Poor Relief Department within the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, and the Social Development Commission are among agencies involved. OPM said teams worked well past midnight, Tuesday, to help those who lost their homes.

“Assistance provided included food supplies, bottled water, toiletries, temporary shelter supplies, tents and lighting equipment. As part of the emergency response, ODPEM mobilised and transported relief supplies directly to affected families, including 40 family-size tents, cots, foam pads, solar lights, care packages, cases of bottled water and sanitary products. The Ministry of Labour will return on Friday, August 14, to provide additional support,” said OPM.

But while grateful for the help, residents said they expect more, and they laid out their demands during Wednesday’s protest.

“There is no way you can demolish a house like this, and no notification. No notification. We need justice,” said Haye, who stressed that many of them had not yet recovered from the devastation caused by last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

“We are not going to stop this [protest] until the prime minister [Dr Andrew Holness] hear. We naw stop. We go come out here day by day because we want justice. It must be a relocation!” she insisted.

Another demonstrator, Sylvia Fisher, said while they understood that the residents could not remain on privately owned property indefinitely, they should have been given notice and assistance to relocate.

“You can’t run in pon people so. And run pon people goods… and then now put you under tent! You have pickney to go back to school. It cannot work,” she said.

She said she has lived in the community for 32 years, while her father lived there for more than 50.

Fisher is adamant that the government has a responsibility to assist affected residents whom, she said, voted them into office.

“The government need to come see this cause a we the people make the government, and is we the people put politicians in power, and a we the people have power. So they must consider poor people. A no rich man, a poor people put them in a power,” she argued.

“We know we have to go, but please relocate we, relocate we. We live pon the land 20, 30, 40 years you just come pitch we off so. No! Find somewhere and put we. The private man who them say claims to own the land, him fi find somewhere and put we. A him come mash we up,” Fisher alleged.

Even as those who have lost their homes agitate, there are fears that the wrecking crew will return. Among the worried is 69-year-old Stanley Hill, who said he has lived on the property for 51 years.

He said a marker has been placed at the doorway of the small concrete house he has occupied for decades, indicating that it is earmarked for demolition.

“Now to the age a me now, me soon 70, me a 69-year-old. And me live there from me a little boy. Where me going go now as an old man? Me can’t make house again,” said Hill.

“I need somebody to talk to me so me know where me stand. Because me can’t come sleep under tree. And me don’t have no money. Me don’t have no bank account,” he added.

The OPM has given a commitment to keep an eye on what is happening in the community and “coordinate additional interventions”. It said it is aware that those affected include senior citizens such as Hill, children, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable individuals.

Said the media release issued Wednesday: “The Poor Relief Department of the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, along with the Social Development Commission, will undertake further assessments of affected residents and households. Assistance will be provided through the applicable government programmes and support frameworks. Furthermore, the Ministry of Local Government has indicated that drop-in shelters will be available to meet the needs of residents.

“The Government of Jamaica’s response is being coordinated across the relevant social protection, disaster management, child protection, local government and community development agencies, with the immediate priority being to ensure that vulnerable residents have access to essential assistance while individual and household circumstances are properly assessed.”

World.title: US threatens EU over its green reporting rules
World.content:
The dispute centers on two pillars of the EU’s corporate sustainability rulebook: the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, which requires large companies to address human rights and environmental harms linked to their operations and supply chains, and the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, which requires companies to disclose sustainability-related information.

Brussels has scaled back both laws in its drive to cut red tape, but has stopped short of Washington’s demand to shield U.S. companies from their reach.

Last week, Puzder similarly attacked the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism as a tariff on U.S. exporters. On Thursday, the White House also accused the EU and more than 40 countries of enabling Chinese goods to skirt U.S. tariffs by rerouting them through their markets.

A European Commission spokesperson told POLITICO that Brussels had made “considerable efforts” to explain its rules and highlight "its willingness to cooperate with the US to increase trade where possible," but drew a line at changing its regulatory regime in response to U.S. pressure.

“We have been very clear and consistent on the fact that neither our rules framework nor our regulatory autonomy are up for negotiation,” said the spokesperson.

This story has been updated.

Koen Verhelst contributed reporting.

World.title: Le Conseil Constitutionnel censure la loi interdisant les réseaux sociaux aux mineurs
World.content:
“L’interdiction instituée par la loi est susceptible de s’appliquer à des services de communication en ligne dont les risques pour la santé et la sécurité des mineurs ne sont pas établis”, estime encore le Conseil Constitutionnel, insistant sur l’imprécision autour du champ d’application de l’article.

Le risque avait été soulevé au moment de l’examen du texte au Sénat, certains élus de la Chambre Haute ayant tenté d’imposer l’établissement d’une “liste noire” qui définirait plus précisément les plateformes concernées par cette limitation d’accès aux mois de 15 ans – et éviterait ainsi le risque de censure par le Conseil Constitutionnel.

Un élément du texte retiré au moment de son examen en Commission mixte paritaire pour assurer sa conformité avec le droit européen.

Le Conseil Constitutionnel estime par ailleurs que le texte ne définit pas les garanties légales propres à assurer le droit au respect de la vie privée des utilisateurs qui seront contraints de faire vérifier leur âge par les plateformes pour prouver leur majorité.

“Le gouvernement n’a pas assez écouté le Sénat et le risque d’inconstitutionnalité que nous pointions depuis des mois. Désormais, le risque, c’est que le texte soit vidé de sa substance”, a réagi, sur ce point, la rapporteure du texte au Sénat, Catherine Morin-Desailly, auprès de POLITICO.

Un constat partagé par le député socialiste Arthur Delaporte, à l’origine de l’une des saisines du Conseil Constitutionnel.

World.title: French court blocks social media ban for under 15s
World.content:
The French president has also pushed restrictions to the top of the EU agenda, with an expected announcement of bloc-wide measures by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September.

In a statement late Friday, the French presidential office said the government would not be giving up on the bill. It has set a new target date for spring 2027, which coincides with when Macron will leave office.

The statement said Macron “has instructed the Prime Minister to work, as quickly as possible, on a legally sound draft that takes into account” the court's decision. The ruling hinted at what would make the age restriction align with fundamental rights: giving parents more flexibility.

Peter Craddock, a senior Brussels-based attorney advising social media firms, said the French court decision could have far-reaching implications.

"What they're basically saying here is: 'Listen, government, if you want to get this to succeed, you can't just work on the basis of a general ban. There have to be limitations," said Craddock, a partner at Keller & Heckman. "There have to be ways for people to say, 'well, actually, in my case, my son, my daughter is of a certain degree of maturity and is able to use this properly.'"

The government bill had passed through the French legislative procedure after a lengthy back-and-forth earlier this summer. It was set to bring forward Europe's first social media age restrictions, with Greece and Denmark planning to follow suit.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
World.content:
Latvia's military warned that similar incidents may happen again in the future. "While the Russian aggression in Ukraine is ongoing, the recurrence of such cases when a foreign unmanned aircraft enters or approaches Latvian airspace is possible," it said.

An air raid alert was declared in four eastern Latvian municipalities at around 4 a.m. local time. The military urged people to stay indoors and away from exterior walls.

After the drone was downed, Sandra Kapteine, head of the Rugāji village administration, told the Latvian Information Agency that the incident “caused no casualties,” as the drone wreckage fell in a “wooded area.”

There has been an uptick in similar incidents over recent months in countries close to the war-zone. A week ago, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said a Ukrainian-made drone crossed Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded near the village of Kardam.

World.title: Spain and Morocco reinforce border amid fears of fresh Ceuta migrant surge
World.content:
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska traveled to Ceuta on Thursday to inspect border infrastructure and a new sea barrier designed to keep people from swimming into the city. The exclave’s security personnel has also been reinforced with an additional 300 police officers and 2,000 soldiers.

“We do this to dissuade anyone who aspires to enter Ceuta and Melilla irregularly,” said Grande-Marlaska. “None of them will remain in Ceuta, none of them will make it to the Iberian Peninsula, none of them will be given legal status.”

The rumored mass crossing has been cited by critics of Spain’s migration policies.

Austria’s conservative Europe, Integration and Family Minister Claudia Bauer, last week mentioned the rumored Aug. 15 surge in a written statement, demanding Madrid “immediately and significantly reinforce border protection in its African enclaves and ensure that this time it will hold.”

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government also cited the possibility of a mid-August mass arrival last week while justifying its decision to maintain border checks on travelers from Spain.

World.title: Farage’s victory over Binface won’t silence his critics
World.content:
But second-placed this time was Count Binface, a comedian with a trash can on his head who secured — by many thousands — his highest ever vote count in a palpable protest against Farage. None of Britain’s mainstream parties took part in the contest, branding it a circus.

The Reform UK leader’s refusal to turn up at the count to hear the result Friday — a move that would have seen him pictured alongside a cast of comedy characters — underlined the struggle for him to get back on the front foot he is used to contesting politics from.

More significantly, Farage’s triumph means that parliamentary investigations into his financial affairs will now resume. That could lead to another by-election — one in which serious rivals are far less likely to stand aside to allow Farage to face-off against a long list of no-hopers.

Count Binface waits with other candidates for the declaration of the winner of the Clacton by-election at Clacton Leisure Centre, eastern England, on Aug. 14, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

Labour MPs switched out their own leader in part because of Farage’s storming success at local elections in May, but the focus on this contest has also made it harder for Farage to land blows on Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

This week, Labour overtook Reform in POLITICO’s Poll of Polls after months on the back-foot for the governing party.

Snubbing the count

Clacton is Farage’s fiefdom. It was one of the most Brexit-voting constituencies in the country and was the place that first sent him to the Commons on his eighth time of trying.

World.title: Farage probe resumes after he wins Clacton by-election
World.content:
The by-election was called by Farage himself amid mounting scrutiny of his finances.

The right-wing populist has faced repeated questions over a £5 million donation from crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, received before he became Clacton’s member of parliament in 2024, as well as support from convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

Farage has given varying explanations for the support, and billed this election — called at a dramatic press conference railing against the mainstream parties — as a “people versus the establishment” chance for Clacton’s voters to be his judge.

On Friday, the website of Parliament’s standards commissioner was updated to make clear that a paused probe into the Harborne donation has now been resumed.

That tees up the prospect of a further electoral test for Farage in Clacton if he is found to have broken the rules. The Conservatives, likely to be the most competitive challengers, have made clear that they would stand in such a contest.

Farage on Friday broke with tradition by declining to attend the result declaration at Clacton Leisure Centre.

World.content:

World.title: EU pushes back as US revives trade pressure on bloc and accuses Brussels of enabling China to evade tariffs
World.content:
The EU pushed back at renewed trade pressure from the United States on Friday, as Washington said the bloc was enabling Chinese evasion of US tariffs and stepped up calls for it to roll back flagship green rules on businesses.

 

Washington's ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, called on the bloc to "align" the provisions of two landmark new laws on environmental and human rights supply chain standards with the EU-US trade deal struck last year.

"Now it's time for the EU to deliver," Puzder posted on X, along with a US government document detailing a long list of "concerns" with the rules.

"The United States will take any actions necessary to address unreasonable burdens on US commerce absent a solution that addresses these concerns," the document warned.

Responding to Puzder's message, European Commission spokesperson Arianna Podesta said the EU continued to "exchange on both tariff and non-tariff issues" with the United States, calling the process "constructive."

But she added: "We have been very clear and consistent on the fact that neither our rules framework nor our regulatory autonomy are up for negotiation."

The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) requires large companies to fix the "adverse human rights and environmental impacts" of their supply chains worldwide, while the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) requires them to provide information on their climate impact and emissions and steps to limit them.

"The directives' extraterritorial reach and costly and onerous supply chain due diligence obligations will adversely impact the ability of US businesses to compete on a level playing field in the EU market," read the US document.

The EU has already dialled back the scope of both laws under pressure from businesses both inside and outside the bloc, delaying implementation and sparing smaller firms, but the US document said that did not go far enough.

Puzder's comments came a day after he hit out at the bloc's carbon border tax, CBAM, which he charged was "a tariff in substance, no matter the 'climate policy' label."

Separately, the EU was among dozens of trading partners flagged in a White House report on Thursday as risks regarding "illegal transshipment" from China, where goods are sent through third countries to avoid paying sweeping levies imposed by President Donald Trump.

US President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the Trump Turnberry golf course in Scotland, 27 July, 2025 AP Photo

The report, which also targeted Mexico, Canada and Japan, vowed to tap artificial intelligence to help detect illegal practices in future.

"The EU shares the US objective of tackling customs fraud," the commission spokesperson said in response to the accusations.

Podesta said Brussels was "engaging" with Washington to better understand the report's "potential implications for the EU," while noting that the document found the EU transshipment risk to be "embedded within broad legitimate trade flows."

World.title: Jason Arday, former Cambridge University professor at centre of plagiarism scandal, found dead at home
World.content:
Jason Arday, the former Cambridge University professor at the centre of a plagiarism scandal, has been found dead at his home in Battersea, UK media reported on Friday.

 

Arday resigned from his post at Cambridge University last week shortly after the prestigious British institution announced a probe into the various accusations against him.

He made headlines when the university appointed him as its youngest black professor in 2023 but he since faced snowballing claims he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis.

Questions also emerged about some of his stated achievements, with Arday and his defenders claiming racism had motivated parts of the scrutiny.

In a letter posted online, he said that quitting was "the only way" to end a "difficult period," but insisted the decision should not be "mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

"It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure," he wrote.

Arday said he was resigning from his positions as a Cambridge sociology of education professor and a fellow at the university's Jesus College, with "immediate effect."

The university had robustly defended Arday in June, claiming "a vile campaign to undermine his credibility" and insisting plagiarism claims regarding his "thesis and journal publications" had been probed and dismissed by "the relevant institution" and journals.

This is a developing story and our journalists are working on further updates.

World.title: Russia admits new petrol shortages amid ongoing long-range Ukrainian strikes
World.content:
Russian authorities acknowledged on Friday that some regions face new petrol shortages, as Ukraine steps up attacks on the country's oil refineries.

 

Ukraine has been targeting Russia's energy sites with drones and missiles for months, hoping to hit a vital source of revenue for the Russian army.

Russia has shut down one major refinery at Orsk, around 1,300 kilometres from the front line, for six months after it was attacked this week.

"The situation remains tense in several regions of the country regarding fuel supplies to service stations," the government said in a social media post.

Oil companies are "taking the necessary measures to increase deliveries to the most vulnerable regions," according to the statement.

It said a government meeting had been held on the shortages and the Deputy Prime Minister responsible for energy, Alexander Novak, has ordered that fuel prices be monitored.

Companies and car drivers have suffered repeat shortages in recent months because of the conflict.

Vehicles line up at a Rosneft gas station in Moscow, 29 June, 2026 AP Photo

Nearly every Russian region has at some point had to limit fuel sales or impose other kinds of rationing, such as banning the filling of jerry cans.

The Krasnodar region on the Black Sea, known for its tourist beaches, has been one of the worst hit.

"The situation regarding petrol supplies at service stations has become complicated," regional governor Venyamin Kondratyev said.

Oil companies "have again started imposing restrictions on the amount of fuel supplied and reduced service station opening hours," he added.

"This is causing concern among the region's residents and visitors," the governor added, stating that he had asked the authorities to send more fuel.

The governor of the Orenburg region, where the Orsk refinery is located, said on Thursday it had been shut down and repairs would take months.

Russian President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow, 14 August, 2026 AP Photo

Rare admission

Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged for the first time in June that his country was facing a “certain deficit” of fuel.

Speaking at a meeting with officials that focused on the fuel situation, Putin admitted that the country was “going through a difficult period,” but insisted that Moscow would “honour all its social obligations.”

Shortly after, he told state TV that the country's arms industries will quickly ramp up production of air defence systems to fend off Ukrainian attacks.

Claiming the issues that arise are not critical, Putin also said that Russia will import more fuel and speed up repair works at oil facilities to end the “temporary deficit.”

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has referred to strikes on Russian energy sites deep inside Russia as “long-range sanctions.”

World.title: Luigi Mangione admits shooting healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York court
World.content:
Luigi Mangione admitted on Friday to gunning down UnitedHealthCare chief executive Brian Thompson, as he appeared in US federal court to change his plea to guilty.

 

"On the morning of December 4, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione told a federal judge.

Mangione also pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges, admitting matter-of-factly that he trailed the executive to an investor conference in 2024 and gunned him down in the street.

Mangione, 28, said he even used a ruse to glean information about the event, contacting the health insurance company ahead of time under the guise of being an investor at a multibillion-dollar firm.

Mangione is set for sentencing 18 December. When US District Judge Margaret M. Garnett asked whether he understood that he could spend the rest of his life in prison, Mangione answered neutrally: “Yes.”

Mangione entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court, resolving one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s death.

Luigi Mangione appears for a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan Criminal Court in New York, 11 August, 2026 AP Photo

Mangione's lawyers are now seeking to have his separate New York state murder case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.

“Mr. Mangione has accepted full responsibility for the death of Brian Thompson,” defence lawyer Karen Friedman said outside the court, arguing that her client shouldn't face two prosecutions over a “single tragic event.”

Surveillance video of the ambush showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson, 50, from behind.

Police say “delay, deny, depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims.

That detail and revelations that Mangione's private writings lambasted health insurers as greedy, according to authorities, made the case a fulcrum for debate about the industry and made Mangione a celebrity for some of its critics.

Stickers are displayed on a pole in front of Manhattan federal court on the day of a hearing for Luigi Mangione, 14 August, 2026 AP Photo

Mangione told the court on Friday that he pursued Thompson “after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system.”

Mangione was never a UnitedHealthcare customer, according to police and the company.

A University of Pennsylvania graduate from a wealthy Maryland family, he was arrested five days after the shooting, when he was spotted at a McDonald’s in Pennsylvania.

Thompson led one of the United States' largest health insurers, but he wasn’t well known outside the industry.

Trained as an accountant, he had worked at parent company UnitedHealth Group Inc. for 20 years and became CEO of its insurance arm, UnitedHealthcare, in 2021. He and his wife have two sons, who were in high school when their father was killed.

Both the federal and state cases could lead to a life prison sentence for Mangione. A federal judge earlier this year tossed out additional charges that could have exposed him to a potential death penalty.

Mangione had complained about the prospect of two trials, telling a judge in February: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any commonsense definition.”

Under New York law, a state prosecution could potentially be barred if the federal case is resolved first.

The state’s double jeopardy protections kick in if a jury has been sworn in a prior prosecution, such as a federal case, or if that prosecution ends in a guilty plea. Mangione’s cases involve different charges arising from the same course of conduct.

In a letter last month, state prosecutors objected to the possibility of a guilty plea in the federal case wiping out the state case.

Members of the media wait in line outside of Manhattan Federal Court on the day of a hearing for Luigi Mangione, 14 August, 2026 AP Photo

Garnett has delivered some setbacks to the defence, including ruling in January that prosecutors could use items collected from Mangione’s backpack during his arrest as evidence against him.

They included a 3D-printed pistol that investigators said matched the one used to kill Thompson and a notebook in which authorities say Mangione described his intent to kill an insurance executive.

In June, Mangione’s lawyers said they would pursue a psychiatric defence in the state case but reversed course a day later.

The defence, involving claims that he was suffering from extreme emotional disturbance at the time of the killing, isn’t allowed in federal court.

World.title: Italian police recover stolen Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse artworks worth millions
World.content:
Paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth over $10.4 million (€8.9 million) which were stolen from an Italian museum in March have been recovered, Italian police said on Friday.

 

The paintings were taken by thieves from the villa of the Magnani-Rocca Foundation, near Parma in northern Italy, in a heist that lasted under three minutes.

Parma chief of police Andrea Pagliaro said the investigation centred around a gang of nine Moldovan suspects.

Five are accused of carrying out the theft, he said.

Video footage released by police showed two thieves wearing headlamps and with their faces covered entering the villa by breaking through a window.

They headed straight into a room where the three paintings hung and took them off the wall, before heading back to the window and passing them through to an accomplice waiting outside.

Italian newspapers carry the news of the heist of three paintings from a museum near Parma, 30 March, 2026 AP Photo

They made off with "Fish" by Auguste Renoir, "Still Life with Cherries" by Paul Cézanne and "Odalisque on the Terrace" by Henri Matisse.

The Renoir is worth €3 million, the Cézanne €6 million and the Matisse around €20,000, police said.

The paintings were recovered at the house of one of the suspects, police chief Pagliaro told the AFP news agency.

The Magnani-Rocca Foundation, 20 kilometres from Parma, houses the collection of art historian Luigi Magnani, which also includes works by Durer, Rubens, Van Dyck, Goya and Monet.

The theft is the latest in a series of robberies targeting European museums.

Last October, thieves broke into the Louvre in Paris in broad daylight, escaping in less than eight minutes with jewellery worth €88 million.

World.title: US backs Japanese sovereignty over disputed islands after Putin visit
World.content:
The United States has backed Japan's sovereignty over four islands controlled by Russia after Vladimir Putin became the first Russian president in 15 years to visit the disputed territory, prompting Tokyo to summon Moscow's ambassador and describe the trip as "absolutely unacceptable."

 

"The United States remains unwavering in its support of its most important ally and in its recognition of Japanese sovereignty over the Northern Territories," the US ambassador to Tokyo George Glass said on X.

"At a time when the US-Japan alliance is dedicated to cultivating prosperity across the Indo-Pacific, we strongly oppose any action that undermines its peace and stability," Glass added.

Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by the four southernmost islands in a volcanic chain off the coast of Hokkaido seized by the Soviet Union following an invasion in August 1945, in the final days of World War II.

Moscow broke its formal neutrality with Japan just days before the invasion.

The Japanese government maintains that the four islands and groups of islets that make up the Northern Territories — Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and Habomai — are part of its territory that the Soviets illegally occupied and Russia has continued to occupy since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.

The dispute has kept the two countries from signing a peace treaty that would formally end their hostilities. They terminated the state of war in 1956.

Moscow has reinforced its military presence on the islands as recently as December 2021, when it deployed Bastion coastal defence missile systems on an uninhabited volcanic island in the middle of the chain.

FILE: Bastion missile launchers move to their positions on the disputed island chain near Japan, 21 December 2021 AP Photo

The island hosted a Japanese army base prior to the Soviet occupation. A Soviet base there was shut down amid funding shortages in the wake of the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Moscow previously deployed Bal and Bastion missile systems on two of the four southernmost islands in 2016.

In the following years, Moscow further beefed up its arsenal on the islands by sending top-of-the-line air defence missile systems, setting up an air base on Etorofu Island, and deploying fighter jets.

The sparsely inhabited islands are strategically significant to the Kremlin as they sit at the entrance to the Sea of Okhotsk and give Russia's Pacific Fleet access to the open Pacific without passing through Japanese-controlled waters.

Putin's visit was the first by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.

'Absolutely unacceptable'

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters "the Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory, both historically and under international law."

Putin's visit "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable," she added.

Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said his country “strongly protests” Putin's visit to the largest of the islands, Etorofu.

“The Northern Territories, including Etorofu Island, are Japan’s inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law,” Motegi said in a statement.

He summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to the ministry in Tokyo and lodged a strong protest over the visit, requesting that he "promptly report the message back to Moscow,” the minister told reporters afterwards.

FILE: Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks during a news conference at the prime minister's office in Tokyo, 18 February 2026 AP Photo

Russia's embassy in Japan said the ambassador reiterated Moscow's claim that the islands are part of Russia and that Putin's trip there was not "a matter for discussion with foreign states".

The Kremlin boasted about the visit by posting a video of Putin on one of the four main islands. Russian state-run media said he had visited a fish-processing plant and showed him trying local caviar.

Takaichi said the visit was a further blow to the already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.

Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

It also placed export controls on technology with military applications and provided financial support to Ukraine. Russia responded by designating Japan an "unfriendly state".

Tokyo is now considering strengthening those sanctions as part of its countermeasures in response to Putin's trip.

“We must say this visit has further hardened Japanese public sentiment toward Russia and has made it more difficult to restore bilateral relations in the medium to long term,” she said.

“We hope the Russian side fully understands the seriousness of this.”

World.title: The rise of 'conscious' festivals, where music, spirituality and nature meet
World.content:
The Medicine Festival brings together more than 10,000 people in the United Kingdom for four days of music, ceremony, spirituality and environmental activism.

 

The festival in Berkshire reflects a growing interest in alternative ways of connecting with oneself, others and nature.

The sixth edition of the festival features a full programme of events, including concerts, yoga classes, ways of exploring movement and spiritual awareness and traditional ceremonies.

Main stage at Medicine Festival. Berkshire, United Kingdom. Ana Torres

Many Europeans have crossed the border to attend. Ayla, from the Netherlands has come to the festival for the first time.

“What I like about Medicine is the sharing of wisdoms. I hope I get out of here inspired, rested and motivated as well," she told Euronews.

In Europe and around the world, there is a growing interest in "conscious festivals" such as Medicine, which encourage people to explore their inner self, reconnect with nature and create a sense of community.

“We see ourselves as part of nature," explains Joshua Dugdale, Co-Founder of the Festival.

Jamming session at Medicine Festival. Berkshire, United Kingdom. Ana Torres

“We promote the medicine of dance, the medicine of music, the medicine of community, but also seeing people who have maybe a different world view and engaging with that, learning new skills, understanding new ways of seeing the world, we would call it a sacred festival”.

To date, the Medicine Festival has donated over one hundred thousand euros to support the environment and indigenous communities.
