The government's Yusril Ihza Mahendra said the state did not "reduce a person's constitutional rights because of their sexual orientation and gender identity".

Trans women part of Indonesia's history

Sonny Sudarma won Jakarta's inaugural beauty contest for transgender women in 1969. (Supplied: The Antara Photography Archives)

The attack on trans women comes despite the LGBTQIA+ community long being part of Indonesia's social fabric.

Benjamin Hegarty, an anthropologist with expertise in queer theory and transgender studies, said people who might now be understood as trans had been documented across the archipelago for centuries.

"Trans people have always been there," he said.

"They've always been in Indonesia in one form or another, stretching back many, many years … to the pre-colonial period."

Benjamin Hegarty says trans people are part of Indonesian history and society. (Supplied)

Dr Hegarty said colonial observations from the 19th century documented how people now understood to be trans women were part of life in the markets and at theatres.

"The Indonesian context appeared to be one where there was greater tolerance … of trans women in public space across that period, especially compared to Europe," Dr Hegarty said.

However, in the late 1940s and early 1950s, Dr Hegarty said press reports associated trans women with the streets at night, prostitution and public nuisance.

Despite that, by the 1990s trans women began to emerge and be embraced in popular entertainment industries in Indonesia.

Trans women and gender-nonconforming performers became familiar faces across stage shows, comedy, film and television, from the Fantastic Dolls and Dorce Gamalama to figures such as Ade Juwita and Tata Dado.

Dorce Gamalama became one of Indonesia's most prominent trans celebrities. (Instagram: @dg_kcp)

But while well-known trans women enjoyed greater acceptance, street-based trans women did not, Dr Hegarty said.

Professor Marzuki warned that violence could also become more severe as three factors overlapped: labelling of LGBTQIA+ people as a threat, mobilisation of vigilante groups and weak law enforcement.

"When those three elements come together, violence can escalate very quickly," he said.

Mr Gonzales, from Pelangi Nusantara, said he feared violence against vulnerable groups would increasingly be seen as "normal" if the attacks continued.

"The government has an obligation to protect all of its citizens without exception," he said.

" We do not want to wait until a trans woman dies before everyone takes this seriously. "

World.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the UAE are looking to Africa
World.content:
The European official smiled intently and asked a rather surprising question: "Have you been thinking about Djibouti?"

It was 2017 and there was a certain frisson of alarm going around the world about China and its ambitions for global power.

There was certainly alarm in Australia at a regional level: the South China Sea; China's massive 'Belt and Road' Investment spending initiative across the Pacific and the wider region.

And there was alarm across Europe too, where the Poles found themselves at the junction point for a Chinese-funded railway across Central Asia; where the Germans pointed out that Berlin is closer to Beijing than Sydney; and where a newly elected French president, Emmanuel Macron, was attempting to lift and expand French ambitions in foreign policy.

All reasons why all roads led to Djibouti. Or, more correctly, why all undersea cables led to the small kingdom on the north-east coast of the Horn of Africa.

Between 10 and 12 international cables land in Djibouti, making it a critical digital hub connecting Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

From about 2013 onwards, Chinese state-owned enterprises began making huge investments in local ports and infrastructure in the tiny Republic. By 2017 it had opened a significant military base there — following the French (the former colonial power) and then, post 9/11, the Americans.

It's not just the submarine cables that make Djibouti such a crucial location. It sits on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow stretch of water linking the Suez Canal, Red Sea and Indian Ocean — which daily threatens to come more into play as the deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz continues.

The Iran-backed Houthis, who live on the other side of the strait in Yemen, announced on July 20 that they were imposing a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, and there is anxiety that they might try to impose a total blockade on Bab el-Mandeb.

Which is why the rapidly changing geopolitics of the region have to be seen in a wider context than just the conflict between the US and Israel and Iran.

The "Bab el-Mandeb" Strait means, quite literally "the gate of tears" in Arabic. (Reuters: Nasa Worldview/Handout)

A new maritime alliance

Another party that had spoken recently of building a military facility in Djibouti is Saudi Arabia. Given it has been getting around the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz by shipping oil to its western coastline on the Red Sea, it has a particular current interest in that shipping route staying open.

But rather than proceed with the military base, Saudi has now pivoted to establishing a 13-country maritime alliance to safeguard security in the Red Sea which includes Pakistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Somalia and Yemen.

Unpacking a NATO-like defence pact A NATO-like defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan has landed like a stone thrown into an already rippling Middle East pool.

Turkiye this week confirmed it was also joining the alliance — a move which follows the announcement of the collective security obligations agreed to earlier this month in the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi, Pakistan and Turkiye.

While early analysis of the Mecca deal focused very much on what it meant for conflict with Iran, the collective actions of this group in keeping shipping moving in and out of the Red Sea will be the first real test of the arrangement.

But the testing of the new alliances in the Red Sea also shifts the focus of all these countries' interests — and those of others in the region — to Africa more broadly.

We don't hear much about Africa in Australia, unless its humanitarian crisis or a civil war.

But even in states which are seemingly failures, there has been the most extraordinary surge of investment and commitment by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkiye. It is no longer just a battleground for influence between China and Russia.

There has been a surge of investment and commitment to Africa by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkiye.

A new 'Scramble for Africa'

There is a new Scramble for Africa of sorts going on: not like the period of invasion and colonisation of its earlier namesake in the lead up to World War I but a tussle for footprints in infrastructure which is at least in part driven by estimates that Africa could be home to around 15 per cent of the world's rare earths.

What makes this particularly fascinating is that African nations are getting better at extracting outcomes from all this investment — for example, in the form of higher revenues, or commitments to manufacturing.

Global Policy Institute analyst Bob Savic notes that "nations like the Democratic Republic of the Congo which controls more than 70 per cent of global cobalt production, have instituted 'super-profit' taxes, while Zambia has repeatedly raised its mining levies".

"Zimbabwe has rapidly followed suit, banning exports of raw lithium — a mineral critical for electric vehicle (EV) batteries — in a bid to end the export of wealth in unprocessed form," he says.

"Across the continent more broadly, governments have increasingly embraced resource-nationalist measures."

Saudi Arabia has pledged over $41 billion in investments in industrial zones, development finance and export credits with African nations.

While it is heavily focused on the Red Sea and Horn of Africa, it has also been buying arable land for food production across East and West Africa as well as contracts for copper, cobalt and lithium.

Turkiye, meanwhile has also dramatically expanded its footprint across Africa, both through a massively expanded diplomatic footprint, new air routes, an eight fold increase in trade, (particularly driven by defence exports) and in infrastructure investments. It has also intervened in the past six years in conflicts in Libya; in confronting piracy off the coast of Somalia and to secure mining infrastructure in Niger.

But both these countries' investments, and interests, are dwarfed by the effort put into Africa by the United Arab Emirates.

Loading

UAE's massive African investment

The Financial Times reported last week that by since 2017, the UAE has announced "investments worth upwards of $US168bn [$237bn]" in Africa.

"The UAE's projection of power spans the continent, ranging from ports to green energy projects to industrial-scale farms," the FT wrote.

The massive state-owned logistical company DP World now operates or is developing ports, inland terminals and free zones in 13 African countries.

Houthis attack Red Sea cargo ship, sources say A small cargo ship was attacked by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, sources say.

The FT says the UAE "has leased millions of hectares of agricultural land to bolster food security".

"It has acquired mining rights from DR Congo to Guinea to secure critical minerals for the energy transition and for its burgeoning defence sector. "

However, it notes "that engagement also comes at a price".

"The UAE is creating a complex system of commercial, industrial and military entanglements that sometimes reinforce but also undermine the sovereignty of fragile states — most notably in war-torn Sudan," the paper reported.

While Saudi Arabia is enmeshed in the conflict with the Houthis in its southern neighbour Yemen, the UAE's presence in the horrific war in Sudan is particularly troublesome.

The Emiratis categorically deny all claims of providing military, financial, or operational support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan — one of the two militia groups that have been fighting a civil war for control of Sudan.

But it is regularly accused of doing so, backed by analysis from intelligence agencies and human rights groups, and the RSF is also accused of committing documented war crimes on a vast scale.

The expansion of strategic ambitions by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the UAE into Africa, with the added factor of competition for rare earths, gives us another example of just how quickly global forces are shifting.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: What dozens of empty chairs revealed about Australia's racism inquiry
World.content:
A family who are alive only because a bomb that landed at their feet didn't explode.

An Olympian forced out of the sport that changed her life after being belittled and bullied.

A mother questioning whether sending her children to school is doing them more harm than good.

An elder who is too scared to gather with community in public after another attempt on their lives.

This is just some of the harrowing testimony given at the inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at First Nations people.

Day after day, witnesses relived some of the darkest moments of their lives. Some spoke of violence. Others of fear, humiliation, and grief. Many did so publicly, knowing the personal cost, like former Olympic boxer Marissa Williamson-Pohlman.

"Institutions celebrate Blak excellence when it is convenient, but abandon us when it matters most," Williamson-Pohlman told the inquiry.

"I wonder where my energy would go … if not so much time was spent with me fighting the very system that was created to 'support' me and make my dreams come true."

Her story was one of many detailing personal and systemic harm through racism, but many of those invited to listen, explain, or respond never appeared.

The inquiry drew heavy hitters, including a former federal minister, lawyers, professors, land councils, and policy advocates, but in many places the absences were just as notable as those who attended.

Dozens of politicians, government officials, and national powerbrokers were asked to attend each hearing.

Most didn't show up.

Victorian Senator Jana Stewart has described the NT government's absence from the inquiry's public hearings as "disappointing" and a "missed opportunity". (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Inquiries are not just for fact-finding

"It's disappointing. I think the public expectation would be if you are a big organisation, if you are a government service, that you front up to inquiries like this and you are accountable," Senator Jana Stewart told me in between sessions in Melbourne.

"I think the least they could do is show up."

As the senator put it, attendance matters because parliamentary inquiries are not merely fact-finding exercises. They are one of the few opportunities for people with little institutional power to speak directly to those who hold it.

The hearings make for hard listening, with First Nations people speaking plainly about the racism, violence, and abuse they suffer on a daily basis.

Now that the hearings have wrapped up, the weight of expectation is palpable, but the reality of repeated disappointments looms large, as Arrernte woman and chief executive of the peak body for Aboriginal and Islander childcare Catherine Liddle put it.

"I'm here because the story of racism is one of harm. It's a story of hate, it's a story of unfathomable damage — and it's a story that we can change," Liddle told the inquiry.

"Racism is pervasive and it always will be until we front up to reality."

Hanging over the inquiry is a thorny question: how can this process make change, when so many change makers didn't turn up?

Renae Isaacs-Guthridge told the inquiry the bomb landed at the feet of her, her daughter and her daughter's friends. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

A tale of two inquiries

Running in parallel to the national parliamentary inquiry has been the royal commission into antisemitism, stood up in the wake of the Bondi terror attack.

Like the royal commission, the First Nations racism inquiry came on the heels of an alleged terror attack.

A fragment bomb, filled with ball bearings and screws, was lobbed into a crowd of Indigenous people on January 26th.

It is not hard to imagine what would have happened had it exploded as intended, something Noongar and Yamatji woman Renae Isaacs-Guthridge has thought about often.

Threats lead First Nations journalists to leave Former Today show presenter Brooke Boney has told the federal racism inquiry she was forced to leave the media industry after receiving "menacing" threats, including the doxxing of her email and home address.

"We should be dead because it landed right in front of us," Isaacs-Guthridge told the hearing in Perth.

The trauma of a near death experience, was compounded by what she described as antipathy from leaders, police, and the media.

"In the days and weeks that followed, as we found out it was a confirmed terrorist attack on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and our allies … there was a distinct pattern of people who said absolutely nothing," Isaacs-Guthridge said.

"I believe because we were an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander crowd, there is an underlying hate against us and so we're not taken as seriously."

Those sentiments have been echoed across the country as the inquiry travelled, with little acknowledgement outside the hearings themselves.

"We are First Peoples, where is the love and respect for us?" Aunty Muriel Bamblett asked in Melbourne.

Comparisons with the reach and scale of the antisemitism royal commission were unavoidable, despite warnings that measuring the pain of one community against another does little to address the root cause of racism.

"Why is antisemitism put on a pedestal compared to racial discrimination?" Biboolmirn Yorga woman Corina Abraham asked the inquiry in Perth.

"What about what First Nations people of our country go through? Why are we still down below?"

Ken Wyatt told the inquiry he wants national cabinet to give the same weight to its findings as to the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, set up in the wake of the Bondi terror attack. (ABC News: Dana Morse )

Failed referendum raises new problems

The silence that surrounds the Indigenous experience of racism and hatred from the broader community was noted by many, including inquiry chair Jana Stewart.

"We've certainly heard through lots of the evidence… the experiences of First Nations people aren't elevated or aren't talked about with the same level of importance as other parts of our community," Stewart told me.

"You can see that playing out probably in the experience of this inquiry as well."

But there are those who see the simultaneous inquiries as a built-in accountability system, like former federal minister Ken Wyatt.

"I suspect out of [the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion] will come a number of recommendations to do with changing attitudes and racist behaviour towards the Jewish community of Australia," he told me after he gave evidence in Perth.

"If we're prepared to do that, then we need to put just as much effort and energy into addressing racism that is faced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country. They are the First Peoples of the nation."

The existence of two separate inquiries into hatred directed at minority communities has prompted broader questions about the state of social cohesion in Australia, and what has led the nation to this point.

Some have pointed to the example set by politicians, with many years of culture wars and populist politics souring national discourse.

The referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament was described by many as "lifting the lid" on racism directed at First Nations people, as Apunipima Cape York Health Council Chief Executive Deborah Malthouse told the inquiry in Cairns.

"The outcome of the Voice to Parliament appears to have given mainstream Australians permission to be overtly racist," Malthouse said.

"Those who would otherwise stay hidden now have the courage to share their racist views openly and widely under the belief that their actions are unlikely to be challenged by wider society."

Loading

Great expectations

A Wemba Wemba and Mutthi Mutthi woman, senator Stewart is acutely aware of where the inquiry she is leading may go.

"I do not want to see another report gather dust on a shelf," Stewart told me during one of the hearings in Darwin.

"I think that it absolutely should be acted on with a sense of urgency that people have asked us to in this process."

Many previous inquiries, including a national report on racist violence, the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody, and the Bringing Them Home report, all laid out plans to make Australia a better, safer, more reconciled place for First Nations people.

But after three decades, most of the recommendations put forward have been ignored, or in some cases explicitly acted against.

Outcomes are also on the minds of those who gave evidence, like Minang-Goreng Noongar elder Dr Jim Morrison.

Federal inquiry hears of entrenched racism Aboriginal community-controlled organisations have told the federal racism inquiry that racial bias on the part of child protection workers and police is harming First Nations women and children.

"This committees recommendations risk becoming another report that acknowledges harm without addressing it," Morrison said.

"We urge the committee to ensure its recommendations translate into funded, practical action, direct investment in community-controlled truth-telling and healing infrastructures, not another report that sits alongside the many that have come before it."

Last week, in one of the final sessions, Yorta Yorta elder Monica Morgan gave detailed evidence on her landmark case that proved she had been racially vilified — the first Indigenous person to win such a case in Victoria.

She then had a question for the committee.

"What is going to happen as a result of your inquiry? Will there be change?" Morgan asked.

"We hope so, absolutely," Stewart replied.

"We hope that recommendations and evidence given to this process and through this committee is honoured with action."

The survivors who gave evidence have now gone home, but their stories sit in the parliamentary records, proof that we cannot say we didn't know.

The question is whether those empty chairs will remain a symbol of indifference, or whether those who left them vacant will act on the inquiry's final report.

World.title: Sean Dorney was a roaming ABC reporter. Now, just getting out of bed is a struggle
World.content:
Sean Dorney was a familiar face on Australian TV screens for three decades.

Sean Dorney was the ABC's first PNG correspondent and spent decades reporting from across the Pacific.

As the ABC's long-time correspondent for the Pacific, he covered coups, elections and conflict.

These days the news for Sean isn't good.

Sean now needs assistance with most tasks. ( )

Like nearly 100,000 other Australians, he's waiting on an assessment for aged-care funding. It could mean the difference between staying in his home or going into an aged-care facility.

Sean's world changed dramatically about 10 years ago when he was diagnosed with motor neurone disease.

Though the disease's progression has been slow, Sean is now largely confined to his Brisbane home. He can still move his head and neck, but is slowly losing the ability to control his fingers, and with that, the touchscreen of his phone.

Sean, now 76, was diagnosed with motor neurone disease 10 years ago. ( )

"Motor neurone disease is not very pretty. I need a lot of help to do almost everything," Sean says.

In the mornings it's Sean's 69-year-old wife Pauline who must lift him out of bed into a wheelchair.

Pauline pulls Sean up from his bed. ( )

Sean no longer has use of his arms or legs. ( )

Loading...

Showering, dressing, meals. Most of the week it's up to Pauline.

"I'm exceptionally fortunate I've got the wife I have," Sean says.

Sean and Pauline, a fellow broadcaster, met in Papua New Guinea in 1975, and married the following year.

"I was extremely attracted to her and she wasn't so attracted to me," Sean says with a chuckle. "I wore her down in the end."

Pauline Dorney. ( )

Sean missed out on NDIS funding because he was too old when diagnosed, meaning he relies on funding from the aged-care system to keep him at home.

Had he qualified for the NDIS, Sean could have received three times as much funding as the maximum under aged care.

Sean's aged-care budget can only afford six hours of care a week because he needs two carers at a time.

They come three mornings a week for two hours to shower, dress and feed him.

Carers shower Sean. ( )

Sean is dressed after showering. ( )

Sean can only afford to have carers come six hours a week. ( )

The rest of the time it falls to Pauline, who admits it's getting harder.

"That constant sort of routine of showering, dressing, it's a lot of work," she says.

"The time will come when I'm going to need night care as well because I'm doing all the night care and there's times when it's really exhausting."

Sean had been on the top level of funding, about $65,500 a year, but last year's Support at Home reforms mean a higher level, just over $80,100 a year, is now available.

Pauline says the extra funds could help to pay for carers to come two extra mornings a week, relieving her of the most taxing physical tasks.

To qualify, Sean first needs to be reassessed.

Eight months after calling to make an appointment, they're still waiting.

"The whole purpose of getting a reassessment is to allow there to be greater care so that Pauline gets a bit more help during the week for just everyday things to help me survive," Sean says.

Loading...

The couple isn't alone in their frustration.

There are 98,606 Australians waiting to be assessed, hoping for a government subsidy that can help them stay at home longer, rather than move into residential care.

The federal government partly privatised the assessment system late last year as part of its "once in a generation" reforms.

Contracts worth more than $1 billion were awarded to more than a dozen organisations — three of them owned by private equity — to do assessments in the home.

Assessments in hospitals are still the responsibility of teams attached to geriatric units.

Government figures show the median wait time for comprehensive assessments in the home is 36 days, down from 43 days in 2024-25.

Asked why someone would be waiting eight months, Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said there could be longer wait times due to "geographic distribution and availability of assessors".

"Where there are individual cases where people are waiting an unnecessarily long period of time, I'm always happy to follow them up personally," he said.

Sean and Pauline have been waiting eight months for an appointment. ( )

'If I go, he goes'

The fear for Sean is that if something happens to Pauline and she can no longer care for him, he will need to go into a residential aged care facility.

"That's not something I can say that I'm really looking forward to, but I think that's the inevitable thing if something does happen to her," he says.

Pauline puts socks on Sean. ( )

The couple fear if something happens to Pauline, Sean will need to go into a facility. ( )

Pauline says the work can be exhausting. ( )

Residential aged care costs taxpayers four times more than home care.

For someone to remain at home, the government subsidy averages less than $30,000 per person per year. That's compared with more than $117,000 in residential care.

"There is clearly an economic imperative to keep people aging at home," says Natalie Siegel-Brown, who recently resigned as the Inspector General of Aged Care.

"We are facing an urgent imperative to rethink the way we are administering this aged-care budget and supporting people to age in place."

Insiders who spoke to Four Corners as part of its investigation into the sector say their fear is that people waiting for Support at Home assessments can deteriorate and end up in hospital, putting more pressure on another part of the system.

There are close to 3,000 "stranded" patients in public hospitals around the country. These patients are too unwell to go home but are unable to secure a nursing home bed.

"This is absolutely a crisis," says geriatrician Chloe Furst, the medical director for acute and urgent care at the Royal Adelaide Hospital.

The Department of Health and Ageing estimates Australia needs 10,400 new aged care beds per year. In 2024-25, only 802 beds were added.

This year the federal government said it had committed to investing $1.7 billion to incentivise the construction of up to 5,000 new residential aged care beds a year across the country.

But Dr Furst says that doesn't address the long wait lists for assessment and Support at Home funding.

"We're still seeing that there are long delays to access home care and the home care that is provided is often not meeting the needs of the individual at question," Dr Furst says.

Pauline says the extra funds could help to pay for carers to come two extra mornings. ( )

Sean is no longer able to type but can play cards on his laptop. ( )

Asked whether budget constraints in Support at Home were pushing more people into hospitals and nursing homes, the federal minister acknowledged there was "more work to be done" despite increased investment.

"Investment in the aged care system has grown by 40 per cent since we were elected in 2022," Mr Rae said.

"We're seeing wait times coming down."

The government announced earlier this year that people with motor neurone disease (MND) would be classified as "urgent" and receive the Support at Home funding they had been approved for within a month.

However, people with MND are not fast-tracked for assessment, which has left Pauline and Sean waiting, counting the months, and hoping.

Sean says he's "exceptionally fortunate" to have Pauline. ( )

"I've been lucky so far with my health," Pauline says.

" But if I go, he goes. "

Watch Four Corners' full investigation The Waiting Game on Monday night from 8:30pm on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: What went wrong for the Suns this year and how 2027 can be much better
World.content:
Sometimes an essay is needed to describe what has happened on the footy field. Sometimes a book will only start to scratch the surface.

But sometimes a single word will do it best. As the Gold Coast Suns filtered off a frigid Manuka Oval after beating GWS, one word seemed to sum up the mood in a nutshell: Finally.

For the first time since May 15, the Suns had entered the winner's circle. At the time of their last win, the Suns sat fourth on the ladder, with many believing they were poised for a real shot at a deep finals run.

But as the weeks drew shorter and the nights colder, their hopes faded.

By the start of July, the hopes of a top-four finish had effectively vanished. Two weeks later, their finals hopes were on life support. By the end of the month, even the wildcard spots were taken off the table.

Damien Hardwick summed up the year via the slightly misheard words of one of the big four of American thrash metal.

"There's a great line by Metallica that I'm going to butcher, where 'sometimes you can see the light at the end of the tunnel, but it's a freight train coming the other way'. That's how it's felt this year. That's the reality of it," he said.

Despite the season being lost, both Hardwick and his playing staff were overjoyed with the win.

"It's been … it's been a while. The boys were really hungry for a win today and I thought we brought the spirit and it was great to sing that song again," Suns star Matt Rowell told ABC Sport after the win over GWS.

For one week, everything worked as it should for the side many thought to be a premiership contender. The win wasn't just one in isolation, it also practically ended the season for their Expansion Cup rivals the Giants.

For both sides, the hope is that a small slice of pain in 2026 will set them up for success in 2027. But to do so, there has to be an understanding of what exactly went wrong.

Hardwick's hard year with Gold Coast

Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.

It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks, there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after mentoring by a few others.

Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted, and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.

It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after a few others have mentored them.

Few coaches have been more highly credentialed in recent years than Hardwick. Beyond the three flags the Tigers won under his guidance, his impact across the league is clear.

While Hardwick served an apprenticeship under a more kick-mark style operator in Alistair Clarkson, his own method differed to that of former co-worker Chris Fagan. Instead, the influence of Hardwick is best seen through the defensive-first-yet-free-flowing styles exhibited by Collingwood and GWS under former Hardwick assistants Craig McRae and Adam Kingsley.

Hardwick's teams have an idiosyncratic stylistic footprint. Under his reign at Richmond, the Tigers overhauled teams with chaos, not control. The side often lost the marking battle but played surge football, running on adrenaline and enthusiasm. Instead of a side built on winning and scoring from clearances, their drive came from scoring on the intercept.

McRae and Kingsley, alongside West Coast's Andrew McQualter, have regularly influenced proceedings in September. The Hardwick school sits as a counterbalance to the way that sides such as Brisbane pick through defences by controlling the ball.

Despite being so influential to how football is played in 2026, Hardwick is quick to note that this may not have been his finest year.

"I feel I haven't had my best year as a coach with regard to bending a little bit of my system of how we want to play," he said. "So those realisations are very, very important. And these are the things that actually your greatest growth comes from."

In the wake of teams inspired by the control-heavy game styles influenced by Alistair Clarkson's Hawthorn sides, Tigerball was risky, dangerous and exciting.

All good coaches evolve over time. And all good "brands" are strategised against and countered. Football is not a solved game with a perfect way to play.

The developing Suns Hardwick inherited were quite different from the Tigers he left. Instead of building from a rock-solid counterattacking defensive unit, they led with the contested, stoppage game the premiership Tigers largely eschewed.

In 2025, Hardwick bent to accommodate both strands, leaning on rising stars Anderson, Rowell, Miller and Humphries to dominate in the middle and using Noble, Rioli and Jeffrey to provide drive on the counterattack.

There were clear parts of the game plan that held strong across both seasons. Gold Coast continued to lean on handball more than most and played into chaotic situations.

But the other part of the balance, that of the stoppage game, fell away.

Last year, the Suns finished +3.3 in clearance differential and third in the league for scoring differential from stoppages.

This year — with a group in flux with early season injuries to Matt Rowell and the incorporation of Christian Petracca — the Suns sit last for clearance differential and fourth-worst for stoppage scoring differential.

Notably, the win in Canberra came in one of the hardest, most contested games of the season. The game was cold, wet and physical and played largely at ground level. The sides combined for just 96 marks all day — about half of the average game this year.

"We love the wet weather footy, as you can tell, and I think it really suited us today," midfielder Bodhi Uwland told ABC Sport post-game.

ABC AFL Daily podcast Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron are joined by a rotating cast of AFL legends, including some of the sharpest minds in the game, to pull apart the biggest stories in Aussie Rules.

"We like being a contested team, that surge mentality, like getting the ball forward. And I think we really showed that today and we're able to really adapt to the conditions."

The Suns played for territory first and results later in Canberra. Despite dominating hitouts and clearances, the Giants still scored more from stoppage. But the high defensive wall that the Suns were able to establish helped the Suns re-enter the winner's circle.

Reigning Brownlow Medallist Rowell led the way for the Suns with one of the finest games imaginable in tough conditions. Despite the number of accolades he has already accumulated in his short career, the game may have been one of his best yet.

"That's one of the best performances I've seen from Rowell, to be honest, like, especially from behind the ball. Seeing him u-turning out of stoppage, shrugging tackles and just getting it forward … and he did it so consistently throughout the game. It was an amazing performance." Uwland said.

It wasn't just his teammates who were effusive about his effort.

"Yeah, he's a difference maker. It's a pleasure to have a guy like that in our footy club who, you see, the way the game plays today." Hardwick added.

"You know, it's 40-odd possessions, 22 contested, I think 18 tackles and 12 clearances as well. It's just one of those games you go, 'Wow'.

"You know, they're video game numbers, but he revels in those conditions. You know, that's the way he plays the game and it's such a pleasure to watch those players that give absolutely everything."

Rowell's preseason Origin injury threw the Suns' midfield balance off at the start of the season and left the side looking for what was their best look through the middle as the season developed. The Suns are blessed with highly capable players at the contest, with more bodies than opportunities most weeks.

The game in Canberra was a hint of what it could look like when it worked for the Suns.

Despite reports in the media of a loss of connection in recent weeks, at least in wake of the win the connection between coach and group seemed to be growing and evolving through the adversity.

"We haven't had the year we've wanted, but I think he's been really impressed by the way we've kept our spirit as a group," Rowell said.

"Even though we can't make finals, we've still got a lot of pride as a group. I think that really showed today. Yeah, Dimma's (Hardwick's) connection with the group is growing each game."

Suns keen to rise in 2027

In the wake of the Canberra game, attention for both sides turned, at least a little, to next season. The balance between running out a season where a premiership is an impossible task and preparing for the next one is a tough balance to strike for all teams.

"Yeah (2027 starts now). We have spoken about that. You look at Sydney — a great example from last year. You know, they had a disappointing year, much like we have this year, and they sort of went to work on some things. Look where they are now." Hardwick said after the game.

"That was our challenge. We spoke to the players about it. Noah and his leaders have just been absolutely leading the charge in that space."

Given how few competitive games there are each year, not a single one needs to be wasted. A flag is always the goal for each of the league's 18 clubs, even if it's not this year's.

Having shown the quality to win a final last year, Gold Coast's prospects of recovery look reasonably bright. Roughly half of the teams in the 18-team era to win a final then dip to double-digit ladder placings returned to finals the following year.

Most of the rest took two years to get back, with Melbourne and Collingwood grabbing the 2021 and 2023 flags. Most encouragingly, only three times since 2012 has a finals-winning team immediately crashed down the ladder and failed to recover at all.

These gap years have almost become routine as footy becomes ever more even and competitive. Almost every year since 2020, at least one side has found itself dipping and another recovering from such a dip.

The one slight pause for both the Suns and Giants is the relatively low placement of all four of the Hardwick-styled teams in 2026. Of the four, only McRae's Pies will play finals, entering via the wildcard round. As always, the question will be whether that style of play is conducive to winning football in 2026 and beyond, or whether the next evolution is upon us already.

Still, the Gold Coast list might be the most talented in the league. If they can get the strategic balance right, and a little luck to fall their way, the sky is the limit for this Suns group.

World.title: Luigi Mangione admits killing insurance CEO, asks to void state murder trial
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaCrime Luigi Mangione admits killing insurance CEO, asks to void state murder trial Michael Koziol Updated August 15, 2026 — 5:55am ,first published 2:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Luigi Mangione admitted to fatally shooting health insurance chief executive Brian Thompson, pleading guilty to federal charges and immediately filing to have his state murder trial voided under double jeopardy provisions. The 28-year-old told a federal courtroom in New York on Friday (US time): “On the morning of December 4, 2024, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan, and he died.” A courtroom sketch depicts Luigi Mangione sitting between his attorneys on August 14. AP He pleaded guilty to stalking the insurance executive resulting in death - serious charges that could result in a lifetime prison sentence, as US District Judge Margaret Garnett reminded him on Friday. The brazen crime, early in the morning on a midtown Manhattan street, shocked the world. It also generated sympathy for Mangione from parts of the community amid broader controversy over access to healthcare in America. For some people, he became something of a pin-up or political prisoner.



In court, Mangione said he researched details of UnitedHealthcare’s annual investor conference in December 2024 after suffering a broken back and navigating the health insurance system. He said he then used a 3-D printer to make part of a gun and travelled to New York with the intent of killing Thompson. There was no plea agreement, and federal prosecutors noted they were free to seek the maximum penalty under the law. Luigi Mangione’s lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said she immediately filed to have the state charges dismissed. Bloomberg Later, outside court, Mangione’s lawyer Karen Friedman Agnifilo told reporters she had immediately filed to have Mangione’s state charges - including second degree murder - voided under double jeopardy laws. “Mr Mangione has accepted full responsibility for the death of Brian Thompson,” she said. “He endured years of severe debilitating pain … He believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life.”



Agnifilo said her client had been unfairly treated since the outset, noting he successfully fought off terrorism charges and other federal charges that carried the death penalty. “It was a single tragic event, yet he is being prosecuted twice for the same conduct … New York law does not allow a person to be prosecuted and punished twice for the exact same crime.” Luigi Mangione appears for a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan Criminal Court in New York on August 11. Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post via AP New York district attorney Alvin Bragg is set to oppose Mangione’s attempt to void the state trial. Jury selection is due to begin on September 8, though it will likely be delayed. Garnett set sentencing on the federal charges for December 18. It was widely expected Mangione would plead guilty to the federal charges and attempt to have the state trial voided after prosecutors and the defence scheduled Friday’s unplanned hearing.



Thompson’s widow sat in the front row of the gallery with other members of his family, and there was a large media presence inside and outside court. Federal US attorney Jamie McDonald, whose office led the federal case against Mangione, told a news conference that there could be no justification for the actions the 28-year-old had admitted. US attorney Jamie McDonald said “there can be no celebrity in assassination”. Bloomberg Mangione prepared carefully, tracked Thompson’s whereabouts, conducted surveillance and used a silencer, McDonald said. After shooting twice at close range, he ran away and left his victim to die. “This was not a spontaneous act of violence. It was deliberate, calculated and premeditated,” McDonald said.



“The defendant committed this murder in an attempt to draw public attention to his dislike of certain businesses. But we live in a civilised society governed by the rule of law. We debate, we disagree, we protest. We do not commit murder. Related Article Crime Luigi Mangione is tipped to plead guilty to stalking. What does that mean for his murder trial? “No grievance, political belief or ideological cause can ever justify murder. There can be no celebrity in assassination. Any person who celebrates, encourages, or excuses actions like these is fundamentally wrong.” Mangione had previously pleaded not guilty to the federal charges, which at the time included murder and weapons offences carrying the death penalty. Those two were later dropped. Experts say it is legally complex whether Mangione will be able to escape a state murder trial. The key legal question is whether the offences are considered distinct enough to mean that double jeopardy provisions do not apply.



A man holds a sign outside Manhattan’s Federal Court. Inside, Luigi Mangione admitted to killing health insurance executive Brian Thompson. AP Photo/Ryan Murphy “It’s actually a pretty interesting legal question,” former New York prosecutor Berit Berger told this masthead ahead of Friday’s hearing. “New York’s a little different than other states. My guess is this will not preclude the New York case from going forward, but it’s a little bit more complicated.” New York has stronger protections for the defendant not to face dual proceedings than many states, Berger said. In most cases, these circumstances would at least delay the state trial, but the court would be under pressure not to delay it too long given the public interest, she said. World.title: The most underrated film of the 21st century? It’s nice, guys
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict The most underrated film of the 21st century? It’s nice, guys In this column, we deliver hot (and cold) takes on pop culture, judging whether a subject is overrated or underrated. Tom W. Clarke August 15, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The best film of 2016 was a stylish homage to old school Hollywood and a Los Angeles lost to time. A love letter to a type of movie they don’t make any more, brought to life with a brilliant original soundtrack, rapid-fire dialogue, and a star-studded cast led by Ryan Gosling. No, not La La Land. Ryan Gosling and Russell Crowe in The Nice Guys, a guaranteed fun time. Sydney Morning Herald It’s The Nice Guys, the criminally under-seen neo-noir comedy, starring Ryan Gosling and Russell Crowe. Unlike La La Land, it absolutely bombed at the box office, and unlike La La Land, it didn’t almost win best picture at the Oscars. However, it’s well overdue for a re-evaluation: this is the best cinematic comedy of the past 15 years, and the most underrated film of the 21st century. It has everything you could ever want in a movie: comedy, drama, action, mystery, amazing stunts, fun outfits, outlandish twists, endlessly quotable dialogue, and two of the most acclaimed male movie stars operating at the absolute height of their powers.



The Nice Guys is a story of private eye Holland March (Ryan Gosling) and enforcer-for-hire Jackson Healy (Russell Crowe) who reluctantly team up to investigate the disappearance of a young woman, Amelia (Margaret Qualley), getting hilariously lost in the seedy underbelly beneath the glamour of 1970s Los Angeles, and unwittingly stumbling into a massive web of conspiracy and corruption. Angourie Rice, then just 13 when she started filming, holds her own against Gosling and Crowe. As the writer of the Lethal Weapon films and Last Action Hero, and director of Kiss Kiss Bang Bang and Iron Man 3, Shane Black had established a reputation for tight, exciting scripts and upending the expectations of action movies. The Nice Guys is his masterpiece, taking the Shane Black experience to the mountaintop and riding a flaming dinner tray straight down it. The script crackles with the kind of dialogue that leaves you breathless, both from laughter and sheer pace. The labyrinthine mystery box plot is twisty enough for you to get lost in, without ever feeling stupider than our loveable protagonists. Gosling flexes his comic chops years before his himbo Ken, while Crowe is pure charisma as the gruff straight man. AP



And Black recreates old school LA as well as, if not better than, Tarantino’s Oscar-winning Once Upon a Time in Hollywood would a few years later. As our hapless investigators fumble their way around town, we are treated to a vivid dreamscape of the glitz and glamour of Hollywood’s elite, as well as its dirty, desperate backstages. The supporting cast is outstanding. Australia’s Angourie Rice has her breakout as the precocious Holly, more than holding her own against Hollywood heavyweights. Qualley stuns in just her second film, and the ever-enjoyable Matt Bomer shows up as a vicious assassin with an unfortunate haircut. Ultimately though, the film is elevated into true classic territory by the unlikely chemistry between Gosling and Crowe. The mystery is fun, the big set pieces are impressive, but it all takes a back seat to the sheer delight that is watching the two actors bicker like an old married couple as they fall through fences, crash cars, and barely avoid being murdered by assassins. Their dynamic is pure gold, in the vein of other unlikely buddy action-comedies like 1982’s 48 Hrs and 1988’s Midnight Run. Gosling, in a bad tie and glorious moustache, a cigarette dangling loosely from his lips like a part of his body he’s never used before, is so accident-prone and easily overwhelmed it’s hard to imagine a worse job for him than private investigator. Crowe, the straight man, a cynical bruiser whose heart is slowly cracked open, is a man who lets his fists do the talking out of preference rather than lack of intelligence.



Related Article Opinion

The Verdict Eight-episode seasons are ruining TV. Bring back the 22-episode binge Gyan Yankovich Lifestyle Editor Gosling finds the outer edges of his remarkable comedic chops, going for broke in every scene, throwing himself into prat falls and cartoonish sobs, and giving the first glimpse of the empty-headed himbo that would become his iconic role as Ken in Barbie. Bouncing off Gosling’s frantic, trembling energy is Crowe in the best performance of his career. As opposed to his award-winning and Very Serious turns in Gladiator and A Beautiful Mind, here his natural charisma shines through and he finds more layers than any of his previous Oscar bait ever did. Had it found a larger audience, it might be just as oft-quoted as the likes of Anchorman, Superbad and Step Brothers. Perhaps The Nice Guys is destined for a slower revelation, a cult hit that finds its audience years later, a la Office Space. Either way, it’s a guaranteed good time. World.title: Before he was Anthony Bourdain, he was a ‘young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking’
World.content:
Dominic Sessa stars in Tony, a film about the making of the man and myth that was Anthony Bourdain.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In Sydney, in Melbourne, in Boston and New York, haloed murals of “Saint Tony” – the beloved chef, writer and TV personality Anthony Bourdain – pay tribute to his rebellious spirit and moral integrity. On Instagram and Reddit threads, fans cite his quotes like ancient scriptures that hold the meaning of life: “Your body is not a temple, it’s an amusement park. Enjoy the ride.” After his tragic death in June 2018, aged 61, Bourdain’s mythical pull has only intensified. It’s amusing then that, in the face of such reverence, A24’s new film Tony beckons cinemagoers with an unsuspecting whisper: You love Anthony Bourdain? Come, let us tell you the story about when he was a young piece of crap. Dominic Sessa laughs mischievously at my summation. Before making the film, he couldn’t have picked Bourdain in a police lineup, anyway. “I know he means something important to so many people, but for me, I wasn’t a huge fan. He didn’t exist in my life the way he does for millions of people. And that was the reason I felt comfortable doing it,” says Sessa of taking on the role of a man who, even from the beyond, remains a daily household fixture in reruns of his hit TV series, No Reservations and Parts Unknown. Bourdain was 19 when he fled to Provincetown, about the same age as Sessa when he started working on Tony. Bob Gruen Tony is a film that could be subtitled “Bourdain: The Incel Years”. It takes the early chapters of Bourdain’s bestselling 2000 book Kitchen Confidential – mainly his evocative telling of absconding at 19 to Provincetown, off Cape Cod, where his kitchen journey began – and crafts an affecting coming-of-age tale. When we first meet Sessa’s Bourdain, he’s bloviating to college literary professors about his plans to update Orwell’s Down and Out in Paris and London. He stalks bars with a pair of nunchucks in his pants, hitting on sorority girls and bartenders with uncomfortable desperation. Painfully insecure, he lies and lies and lies. With the notch turned up slightly, he’d be Rick from The Young Ones.



You’d imagine this was an odd invention from writer-director Matt Johnson (in Johnson’s hands, even Bourdain’s infamous oyster awakening gets twisted towards shame), if it wasn’t all there in Bourdain’s own writing. From the beginning of his public profile, Bourdain never hid his demons and was quick to self-scrutiny. An “insider’s edition” of Kitchen Confidential, released in 2013 and featuring scribbled footnotes from the author, finds Bourdain furiously taking the piss out of sentences he’d written just over a decade before, fed up by a tone he now saw as pompous and self-important. The film revels in that disposition – the man on the way to the man – taking as its starting gun a quote from the same book where Bourdain summed up his own youthful (un)appeal. “I was a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive, and thoughtless young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking.” Sessa with director Matt Johnson on the set of Tony. A24 via AP In a culture struggling to salvage young men from the clutches of toxic masculinity, it’s a loaded launch. After #MeToo, Bourdain apologised for how Kitchen Confidential – full as it was with fighting and f—ing, as much as food – might have contributed to the era’s “boys will be boys” permissiveness. But in the film, he’s still a young scrub in search of a role model, latching onto mentors both bad (Leo Woodall’s drug-abusing, womanising line cook Sal) and good (Antonio Banderas’ wizened, zen-like Chef). For Sessa, this was the appropriate entry point. “I can’t relate to the Bourdain everyone knows, this guy who is writing novels and working in kitchens in a professional sense, but I can relate to being an impressionable young person with pessimistic views on the world and a sense of entitlement. I know what that feels like,” he says. “For the first time in his life, he saw like, ‘Wow, I can live my life this way? I can party and drink and do drugs and have sex and also make incredible food at the same time?’ It was in that excitement, at that moment of being opened up to this, where this person was formed.”



Sessa is speaking over Zoom from high above the Los Angeles skyline, in the office headquarters of film distribution darling, A24. The sun is beaming in LA, but with his mussy hair and sunken eyes – a ’70s character actor out of time – Sessa looks exhausted. Deep into the film’s press campaign, he’s been answering the same inane questions about his cooking skills for days. Well, he’s not getting a reprieve from me. How are his cooking skills now? “About the same,” he says. “I mean, I can shuck an oyster and I can sauté some vegetables. I know how to make a paella now, thanks to Antonio Banderas. Not an incredibly difficult thing, but it feels good. And I know how to hold a knife a little bit better, which is encouraging.” At 23, Sessa is only marginally older than Bourdain was when he took up the dishwashing job that set the path to his life in food. Born in New Jersey to a teacher mother and a father who worked in payroll (his father died when Sessa was 14), in tenth grade he earned a scholarship to the elite boarding school Deerfield Academy in Massachusetts to play ice hockey. When he broke his femur before his first season, he shifted his interest towards drama classes. He was still at school when he landed his first professional role in Alexander Payne’s The Holdovers, where he held his own against prime Paul Giamatti. “In the same way that Tony is in the movie, I’ve felt myself role-playing some sort of version of myself that I thought I had to be in order to be respected,” says Sessa. “When I was in high school, I put a lot of pressure on myself to seem smart and capable. But it wasn’t until I started acting that I was like, ‘Oh, I actually could be good at this in real life, not just in my head.’ Antonio Banderas plays Chef, a kind and disciplined mentor for young Bourdain. A24 via AP “That’s sort of the moment that Bourdain is having in this movie. For so much of it he’s telling people, ‘I’m good at writing, I’m going to be the next great American novelist’, but he has nothing to show for it. And then he has this experience working in a kitchen where he actually does something and gets better at it. He learns how to make a Lobster Thermidor! I think that’s pretty relatable for people. When you’re able to work with integrity and honesty, it changes your life. It happened for me and it happened for Bourdain, and I hope it encourages people to participate in voluntary hardships.”

World.title: It’s my first day with my new family, and I’m already running the show
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPets Opinion It’s my first day with my new family, and I’m already running the show Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist August 15, 2026 — 5:30am

August 15, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The diary of a dog, day 1: It’s my first day with my new family. I don’t even know my own name. They seem to call me all manner of things – Sweet Pea, Lovely One, and No Chewing. Actually, I think No Chewing must be my name, as it’s the thing they say to me most often. Maybe they’re Native American. Meanwhile, the female one oversees the food and does a nice line in chicken pieces. They are served during what she calls a “training session”. Every time I sit down, she gives me a small piece of chicken. By the end of day 1, the chicken is basically raining down on me. I’m running the show. I’m sitting down before she even says “sit”. It’s Pavlov’s dog, except I’m not the dog. All the same, I wonder if I could impress upon her the need for a better name. No way do I want to make my first appearance at the dog park and be introduced as “Our new puppy, No Chewing”. It’s time to say hello to Frank (aka “No Chewing”). Day 2: I’m now hearing the word “Frank” on high rotation. I have a funny feeling it may be my name. What exactly do they want me to be “frank” about? Perhaps that I love chewing!



The training continues to go well. I’ve moved on to demanding chicken by means of a “down”. I lie down, the woman says “down” about a millisecond later, and then I get chicken. It’s a reward for indolence, sure, but everyone seems happy with the arrangement. Maybe if I leapt onto a chaise lounge and started snoring, she’d give me the whole chicken. Day 3: I’ve been trying to help the male one with his wardrobe choices. I discovered, hanging on the back on his bedroom door, a flowery shirt that could be highly fashionable. It could be highly fashionable, if he were somewhat younger and somewhat thinner. By standing on my back legs, I managed to grab hold of the cuff and pull it to the ground. I then expressed the full fury of my fashionista feelings, at which point I feared my name had reverted to “No Chewing”. In the end the man took the destruction quite well, explaining that he hadn’t liked the shirt anyway. The female one had made him buy it. He then tickled me under the ears in a way I can only describe as “conspiratorial”. Day 4: The whole naming issue remains problematic. I now understand my name is Frank, but now and then they mistakenly call me “Clancy”, after which they immediately sigh, apologise, and then go a bit weepy. I feel I’ve been co-opted into a Daphne du Maurier novel. They may as well cut to the chase and call me Rebecca.



Nonetheless, I sense this Clancy was a dog to admire and, as a puppy, it’s always useful to have a role model. I’m certain he’d have taken the same stern action against that floral shirt. It really is ghastly. Sorry, was. Frank with Richard Glover: You never forget your first kill. Day 5: Two small visitors arrive. It’s nice to have fans, real fans, fans who – upon seeing me – instantly screamed and ran about as if I were the greatest thing since Taylor Swift. They danced about me, fighting among themselves as to who got to hug me first, and then taught me how to play soccer, a game in which my skills proved superior to their own. Sure, the younger one is just two years old, but I only have 10 weeks on my own clock. By the time I’m fully grown, based on this first-timers’ game, I’ll probably be inducted into the Socceroos. (I’m assuming that, by then, they’ll have removed their baffling ban on dogs being included in the squad.) I nose two balls into the goal, sidestepping the two-year-old, then totally defeat the five-year-old in a tackle. I’ve earned a rest and accept the young people’s congratulations and cuddles.



Related Article Opinion

Parenting Let me now bring before the court the case of the ungrateful child Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Day 6: I have to give credit to my new family. They’ve obviously installed dog-friendly features to keep me occupied. It’s like a Disneyland for dogs. So considerate! There’s the pantry with the child-proof barrier – but set at a height that still allows easy access for me. And then the books, thousands of them, many of them within reach of my teeth. They’ve also hung floor-to-ceiling curtains in the living room, I assume in preparation for my arrival. Certainly, they are perfectly designed for me to grab with my mouth, running this way and that, the curtains moving on my command, back and forth, making the most delightful sound. I assume they bought it last week at Pet Barn. God knows what it cost because that place is expensive! It would be ungrateful of me not to put it to constant use. I do so, roaring up and down, sampling the fabric with my teeth, hanging on like some trapeze artist from Cirque du Soleil. Then there’s that phrase again: “No chewing”. That’s not my name. A week in, I’m sure of my name. And of my place. My name is Frank and I’ve arrived. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: AFL executive salaries are ‘indefensible’: Former commissioner takes aim at head office
Five emergency money moves that could save you thousands
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingBudgeting Opinion Five emergency money moves that could save you thousands Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor August 15, 2026 — 5:01am

August 15, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Everyone knows that person right now – the one who is struggling with their finances. Maybe they have told you. Or more likely, you can see it on their face or feel it in their interactions. Perhaps, it’s even you. Photo: Aresna Villanueva Well, there are five little-known money repair moves that can give you breathing space – and then simpler-than-you-think strategies to get clear and comfortable. Repair move 1: Park your credit card debt. At a typical 18 per cent interest rate or more, even if you never spend another cent, this liability could be spiralling out of control.



But know that there are other credit cards to which you can transfer your existing card balance and pay no interest on it. These are for new customers only, and the idea is to lure your business across. However, used cleverly, you can think of them as get-out-of-debt-jail-free cards. You can currently get up to 25 months at 0 per cent on a transferred credit card balance, which gives you a 25-month window of opportunity to clear it – divide your balance by the number of months and see if you can repay that amount. These are simple solutions that will make a huge difference to your future. If you can’t manage that, though, such a card will at least cap your debt at its current level. The traps to these – of course there is some nasty fine print – are that any new spending will be charged at an astronomical interest rate, and you’ll also pay through the nose if you still have debt when the 0 per cent period ends.



So, never use these cards for spending and close them – even if you need to transfer your debt to a second no-interest product – when the introductory period expires. Chop up the old card, too, if you can’t trust yourself not to rack up more debt. But what if you face a sudden, unexpected expense? Editor's pick Opinion

Home loans Three steps to protect your home loan from a falling market Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor Repair move 2: Try the no-interest loan scheme (NILS). This is one of those seems-too-good-to-be true things, but it’s legit. The good people at not-for-profit Good Shepherd Microfinance offer no-interest (and no-fee) loans of up to $2000 for unexpected expenses such as a busted washing machine, kaput car, education expense like a laptop or even a big dental bill. Note this is far better than a white goods rental contract that can end up costing you multiples of the appliance’s original value.



The money is paid straight to the supplier – not in cash. To qualify, you need to have a healthcare or pension card, or earn less than $70,000 before tax as a single or $100,000 if you have a partner or dependents. You can also borrow up to $3000 for a rental bond or for recovery from a natural disaster. But as the site says: be aware of scams and imitators. The real address is goodshep.org.au and is a far cry from all the predatory small contract or payday loans online, more accurately thought of as loan sharks. These will often say “no interest” but with fees, can have an enormous effective interest rate. Repair move 3: Access financial hardship. If it’s everyday bills applying far too much pressure, realise that all utility and credit providers must have dedicated “financial hardship” departments. They also must extend you a degree of help if you need it. So, as foolish as it might sound, it’s smart to stick up your hand and say you are struggling … before you miss a bill. That’s the way to protect your all-important credit score, too. Having said that, it’s not widely known that you have leeway days to pay after each bill is due, in terms of your credit score.



The grace period is up to 14 days with any credit product and up to 60 days with any other product (say your electricity). But you will, naturally, make your provider cranky – possibly enough to charge you a financial penalty. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care Half-priced aged care at home sounds like a bargain. Here’s why it isn’t Rachel Lane Money contributor The other thing to note is that post-COVID regulatory updates mean that entering into a financial hardship arrangement with a provider will no longer impact your credit score. All that happens is that the words “financial hardship” will appear on your credit report, and only for one year after that arrangement ends. Repair move 4: Use the National Debt Helpline. Go to ndh.org.au or call 1800 007 007 to access a tremendous network of wonderful, free financial counsellors around the country. There is very likely at least one service in your area. They will go through your finances and find where they can be optimised and streamlined. They can also advocate for you with your providers for financial hardship, help arrange one of those no-interest loans and even liaise with Services Australia if needed.



Repair move 5: Build an emergency fund. None of the above happens if you have a buffer – an emergency cash stash that you can access if stuff goes wrong, which it probably will at some point. An emergency fund can rescue you without the need for credit and without risking debt spiral. Try to build this slowly and steadily over time, ultimately aiming for at least three months’ salary (and an offset account is a smart place to house it if you have a mortgage). You can think of the above repair plays as financial freedom moves – simple solutions that will make a huge difference to your future. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. World.title: Why getting simple super advice has become an expensive nightmare
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementFinancial planning Opinion Why getting simple super advice has become an expensive nightmare Bec Wilson Money contributor August 15, 2026 — 5:01am

August 15, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you walk into a financial adviser’s office at the age of 58, approaching retirement with about $700,000 in superannuation, a mortgage, a few hundred thousand dollars invested outside, what should happen next? And if you walked into a super fund advice appointment, with the same amount of money, and the same mixed picture, what can they do to help you? What can they advise you on, and more importantly, what can’t they? Simple super advice should be easy. So why does it feel like such a maze? Simon Letch Most Australians would expect broadly the same thing from both: help understanding whether they have enough, what sort of retirement they can afford, what to do about the remaining mortgage and whether their super and investments are in the right place, and taking the right amount of risk, and, ultimately, a clear plan for what steps they should take next. But what happens next can really surprise people because, despite starting with the same problem, the two advice models can’t offer the same help.



A comprehensive financial adviser is legally allowed to look across your broader financial life, including your super, investments, mortgage, tax position and retirement goals. But increasingly, many advice businesses are also built around providing ongoing investment management. Part of the reason is that the regulatory burden and the cost of providing comprehensive advice has made smaller, one-off pieces of advice difficult to provide profitably. So what begins as a request for retirement advice can become the start of a much longer commercial relationship, with the client’s super and investments moved onto a platform and managed on an ongoing basis by the advice business or an investment manager connected to it. [Everyday consumers] just want to understand their choices and get trustworthy advice about their retirement. A super fund comes at the same retirement problem from the opposite direction. It already has your money and increasingly, it wants to keep looking after it throughout your retirement. Funds are building retirement products, guidance and advice services to help members make that transition to retirement with them. This could make retirement advice vastly more accessible and affordable for millions of Australians.



But the advice a fund can offer its members has some significant boundaries. It is largely limited to advising on the money invested within the fund rather than the bigger picture of your financial life or the alternatives available to you. That can significantly limit how far they can go in considering things like the age pension, or even your broader retirement picture, to make the journey easier for you. Some funds hold separate financial advice licences that allow them to provide comprehensive advice, charging you personally for that at a higher rate. But that’s not what every member should expect when they contact their funds. These two faces of advice are increasingly colliding with each other. Financial advisers build their businesses by targeting new clients, often from people whose money is currently sitting in a super fund. Super funds are meanwhile trying to build more sophisticated retirement and advice offerings, to serve their members well enough that they think twice about leaving.



There’s nothing particularly surprising about either strategy. They are rational commercial business goals. But somewhere in the middle is the everyday consumer, who doesn’t want to be fought over, and isn’t particularly interested in who wins this battle. They just want to understand their choices and get trustworthy advice about their retirement. Editor's pick Opinion

Retirement living The simple $174,000 question many retirees still get wrong Bec Wilson Money contributor They should be able to get help working out whether they have enough, what their choices are and what they should do next, without having to 



Not in the same way as before Hayne, and not necessarily with the same conflicts, but the principle is worth watching right across the industry. When the person giving the advice benefits from where your money ends up, the incentives matter. And there’s one incentive Financial Services Minister Daniel Mulino should look very closely at: how much of our super can be used to pay for financial advice and how much should be used. Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen The differences are striking. Australian Super allows for an advice fee deduction of up to $7700 or 2.5 per cent of a member’s balance, whichever is lower. Australian Retirement Trust allows up to 2.5 per cent capped at $8800 with an additional $1500 for a new advice relationship. Unisuper allows for $8800 or 2.5 per cent, too. Hostplus caps advice fees at 2.5 per cent of balance or $8000 and HESTA caps them at $5500, or 3 per cent.



Compare that with the platform end of the market, where permitted advice fees can be much higher. And in some cases, there is no fixed dollar cap on ongoing advice fees. HUB24, for example, allows ongoing adviser service fees of up to 4.4 per cent of a member’s total account balance. Higher amounts are possible subject to approval. On a $700,000 super balance, 4.4 per cent is $30,800 per year. ASIC itself is worried about where these limits are heading. Its platform review released in June found one trustee had a dollar-based cap of $25,000 while another was planning to introduce a $30,000 cap. And three of the six platforms it examined had no upper limit on what could be deducted. These aren’t necessarily the fees people are actually paying, but they are the amounts the different systems permit to be deducted from someone’s retirement savings. An adviser may be able to deduct, with the client’s consent, substantially more in advice fees after moving a client from a traditional super fund onto a platform. And because those fees come directly out of retirement savings, rather than the household bank account, consumers may not feel them hitting their hip pocket nearly as hard. The Super Members Council says regulators should take the incentive seriously. It found that platforms that had higher advice fee caps were attracting stronger flows of money from people switching funds, even after accounting for costs, performance and size.



The Financial Services Council offers a different explanation for the strong advice-led outflows from super funds to platforms, saying platforms can provide greater investment choice, tailored portfolios and the ability for advisers to manage super and investments outside super in one place. Editor's pick Opinion

Budgeting Five emergency money moves that could save you thousands Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor Both arguments can be true. A platform can be entirely appropriate for someone who wants or needs that level of investment management. But the SMC data has to raise some legitimate questions about the way advice is paid for influencing where advisers recommend their money goes. And then, alongside this, we have to mention the consumer who’s simply stuck in a pretty ordinary super fund, who’s looking across the market and saying, ‘there must be another fund with better retirement products and services for what I need’ but who can’t find an adviser to help them review their super and move to another fund. That kind of advice should be easy to provide and find on a one-off basis. Instead, the regulatory burden and the cost of providing advice can make it unattractive for advisers unless it leads to a broader ongoing relationship.



There are so few advisers offering this kind of help these days that when I asked the Financial Advice Association Australia to help me find some, even it struggled. That’s an advice gap of a different kind – another one that needs addressing. And that’s the mess that Mulino needs to confront this week, head on. On Tuesday, he is expected to outline the next phase of the government’s financial advice reforms, known as Delivering Better Financial Outcomes. Most people won’t watch. Most don’t even know or care what DBFO is. But they should care about the outcome because these new rules could shape how everyday Australians get financial advice for decades to come. It’s time to finish the job. Australia needs more affordable and accessible financial advice. Super funds need greater scope to help members navigate retirement. Advisers need to be able to provide useful advice without unnecessary cost and complexity. And we must make room for simpler forms of digital advice. But getting more advice to people is only half the job. I’d like to see the government put the purpose of advice properly at the heart of these reforms: helping consumers understand their choices and make informed decisions that help them achieve their real goals. Mulino is going to upset somebody whatever he does. Advisers are worried about super funds moving further into advice; super funds want greater freedom to help members and retain them.



Platforms have billions of dollars flowing in that they don’t want to see slow. The lobbying in the back rooms has been fierce. But that’s precisely why the government needs to stop refereeing the industry’s turf war and tell us what it thinks a trustworthy consumer advice system should look like, because this isn’t it. Please, for the whole industry’s sake and the sake of the consumers, finish DBFO. Give Australians more places to get affordable help. Make the choices, limitations and commercial incentives behind advice transparent. And give advice a clear purpose – for both financial advice businesses and super funds – that puts the consumer at the heart. Bec Wilson is author of the bestseller How to Have an Epic Retirement and the newly released Prime Time: 27 Lessons for the New Midlife. She writes a weekly newsletter at epicretirement.net and hosts the Prime Time podcast.
