World.title: Quick hits: Tempers flare as Aussies wilt, Starc's heart-in-mouth moment
World.content:
Mitchell Starc vents his frustration at a Bangladeshi batter, while a star is born on treacherous Darwin turf.

Here are the quick hits from another torrid day for Australia against Bangladesh.

1. Smith grounds one

Smith downed a chance in the morning session. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

There is toiling, and then there is whatever the Australian bowlers were doing during the first session of day two.

The much-vaunted Aussie quartet, with Cam Green and Beau Webster in support, combined for just a single wicket during the opening two hours of play.

The ball found its way past Bangladeshi willow on a few occasions, but for the most part, chances were at a premium.

So, it was far from an ideal time for the usually so-reliable hands of slipper-supreme Steve Smith to let him down.

But with rookie opener Tanzid Hasan already past 50 and Australia having just taken their first wicket of the day, Smith floored one.

Tanzid edged a Nathan Lyon delivery into the elbow of Alex Carey, the ball ricocheted towards slip, and a diving Smith was unable to gather cleanly.

It was far from a sitter, but one Smith will be disappointed to have missed.

Tanzid given a life on 62.

2. Tanzid Hasan's maiden Test ton

Coming into this series, there were serious questions surrounding Bangladesh's opening pair, with the Tigers having struggled to nail down a reliable top two in recent years.

Up steps Tanzid Hasan, the 25-year-old opener playing just his second Test match.

Tanzid was considered and composed against the much-vaunted Australian attack, providing the foundation for a brilliant Bangladeshi team effort.

Tanzid completed a sparkling maiden century on day two. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

He already had an ODI century to his name, having scored 107 against Pakistan in Mirpur in March, and he also has scored five first class tons for an average of 39.60.

Talk about nervous 90s, though.

First, Pat Cummins whacked the 25-year-old on the arm with a vicious, 140km/h bouncer.

Then, Tanzid almost holed out to the substitute fielder at long off when on 96, skying a Lyon slower ball with a lofted drive that plugged in the outfield after falling just short of the fielder.

He moved to 99 with a neat clip, and then celebrated his century with a push down the ground off Lyon, a superb hundred celebrated accordingly.

3. The Darwin turf bites at the Australians

Starc got tangled in the turf while taking a catch. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

However, Tanzid was unable to turn his maiden Test ton into a truly big one, holing out to Lyon only a matter of balls later.

But Australian hearts were in Australian mouths as Mitchell Starc slid to make the catch and then flipped over ungainfully.

Starc, wincing as he got up, looked to be in some discomfort, and the replays showed that the Darwin turf may have been to blame.

The fast-bowler's knee had been caught in the grass, with a cloud of dust and thatch of grass disengaging from the ground.

Starc was tangled up awkwardly by the Darwin turf. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Thankfully, Starc appeared to recover well, but it wasn't the first time the Marrara Stadium outfield had appeared a little loose, with the ever-energetic Marnus Labuscagne ripping out his fair share of greenery.

With the surface only likely to disintegrate more dramatically over the coming three days, both teams should be wary of not getting twisted up in the outfield.

4. Steve Smith's hat-trick of slip catches

Australia desperately needed something to happen to interrupt the Bangladesh momentum — and it arrived with the new ball.

Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and then Pat Cummins all extracted edges with the new pill, claiming the wickets of Hossain Shanto (84), Litton Das (0) and Mushfiqur Rahim (36) as Bangladesh crumbled from 3-297 to 6-308.

And all three of them were caught by Steve Smith at second slip, making dramatic amends for his earlier fumble.

That trio of catches put Smith level with Joe Root with 218 catches, the most ever by a non-wicketkeeper in Test cricket.

Australia's pacemen are worth their weight in gold, but Smith certainly pays his way in the field to help them out.

5. 'Get off the wicket!'

Tempers flared late on it Darwin. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With that new-ball blitz an increasingly distant memory, and with the Australian bowlers beginning to wilt in the late Darwin sun, the hosts' frustration was on full display late in the evening session.

Into the 103rd over of the innings, Starc was bowling to all-rounder Mehidy, who was well set and intent on seeing the day through.

Mehidy set off for a single and came very close to colliding with the Australian spearhead.

Starc wasn't impressed.

"It's my follow through, not your follow through. Get off the wicket," Starc could be heard saying through the stump mic.

"I didn't see!" Mehidy could be heard saying during the next over, still perhaps apologetic about the near-collision.

But of course, the all-rounder shouldn't be taking the altercation personally.

The Australians' frustration was all of their own making.

6. You call that a knife?

Nathan Lyon used a knife to clean his spikes. (Supplied: Fox Sports)

There's nothing worse as an athlete than getting mud or grass caught between your cleats or spikes.

Nathan Lyon clearly had this issue during the second session, when going through his usual array of warm ups and stretches on the boundary at Marrara Oval.

But what can you do about it when in the middle of a Test match as you're about to prepare for a bowling spell?

Turns out, you ask someone in the kitchen if they have a spare a butter knife they don't mind soiling with some outfield dirt.

Much like the Northern Territory's best known international export, Crocodile Dundee, one can almost imagine one of the locals querying Lyon's choice of implement with quips like "you call that a knife …"

World.title: NRL top eight all but locked in after Souths win
World.content:
Canterbury have been left needing a minor miracle to make the NRL's top eight after succumbing to a 22-6 defeat at the hands of South Sydney.

Led by a rampaging David Fifita, the Rabbitohs took a major step towards returning to the finals for the first time since 2022 with a workmanlike victory at Stadium Australia on Friday night.

But the Bulldogs' hopes of featuring in September are all but over.

Should North Queensland see off Parramatta on Saturday, Cameron Ciraldo's men will be four points adrift of the finals places with just three full rounds of the regular season left to play.

Canterbury take on St George Illawarra, Penrith and Brisbane to round out their campaign and will no doubt look back on this loss to Souths as a game that got away.

Stephen Crichton, Jethro Rinakama, Lachlan Galvin and Jacob Preston were all either held up or stopped short of the line in the first half.

And as South Sydney, who moved up to sixth, pulled away in the second half, the Bulldogs didn't have the firepower to go with them.

The Rabbitohs withstood plenty of early pressure but struck in the 23rd minute when Fifita, who finished with 144m and six tackle busts, pounced on a Cody Walker grubberkick.

Walker was the conductor for their second as the Bunnies shifted from right to left, the veteran playmaker sending Tallis Duncan through a hole to set up Alex Johnston.

The Rabbitohs were far too clinical for the wasteful Bulldogs. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

Souths led 10-0 at halftime after Preston was penalised for a double movement and they moved out of touching distance from the restart.

Dogs hooker Bailey Hayward dropped the kick-off and Duncan crashed over on the left edge on the ensuing set.

Rinakama trudged off with a knee issue soon afterwards and the Bunnies pushed ahead further through winger Campbell Graham.

Missing a recognised goalkicker — Souths converted just one of their five tries — kept Canterbury alive though.

Enari Tuala finally scored on the hour mark but Canterbury's attack didn't have the spark to trouble Wayne Bennett's side, who completed the win with a well-deserved Matt Dufty try two minutes from fulltime.

Earlier, Manly's 'Fozball' fever dream is officially over after the Dolphins became the first team to hold the Sea Eagles scoreless at Brookvale Oval in 33 years.

In a match that failed to reach any real heights, the Dolphins had enough strike to pull away late and win 22-0, leapfrogging them above Cronulla into fourth spot.

The Dolphins' win did come at some cost, with in-form second-rower Connelly Lemuelu limping from the field in the second half with a hamstring injury.

But the story of the night was the Sea Eagles, whose finals hopes are now virtually over after six straight losses.

AAP

World.title: Boxer dies more than a decade after fight leaves him with brain injury
World.content:
Prichard Colón, a former boxer who was left with severe brain damage after a fight more than a decade ago, has died aged 33.

His father, Richard Colón, confirmed his son's death in a Facebook post on Thursday.

The post did not detail the Puerto Rican boxer's cause of death.

World Boxing Organization (WBO) president Gustavo Olivieri posted a tribute to Colón on social media.

"Today, the WBO solemnly joins his family and all those who had the privilege of knowing, supporting, and loving him in mourning his passing," Mr Olivieri said.

What happened to Prichard Colón?

Colón was injured in a boxing match against Terrel Williams in Virginia in the US in October 2015.

Born in Florida, US, Colón kicked off his boxing career in Puerto Rico, where he won five amateur titles.

He was considered a "rising star" in the lead-up to the nationally televised match, ESPN reports.

Here's how a report from Reuters described the match at the time:

"An online video of the fight showed Williams, a 31-year-old fighter from Los Angeles, punching Colón in the back of the head in the seventh round, a shot that appeared to stun Colón, who was briefly examined in his corner. "Williams was penalised for the illegal punch. "Colón was then knocked down twice in the ninth round. "He was disqualified after the ninth round. "His corner mistakenly took off his gloves, thinking it was the final round and that the fight was complete."

After the match, Colón needed assistance to walk to his dressing room after the match.

He said he felt dizzy, vomited and then "passed out", according to a report from the Washington Post.

Colón was rushed to hospital where he underwent surgery to relieve pressure on his brain, spending seven months in a coma.

He was 23 years old.

Prichard Colon, left, and Terrel Williams during the fight. (Getty Images via AFP: Patrick Smith)

In 2016, the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation determined there was no wrongdoing on the part of organisers of the fight, the Washington Post reported.

"No one action [or failure to act] can be identified that is so apparent or egregious to justify holding accountable any one person," the regulator said in a statement.

Signs of hope

In 2017, nearly two years after the fight, Colón was still in what doctors described as a persistent vegetative state, according to an article from ESPN.

He needed around-the-clock care.

At the time, his parents told the US broadcaster they hoped Colón would regain some brain function despite the challenges he faced.

"I do believe in miracles," his father said.

By 2019, Colón had made significant progress, according to another article by the Washington Post.

After months of therapy, he was able to communicate using facial gestures, verbal sounds and a computer that tracked his eye movements.

He could pedal on a recumbent bike, and his competitive spirit was driving him to take steps with assistance in a friendly rivalry with a fellow patient.

"He gets tired and impatient like anyone, and some of his days are better than others," Washington Post reporter Kent Babb wrote.

"What's clear is that he's made it this far, beyond where anyone thought he would, because of good coaching."

'Extraordinary fighting spirit'

News of the former boxer's death triggered an outpouring of grief in the boxing world.

"Prichard's life was defined by courage, perseverance, and an extraordinary fighting spirit," Mr Olivieri said.

"His story transcended the ring and deeply touched the boxing community, which stood by him throughout the years with respect, admiration, and hope."

The WBO paid tribute to Colón's "resilience" as well as "the unwavering love of his family".

Tributes to Prichard Colón were posted to social media after news of his death broke. (Facebook: World Boxing Organization-WBO)

ABC with Reuters

World.title: Australia's Grace Kim makes fast start at LPGA event
World.content:
Australian golfer Grace Kim has continued her hot run with a stellar opening round at the LPGA Tour's Portland Classic.

Fresh off two straight top-10 finishes, Kim is just one stroke behind Colombian leader Mariel Galdiano after the first round at the Columbia-Edgewater Country Club.

Playing an all-out attack, the major champion collected seven birdies and an eagle to finish the day in a seven-way tie for second.

The world number 38 also needed only 24 putts, the fewest of any player in the field.

Kim started with a three-birdie stretch after starting her round on the 10th hole.

"Having that three-birdie start is just a nice feeling to kick-start things," the 25-year-old said.

"A lot of us out here are pretty straight, fairways and greens.

"But in terms of holing all those putts, knowing that the greens roll quite true … it's really nice to just put a stroke on it and see where it would normally go."

Kim is in a batch at 6-under, including Augusta National women's amateur champion Maria Jose Marin, Arpichaya Yubol and Olivia Cowan.

The 20-year-old Marin landed five-straight birdies on the front nine.

"I reached a flow state that I haven't reached in a while," she said.

"After the British Open I didn't play my best golf, and I think getting that confidence back with this round is all that I needed."

One shot behind them and tied for ninth is Australian Robyn Choi (67), who sprang to life on the back nine.

After going out in even par with a birdie and bogey, Choi stormed home with four consecutive birdies beginning on the 12th. She then added another on the 17th to rocket up the field.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Fellow Australian Steph Kyriacou (72) had a solid round of even par, but will have to play well with the cut projected to be around 1-under.

American pacesetter Galdiano's opening 65 featured nine birdies.

Galdiano, a 28-year-old from Hawaii, is making her fourth LPGA Tour start of the year.

"Every start on the LPGA means a lot to me, so just enjoy the moment, really," she said.

AAP

World.title: Fraser officially enters Carlton coaching race after mid-year turnaround
World.content:
Josh Fraser has presented to the Carlton hierarchy after officially entering the club's process to find its full-time coach.

After a stunning run of 10 wins from 12 matches since becoming interim coach when Michael Voss left the club in May, Fraser has Carlton on the cusp of the most unlikely finals appearance.

Although he has delivered a perfect on-the-job audition, Fraser was still required to pitch to the Blues' coaching panel on Wednesday.

Loading...

Untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) have been through the process, with Fraser only formally putting his hand up this week.

"A fortnight ago, the club came to me and asked me to be a part of this coaching process," Fraser said today.

"Then this week, I was in a position to go back to the club and accept that offer to go through the process.

"I presented to the coaching panel this week."

At his first press conference when taking over from Voss, Fraser was adamant he was not interested in being Carlton's coach beyond this season.

But after a wildly successful 12 weeks in charge, buoyed by enthusiastic fans, Fraser could not turn down the opportunity.

"I have said, previously, that I've been ambitious to be a senior coach," Fraser said.

"I've been fortunate to be able to sit in the chair and consolidate some of my thinking; get some opportunity exposure to the role that otherwise you wouldn't normally get.

"It's been something that's been crystallising in my mind and my thoughts.

"Really confident that I'm ready to assume the responsibility of being a senior coach.

"There are 19 jobs to be a senior (AFL) coach.

"I'm as excited about this group as a lot of our Carlton supporters will be."

Joyous Blues fans were chanting "we want Fraser" as the Blues steamrolled St Kilda on Sunday night to put themselves in the box seat to earn a spot in the wildcard round.

If they defeat the Western Bulldogs, who will be without superstar captain Marcus Bontempelli on Sunday, the Blues will lock in their spot in the top 10.

It has been one of the more remarkable in-season turnarounds in AFL history, with Carlton 1-8 when Fraser took over.

"It can disrupt the club at times, when there's a significant change, like when you lose a coach, and you bring another coach in mid-season," Fraser said.

"That speaks to the culture that's been here, but I'm grateful for all the support I've had around me."

AAP

World.title: Bangladesh grinds Australia into the Darwin dirt as rookie scores sparkling ton
World.content:
Australia's much-vaunted bowling attack has been ground into the Darwin dirt, experiencing another torrid day against Bangladesh at Marrara Stadium.

Led by a sparkling maiden Test ton to rookie-opener Tanzid Hasan, Bangladesh lost just five wickets on day two, reaching stumps on 6-351 and 153 first-innings runs ahead of their hosts.

After an opening day that saw Australia bowled out for a well below-par 198, Pat Cummins's men picked up where they left off on day two, struggling for ideas and inspiration against a disciplined Bangladeshi batting line-up.

Mitchell Starc took the only wicket in an energy-sapping morning session for Australia, while Steve Smith was uncharacteristically slow in reacting to a deflected Tanzid edge, that, if taken, would have seen the opener depart for 62.

Tanzid, playing just his second Test match, took 188 balls to reach his century, and brought it up with a push back past Nathan Lyon after a nervous period in the 90s.

Tanzid completed a sparkling maiden century on day two. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

However, the 25-year-old threw his wicket away only a matter of balls later, caught in the deep after mistiming an ill-advised slog against Lyon for 101.

That was the only wicket to fall in the second session as captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, who had shared a 93-run partnership with Tanzid, continued to take the fight to the Australians alongside 39-year-old, 103-Test veteran Mushfiqur Rahim.

Bangladesh's lead by the time the new ball was taken stood at 91, with seven wickets remaining.

Starc instantly got the new ball talking, sending the first ball swinging past the bat and stumps of Shanto to the giant left hander's complete disbelief.

But it was Hazlewood who made the breakthrough in his first over, finding the edge of Shanto to have him caught at second slip by Steve Smith for 84.

Starc got in on the act three overs later, having Litton Das caught behind, also by Smith, for a 12-ball duck.

Then Pat Cummins joined the party to find the edge of Mushfiqur, and give Smith a third consecutive catch, Australia's three great pacemen striking with fearsome force to reduce Bangladesh from 3-297 to 6-308.

That third catch put Smith level with Joe Root on 218 catches, the most ever in Test cricket by a non wicketkeeper.

But Australia once again toiled as the lacquer faded from the new ball, with six-wicket hero from day one, Hasan Mahmud (13 not out), providing able support to all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz, who reached stumps on 32.

World.title: EPL side walks off as Spanish club kicks penalty into open net
World.content:
Fulham's preseason match against Málaga turned out to be not too friendly after the English club walked off and coach Álvaro Arbeloa was shown a red card for complaining to the referees.

The match had finished 2-2, after the La Liga side Málaga FC equalised in the 90th minute.

At full-time, the Premier League outfit walked off the pitch while Málaga stayed on, believing a penalty shootout should decide the winner.

Malaga striker Jauregi then kicked a penalty into an open net before celebrating in front of the home fans.

In a post on X, Fulham said both teams had agreed before the match that no penalty shootout would follow a draw.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

On their club website, Malaga said it believed a shootout was on the cards.

"Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract," the La Liga club said.

Tech.title: Samsung has new Galaxy headphones in the works
Tech.content:
Strings of code in Samsung’s Galaxy Wearable app hint at an upcoming pair of over-ear headphones that could compete with the AirPods Max, SamMobile reports. Samsung’s reportedly referring to the headphones as the “Galaxy H1,” and SamMobile says they could launch sometime in 2027. That would make these the company’s first pair of over-ear headphones since the Level On in 2015, which was released well before Samsung acquired Harman and a number of other audio brands.

Connection status icons in the app standard show the design of over-ear, wireless Bluetooth headphones, but not necessarily exactly what these will look like in the end. Samsung’s main audio device right now is its Galaxy Buds line, but it doesn’t have high-end headphones similar to the AirPods Max or Sony XM series.

Apple released a revised AirPods Max 2 model earlier this year, which looked the same but added a new chip to power more features like adaptive audio and live translation. When the Galaxy H1 launches, as SamMobile points out, we would expect it to include the Samsung Seamless Codec Ultra High Quality (SSC UHQ) codec that works exclusively with 2023 and newer Galaxy phones and tablets, as well as support for AI assistants like Gemini and Bixby that’s similar to what we saw in the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.

Tech.title: A RAMageddon guide to back-to-school laptop shopping
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

If you’re a student looking for an affordable laptop, I have bad news and I have good news. The bad news is that computer prices are out of whack due to the ongoing RAM and storage crunch, making some a little pricier than they used to be and others wildly more expensive.

The good news? Despite that, there are still many great options, including the selection we’ve tested and highlighted below.

Before you go for the cheapest option you can still find, consider biting the bullet on a more powerful laptop, especially if you’re buying for a college student. Prices are likely to continue rising well into next year — especially since all the memory being made through 2027 is already allocated. You can get a mostly tolerable laptop for under $500 and a good one for around $700, but spending more to get something like a MacBook Air gets you better build quality and enough performance headroom to last through four years of college and well beyond. (Many Verge writers and editors are still using M1 MacBook Airs from 2020). But even the modest options below (new or refurbished) should easily be good for more than a few years. The key is to avoid something that feels slow or janky on day one, if you can. It’ll only get worse from there.

If your school or curriculum recommends certain laptops or minimum specs, then you already know what to aim for. If not, our rule of thumb is to go with a Mac running Apple silicon or a Windows laptop running Intel or AMD chips released in the last few years. (For Windows machines, don’t go any older than 2022 or 2023 — Intel’s 13th-gen “Raptor Lake” or AMD’s Ryzen 7000 series.) Snapdragon X chips are also great options unless you’re a college student who needs to run specialized software not compatible with Windows on Arm (or if you want to play games).

But try to get 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage or more if you can — especially for college students. Eight GB of RAM is workable on macOS with the MacBook Neo, but Windows laptops struggle a bit with it. And for the most budget-conscious or anyone shopping for younger kids, a quality Chromebook is still great.

The best cheap laptop

The MacBook Neo is the easy pick for students from middle school to high school. There’s still no beating its balance of build quality and good-enough performance at this price. Students and teachers can get it starting at $599, and Apple offers refurbished models for $599 for the rest of us as well. If you can justify spending an additional $100, it’s worth getting the model with twice the storage and a Touch ID fingerprint sensor, which makes logging in and entering passwords much less of a hassle.

The A18 Pro chip is powerful enough for most high school students (and adults), and everything from its trackpad to its speakers and screen range from good to great, which is not the case for Windows laptops in this price range. Its only shortcoming by comparison is having just two USB-C ports. The 8GB of RAM and 256GB of base storage mean a student eventually pushes the limits of what this laptop can do sooner than a more powerful MacBook Air, but the Neo is still significantly cheaper.

The best laptop for college

The Neo is the best cheap laptop, but the MacBook Air is still the best laptop for most people, and the standard recommendation for college students. Every part of it is a step up from the Neo: It has a much more powerful processor, and it starts with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of much faster storage. And few laptops can match the Air’s overall build quality. It also means spending $1,299 (or $1,199 for students) on a 13-inch model, or $1,499 for the 15-inch. It’s a shame the Air no longer starts at $999 like it did just last year, but it’s still worth springing for if you’re buying for the long term.

The Airs have been so good for so many years now, you don’t miss out on much by buying a refurbished model if it’s substantially cheaper. Keep an eye on Apple’s refurb store, and retailers like Best Buy sometimes have great deals too.

A Windows laptop nearly as nice as a MacBook Air

Asus Zenbook A14 $ 700 $ 1000 30 % off $ 700 Asus’s Zenbook A14 is a bit of a MacBook Air wannabe, but it’s a compelling alternative if you value a superlight Windows laptop with long battery life. The 2025 model sports an Arm-based Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus chip, a nice 14-inch OLED display, and a sleek textured beige finish. Read More $700 at Best Buy

Asus Zenbooks are some of the sleeker, better-looking Windows laptops, and the Zenbook A14 is Asus’ wannabe MacBook Air. It has a good Snapdragon X Plus chip, 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a lovely OLED display in an ultra-light chassis (it’s just 2.4 pounds / 1.09kg), all for $1,000 or as low as $700 on sale. It even has a solid port selection, with one USB-A, two speedy USB4, and HDMI 2.1. I really enjoyed the larger Zenbook A16 version when I reviewed it, but the A14 is even lighter and significantly cheaper. Like its larger sibling, the A14 is coated in Asus’ Ceraluminum finish that gives it a nice textured feel and unique look. (It’s a beige laptop!)

A cheap laptop with a great processor

Acer’s Aspire 14 AI didn’t impress me with its screen, speakers, or build quality when I tested it against the Neo, but for $500 or $600 on sale, which it often is, it’s hard to beat. It has a solid Intel Lunar Lake processor, 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a bunch of speedy ports. Getting two USB-A, two Thunderbolt 4, and HDMI 2.1 on a $600 laptop? Hell yeah.

A Lunar Lake chip means you get great battery life, and you can even do some light gaming. Its screen isn’t pretty and everything creaks, but with the money you save you can overcome some of its shortcomings with a mouse and monitor. Just keep in mind that the appeal of this laptop is what you’re getting for the price. If the deal winds change and Aspire 14 AIs are selling for $700 or more, consider something else.

A formidable 16-incher for about $500

I’m still testing the HP OmniBook 3 for a full review, but I’ve used it enough and I like it enough at around $500 to give it a nod. Its speakers and screen are not good quality, but they’re slightly better than the Acer Aspire above — just don’t look too close, or you’ll notice that its 1920 x 1200 resolution isn’t very sharp at this scale. At 16 inches you’re getting a big screen for cheap, but this laptop doesn’t feel large, as it weighs only 3.65 pounds / 1.66kg and is about 0.63 inches / 16mm thick (at its hinge, where it’s slightly thicker). And its sizable battery and efficient Snapdragon X chip allow it to last long on a charge. Plus, it’s got an ample-sized numpad for you numbers people.

Consider a refurbished ThinkPad

ThinkPads are awesome. They have great keyboards and trackpads, sturdy builds, lots of ports, and even a TrackPoint. They’re typically very expensive when bought new, and they have a reputation for lasting a long time. They’re Lenovo’s business line, so there’s a constant stream of used ThinkPads entering the secondhand market when companies refresh their fleets. That makes them a great candidate for buying refurbished or used. Lenovo sells many refurb units directly, so you know you should be getting something in good shape. Many of them are still expensive, but this ThinkPad T14 is an attractive example, offering a 13th-gen Intel chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage for around $700. Or for a bit more you can get this ThinkPad L14 Gen 5 with a newer Intel Meteor Lake chip for around $1,000.

And for the more adventurous folks out there, you can pick up an even older ThinkPad on the cheap and install Linux to give it new life.

Our go-to pick for a cheap Chromebook

A Chromebook is good for web browsing, doing homework, and nailing the basics of browser-first computer use — when done well. The Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 is a mainstay of The Verge’s laptop recommendations, despite being a few years old. It’s very affordable at just $350, and even with its 12th-gen Intel chip and 8GB of RAM it’s more than serviceable for ChromeOS. Google’s new Googlebooks are coming in the fall, but some early leaks are pointing at those potentially being pricier laptops (making me wonder what exactly their appeal will be).

A great convertible Chromebook

If you can afford a slightly pricier, newer, and better Chromebook than the Asus, check out the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. Its full price of $749 is a bit much, but when discounted to $600 like it is at the time of this writing it can be worth it. The Arm-based MediaTek Kompanio Ultra in this Chromebook paired with 12GB of RAM gives it very good performance and excellent battery life. And since it’s a convertible, it’s also great to use with an optional stylus for note-taking, drawing, and sketching.

Tech.title: Lamborghini’s flagship Revuelto levels up with SV trim
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

A lot of automakers talk about wanting to minimize or eliminate driver distractions so as to make the experience of driving more rewarding and safer overall. Lamborghini has a different strategy; it wants the driver to become one with their vehicle. This helps explain the storied super car maker’s tagline for the new Revuelto SV: the quantum of driving.

“For us, quantum of driving is the moment when you get into the car, you start driving the car, and the car and you become one piece,” said Alessandro Farmeschi, product line director for the Revuelto, the Italian brand’s top V12 powered model. “And you start just thinking about your drive, feeling the adrenaline of the acceleration, braking, the G-forces, you know. You feel everything and you basically forget about the rest because you are so concentrated and you enjoy so much this experience.”

Be the car! What better way to be less bothered by all of modern life’s distraction? I can’t speak from experience, having not driven the Revuelto yet, but standing next to the sharklike SV version, you can certainly begin to understand where Farmeschi and his colleagues are coming from. Be the car? Sure, I’ll be this car. And I’ll eat all others on the road for breakfast.

SV stands for Superveloce or “superfast,” which dates back to the iconic 1971 Miura SV. Lamborghini has also used the designation on higher-performance versions of the Diablo, Murciélago, and Aventador — and now the Revuelto, it’s flagship V12 supercar.

Previous Next







1 / 5

It’s a high-performance evolution of an already very fast, very high performing vehicle, which begs the question: How much is too much? The Revuelto SV’s hybrid-electric powertrain still features a 6.5-liter naturally aspirated V12 and three electric motors, which can put out 1,065cv (around 1,050 hp), or around a 50 hp boost over the standard Revuelto. The additional capability is supported by a revised battery package that retains the same basic shape and geometry but increases energy capacity by 7.3kWh and provides higher power output.

The battery improvements are intended not simply to produce a higher peak figure but to make the car’s performance more consistent during hard driving. Lamborghini wanted the SV to deliver a flatter and more consistent level of performance throughout a lap rather than experiencing larger variations in output, Farmeschi explained.

The transmission shifting time has also been reduced by 30 percent for a more responsive and effective acceleration. Carbon fiber is used extensively throughout the vehicle to shave crucial kilograms. The front bumper is completely new, while the rear wing, door panels, and new racing seats also use carbon fiber as part of the effort to slim down and improve performance. The result? The Revuelto SV posts a power-to-weight ratio of 1.66 kg/CV, as compared to 1.75kg/CV for the standard Revuelto. Every milligram matters.

Downforce has been increased by 80 percent, thanks to the new front bumper and rear wing, which Farmeschi explained incorporates two wing designs into one. The front-end changes alone provide a 100 percent increase in front downforce compared with the standard Revuelto, which gives the car greater stability as it enters corners and begins turning, effectively helping to “glue” the front of the car to the track. This enables a 0–62mph acceleration in just 2.4 seconds — on par with the limited-edition Fenomeno, which Lamborghini previously described as its “fastest” in production. (I guess the Fenomeno will have to share that distinction now.)

Previous Next







1 / 5

But for Farmeschi, it’s not just about track performance metrics — it’s also about emotion. “Because emotion is driving the car, it’s being so fast… enjoying the car, going beyond even your limits because the car also helps you to manage the performance,” he said.

Of course, enhanced acceleration and performance also demands enhanced braking. The Revuelto SV features a new CCM-R Plus braking system, as compared to the carbon-ceramic brakes used on the standard Revuelto. The discs are thicker and larger in diameter, with radial holes extending along the radius to improve cooling. The result is a braking system capable of handling greater levels of stress while allowing the driver to brake harder and later.

Speaking of driving dynamics, Lamborghini is introducing a new Pilota mode, derived from its GT racing program. The driver can activate Pilota mode using the helmet icon on the steering wheel and then choose one of five levels using the rotary controls. These settings alter how sensitive the car is to its stability systems. The vehicle incorporates ABS and stability-control systems as well as a six-dimensional sensor located in the center tunnel, which measures vertical, lateral, and longitudinal acceleration as well as roll, pitch, and other vehicle movements. Pilota mode uses this information to change the car’s behavior according to the driver’s selected level.

“The customer can select this, like in the race, where you want maybe the car a bit more, let’s say, loose, because you want to, let’s say, manage the car differently, maybe using better the track, the cornering, rather than being more precise,” Farmeschi said, “so it depends on the driving style.”

After scraping its plans to make a purely electric sports car, Lamborghini doubled down on its hybrid strategy. The electric motors in the Revuelto SV allow for better torque vectoring and driving dynamics, Farmeschi said, arguing that those reasons help justify the added weight from the 7.3kWh battery.

The hybrid system also has a practical social benefit, he said with a sly grin. Your neighbors may appreciate the courtesy of rolling out of your driveway silently under electric power, for example. (The idea of anyone living close enough to a Lamborghini Revuelto owner to hear any engine sounds seems slightly ludicrous, but I digress.) The electric-only range is approximately 15 kilometers, or about 10 miles — not enough for a commute, but it can be useful for driving through areas with restrictions on combustion-engine vehicles.

Lamborghini isn’t announcing pricing yet, but come on — we’re already talking a minimum of $612,000 for the non-SV trim. You can expect the new version to set you back at least $750,000 before any options are added in. I can already hear the crypto bros frantically checking their account balances.

There may not be an all-electric Lamborghini coming any time soon, and the public’s reception to the Ferrari Luce underscores the minefield these specialized automakers will need to navigate in the future. But for now, Lamborghini is making the most of its hybrid super cars — emphasis on “the most.”

Photography by Andrew J. Hawkins / The Verge

Tech.title: The X-Files creator Chris Carter wanted to make a more horrific movie
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

The version of The X-Files: I Want to Believe that premiered in 2008 was not exactly the movie co-writer / director Chris Carter intended to make. Carter wanted to bring agents Mulder and Scully back to the big screen with a grisly story about faith and the supernatural. But executives at 20th Century Fox felt that Carter’s ideas were too dark, and he was pushed to turn the project into a PG-13 feature. Now, almost two decades after I Want to Believe’s theatrical debut, Carter is back with a new director’s cut of the film for Hulu that’s much closer to his original vision.

“We got to tell a good X-Files story,” Carter said of the original cut during a recent conversation we had about the new release. ”We just didn’t get to tell it in the way that we had intended.”

The X-Files: I Want to Believe – Vrach Frankenshteyn’s Russian subtitle is meant to clue you into how heavily the movie leans into the series’ monster of the week-style storytelling. Mulder (David Duchovny) and Scully (Gillian Anderson) find themselves unwittingly investigating a string of gruesome kidnappings with the help of a predatory priest (Sir William Connolly) who claims to have psychic visions. Neither of the agents know what to make of the man’s supposed abilities, but they can’t ignore the way he consistently leads the FBI to dismembered body parts hidden in the frozen, West Virginian wilderness.

The new cut of I Want to Believe puts an emphasis on its Frankenstein elements that almost makes it feel like 20th Century Studios wanted to tap into Hollywood’s recent fascination with reimagining Mary Shelley’s seminal sci-fi novel. But Carter told me that he thinks his version is actually exploring some of the real world horrors that are woven into people’s desperate searches for youth and immortality.

“There’s this tech bro idea that if you do the right things and eat the right things, you might be able to live forever and ever,” Carter explained. “But if you’re able to transplant your head successfully onto younger and younger bodies, who’s to say that’s not everlasting life?”

While writing I Want to Believe back in the early aughts, Carter was inspired by the work of Robert J. White — a neurosurgeon and bioethicist who successfully managed to transplant the head of one living monkey onto another’s body in the 1970s. Before White’s death in 2010, Carter met with him in Ohio to speak about his work, and their conversation informed some of I Want to Believe’s beats. With Vrach Frankenshteyn, Carter wanted to highlight the visceral sense of fear that might be felt by someone undergoing experiments similar to White’s. The new cut spends less time focusing on Mulder and Scully’s personal relationship, and puts more of its energy into making you feel the terror of its victim characters.

“You have these women who have been stalked, violently taken from their cars, and then trapped in boxes, where they witness these terrible medical procedures they’re going to be subjected to,” Carter said. “If the audience now comes into this movie thinking about head transplants and this title, plot details like finding an arm in the ice and snow brings them into this story in a different way.”

David Duchovny, Gillian Anderson, and Chris Carter on the set of The X-Files: I Want to Believe. Image: Hulu / 20th Century Studios

Though I Want to Believe was met with mixed reviews when it first hit theaters, the series continued with two revival seasons on Fox that ran from 2016 to 2018. Those seasons and the rise of digital streaming brought a new generation of viewers into the X-Files fandom. Carter told me that he’s regularly surprised to meet young people who feel a deep connection to the world he created even though they weren’t alive when the show was originally airing. Carter appreciates that, for those fans, The X-Files is something they’re experiencing for the first time, and it’s markedly different from the new generation of streaming sci-fi series.

Carter — who’s currently working with his wife, Dori, on a movie about a woman forced to live her mother’s life in the 1950s titled Queens for a Day — knows the pleasure of watching truly original and distinct stories unfold. That’s why he has tried to keep himself in the dark about what Ryan Coogler is cooking up with his own upcoming spin on The X-Files. That said, while shooting Queens for a Day in Vancouver, Carter couldn’t stop some of the members from his production crew from visiting Coogler’s nearby set. And while Carter insisted about being kept in the dark about any “secret inside information,” he has faith that Coogler is going to “bring his stamp” to the franchise.

“Ryan is a filmmaker I completely respect,” Carter said. “I’ve made a point of not reading [his script] because I want to watch it like everyone else. But I’ve got an inkling about what he’s doing with his approach and this diverse cast, and it’s very exciting to me.”

The X-Files: I Want to Believe – Vrach Frankenshteyn is now streaming on Hulu.

Tech.title: You can now turn off Google Gemini’s visible watermarks
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google will now allow you to remove visible watermarks from the images, videos, and music made with AI tools. With the update, you can toggle off a new “Media watermark” setting in Gemini and Google’s AI video generator, Flow.

When toggled off, Google will remove the “sparkle” watermark that appears in the bottom-right corner of content generated with the company’s Nano Banana and Omni models. Though visible watermarks are now optional, AI-generated content will have invisible SynthID watermarks and C2PA metadata embedded in the background, according to Josh Woodward, the vice president of Google Labs, Gemini, and AI Studio. That means you can still verify if a piece of content has one of these markers by asking Gemini or Search if it’s AI-generated.

You can find the “Media watermark” option in Gemini’s settings menu. Screenshot: The Verge

While this change might make it more difficult to quickly discern if an image or video is AI-generated, many users have already been editing out visible watermarks. Other AI image generators, like OpenAI and Meta’s, also don’t apply visible watermarks. Instead, OpenAI relies on SynthID and C2PA to signal whether something is AI-generated, while Meta launched its own Content Seal standard. Anthropic also announced this week that it’s applying invisible watermarks to both AI-generated text and images.

Google plans on rolling out its new watermark setting to Search as well, but the toggle won’t launch in countries that require visible watermarks.

Tech.title: What we know about the alleged Iranian hacks on U.S. water utilities
Tech.content:
Since the end of last month, several water utilities in the United States have been hit by cyberattacks, causing alarm in the country.

For years, water utilities and other critical infrastructure facilities in the power sector, for example, have been targeted by hackers, whether government-backed or individuals. What makes this recent series of attacks—allegedly carried out by Iran—particularly concerning was how widespread they have been, hitting targets in around a dozen states.

The U.S. has more than 150,000 water systems, some of them run by local companies. In theory, that should make it harder for hackers to target several facilities at the same time. But on the flip side, the companies running these systems may not have the resources or cybersecurity expertise needed to protect themselves.

Cybersecurity experts have long believed that Iranian hackers target low-hanging fruit in opportunistic isolated attacks, so this hacking campaign could be a significant escalation.

A lot has happened since news of the initial attacks broke two weeks ago. So we decided it was a good time to recap what we know so far, and what we don’t.

Where have there been attacks?

On July 28, Minnesota authorities announced that water treatment plants in more than 30 communities were hit by coordinated cyberattacks.

Two days later, the FBI said water and wastewater utility companies in “at least seven states” reported incidents, and in some cases the attacks “degraded water operations.” Since then, apart from Minnesota, there have been reported hacks against water facilities in Arkansas, Georgia, New Jersey, and Michigan.

Who is behind the attacks?

The short answer is: we don’t know yet, but the number one suspect is the Iranian government.

As of today, officially, the U.S. government has yet to name the culprit behind the coordinated wave of hacks.

However, the first incidents in Minnesota came days after the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned that Iranian hackers were targeting internet-connected devices in water systems and the energy sector, without saying where those attacks were occurring. (CISA had originally published this warning in April, and updated it before the Minnesota attacks.)

After the initial wave was uncovered in Minnesota, President Donald Trump said he did not think “there was an Iranian cyberattack.” Instead, he blamed the state, perhaps because it is run by democratic governor Tim Walz, who was chosen as Kamala Harris’s vice president in the 2024 elections.

Trump’s claim came a day after Wired reported that the Water Information Sharing and Analysis Center, or WaterISAC, a nonprofit group that distributes cybersecurity information among the water sector, told its members that the recent attacks “aligned” with the hacking campaign CISA warned of—effectively accusing the Iranian government.

Earlier this week, The Washington Post reported that U.S. intelligence agencies “are confident” that Iran, and in particular the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), is responsible. The attribution isn’t public yet, according to the paper’s sources, because the agencies are not sure which specific unit within the IRGC was responsible, and also because officials may be reluctant to contradict Trump’s claim.

Iranian government hackers have a history of targeting critical infrastructure in the U.S., and it’s possible that these attacks are part of its strategy to retaliate against the country because of the six-month-long war.

Until now, Iranian hackers had had only limited success in their cyberattacks against U.S. targets. In March, a hacktivist group called Handala disrupted the operations of medical tech giant Stryker. The U.S. government later accused Handala of being operated by Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Then, the group claimed responsibility for hacking the personal Gmail account of FBI director Kash Patel.

What effects have the attacks had?

The reality is that some systems inside critical infrastructure facilities are exposed to the internet and relatively easy to find. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm Forescout reported finding more than 2,800 controllers in U.S. water systems exposed online. If a system is exposed, it doesn’t automatically mean hackers can take over control and cause real-world effects. But that has happened in some isolated cases in recent attacks.

The FBI said some of the cyberattacks around the country caused loss of pressure, which “could potentially allow untreated groundwater to seep into pipes,” and flooding.

The town of Braham in Minnesota, one of the first ones to report an incident, had to take its water plant offline for a few hours, urging its around 1,700 residents to conserve water. The city of Maple Plain, also in Minnesota, briefly declared a state of emergency. In a county outside Atlanta, Georgia, local officials briefly told residents to boil water before using it as a precautionary measure.

The worst effect, however, may be psychological. These attacks have been widely covered in national and local press, causing people to worry about the safety of a fundamental and basic need like water. That may very well be part of the hackers’ goals: to spread panic and fear.

Tech.title: Read-it-later app Pocket shut down down — here are the best alternatives
Tech.content:
In May 2025, Mozilla announced that it was shutting down the popular read-it-later app Pocket, which it had acquired back in 2017 for an undisclosed amount. That led to a growing demand for alternative apps that could help people save online content, particularly longer articles, that they want to read later when they have more time.

While Mozilla exited the business, saying the way people are browsing the web is changing, the shutdown boosted adoption of a number of other apps, like Matter, Instapaper, and Raindrop.io, among others. It’s supporting the creation of new, indie alternatives, as well.

Many of the apps will support imports. However, Pocket users only had until October 8, 2025, to export their saved articles and other items, including lists, archives, favorites, notes, and highlights.

Below are the read-it-later alternatives that are picking up where Pocket left off.

Matter

Matter is a GV-backed company that makes an eponymous iOS app along with browser extensions for Chrome, Safari, and Firefox. The app lets you listen to articles and transcribes your favorite podcasts.

Though the app itself is free to use, you can pay $79.99 per year to unlock features like improved transcriptions for podcasts and YouTube videos, tools to adjust reading speed, and additional integrations with other apps like notes apps, Gmail, and Kindle.

Image Credits:Matter

In March 2025, the company also added an AI-powered co-reader to answer questions about different topics users might have while reading an article.

Instapaper

Instapaper, which was founded by developer Marco Arment in 2008, is one of the oldest read-it-later apps. It’s available on both iOS and Android, and lets you save unlimited articles and videos without paying any fees. It was acquired by Pinterest in 2016.

Image Credits:Instapaper

However, for $59.99 per year, you can add notes to saved articles, have a permanent archive of articles in your accounts, create a text-to-speech playlist to listen to stories, enable full text search for all saved items, and get the ability to send articles to your Kindle.

The company allowed Pocket users to import their account into Instapaper. Users who imported this way also received an email offering a three-month free trial to Instapaper Premium.

Raindrop.io

Raindrop works primarily as an alternative bookmark manager for web browsers. However, its accompanying mobile apps for iOS and Android allow you to read your saved articles and PDFs. The free version gives you unlimited bookmark saving along with integrations like Zapier and IFTTT.

If you decide to pay $33 per year, you’ll also get AI-powered suggestions for organizing your content better, full text search, reminders for your bookmarks, a duplicate and broken links finder, and a file upload limit of 10GB per month.

Image Credits:Raindrop.io / raindrop.io

Plinky

Former Twitter engineer Joe Fabisevich created Plinky to allow users to save and categorize any kind of link, including articles, videos, recipes, and memes.

The app is available across all Apple platforms, along with browser extensions to save links. Once you’re signed up, Plinky lets you use folders and tags to categorize your links, and even set reminders to read them at a specific time.

Image Credits:Plinky

You can save 50 links, create three folders, and use five tags with the free version. To remove these restrictions, you can pay $3.99 per month, $39.99 a year, or a one-time fee of $159.99. Pro users are able to save unlimited links, create an unlimited number of folders, use an unlimited number of tags, and set an unlimited number of reminders.

Paperspan

Paperspan is a very simple app that offers a reading list across devices, allows you to add notes, and has text-to-speech functionality.

The app is free, but it offers an $8.99 per month subscription to unlock advanced search, as well as the ability to create playlists, show reading stats, and send your articles to Kindle.

(Though the app works, PaperSpan hasn’t been updated for some time, which may not be a good signal about its long-term future. The app is available on both iOS and Android.)

Readwise Reader

Readwise, a tool to add notes and highlights to articles, launched its Reader app in 2021. The app allows you to import RSS feeds, YouTube videos, Twitter threads, and more to read at your convenience. Because of its integration with Readwise, the Reader app offers great annotation features. It also features offline text search and an AI assistant.

Image Credits:Readwise Reader

Plus, you can integrate Reader with knowledge management apps such as Obsidian, Notion, Roam Research, Evernote, and Logseq. The app is free to try for 30 days, and then you have to pay a $9.99 per month Readwise subscription to access it.

Readwise had allowed Pocket users to import their entire Pocket archive into Reader, adding that its app supports a number of features — like PDFs, ePubs, X posts, AI, and filtering — that Pocket never did.

DoubleMemory

DoubleMemory is a newer indie app focused on the Apple ecosystem, offering native apps for both Mac and iOS.

On Mac, you can easily save any link or content by pressing Cmd + C twice. The saved content will then appear in a Pinterest-style tile format.

The app also allows you to read offline and search through text, notes, and tags. You don’t need an account to start using DoubleMemory. And if you have multiple apps, it uses your iCloud account to sync content across them.

Image Credits:DoubleMemory

DoubleMemory is free with in-app purchases. It offers a $3.99 monthly subscription or an annual subscription of $17.99.

Recall

Recall works as a browser extension and offers a mobile app that allows users to save content from the web, including articles, PDFs, blog posts, podcasts, Wikipedia pages, YouTube videos, and recipes.

However, unlike traditional read-it-later apps, Recall uses AI to automatically summarize content, categorize it, and then resurface it when it’s related to something new you’re looking to learn about.

Image Credits:Recall

Designed to enhance your ability to remember information, you can review your summaries from your personal knowledge base on a saved spaced repetition schedule.

Recall is free to try with support for up to 10 free, AI-generated summaries. After that, you can continue to use Recall as a read-it-later tool, or you can upgrade to a $7 per month plan for unlimited AI summaries and other features.

Wallabag

Wallabag is an open-source read-it-later app that is available on major platforms like iOS, Android, and the Web, with support for e-readers like Kindle and Kobo. The app lets you save articles for offline consumption and also export all of your data in PDF, ePUB, .mobi, JSON, CSV, TXT, or HTML formats.

The app has a simple interface and lets you highlight sections and add tags to articles. It also has a reader mode and supports importing data from other services like Pocket, Instapaper, and others.

The app is also available as an €11 per year hosted subscription, if you prefer. The company will use the money to fund its open-source efforts.

Readeck

Open source web app Readeck is designed to help you organize any web content you want to revisit later, whether that’s articles, videos, photos, or anything else. You can also use the service to highlight text, export articles to e-book format, save video transcripts, and more.

Image Credits:Readeck

Readeck works as a browser extension so you can save your bookmarks as you surf the web. Users can host Readeck themselves, but the company says it will offer a hosted version in 2025. It’s also developing a mobile app.

Obsidian Web Clipper

Obsidian‘s web clipping service lets you highlight and capture web pages you want to save with just a click on its browser extension. You can also use templates that customize how certain types of web pages are saved.

For instance, articles are saved with their citations and footnotes, while recipes will include ingredients, steps, and nutrition. You can even set up custom templates to save from your favorite websites.

Image Credits:Obsidian

As an open source app, Web Clipper is free to use, allowing you to highlight text, images, and blocks of content for saving into the Obsidian note-taking app.

Karakeep

Karakeep‘s bookmarking app lets you save links, notes, and images, and then uses AI to automatically tag items and make retrieving them faster. The app includes other features like support for lists, bulk actions, dark mode, full-text search, and more.

Image Credits:Karakeep

The open source app is available on iOS and Android as a browser extension for Chrome and Firefox. You can support its developer here.

Dewey

Dewey is another “save everything”-style app that lets you save and organize web links, videos, and images, including posts from social media sites like X, TikTok, Bluesky, Threads, Reddit, Instagram, LinkedIn, and others.

Image Credits:Dewey

The service offers built-in organizational tools like folders and tags, AI bulk tagging, keyboard shortcuts, automatic syncing to Notion, export, a personalized RSS feed, and more. Dewey offers multiple plans, starting at $7.50 per month, which you can choose to pay annually for $30 off.

Folio

Cross-platform app Folio’s design might remind you of Pocket, in part. That may not be an accident, either, as the app’s creator, Nick Chapman, worked at Pocket as head of product.

Folio’s interface is simple and lets you filter articles using the tagged, favorites, short reads, and long reads tabs. You can easily add articles through the Chrome extension, the share sheet, or by manually adding URLs. Plus, it’s easy to import data from other apps like Instapaper.

Image Credits: Folio Image Credits:Folio

Currently, the app offers premium features like text-to-speech, highlights, custom fonts, and full-text search for free. It also has a discovery section where you can explore articles to read.

Folio is currently on the web, iOS, and Android.

Burn 451

While a lot of apps allow you to save articles, we all know it is easy to hoard articles and not read them. Burn 451 is trying to change that habit. It will let you save an article, but you have to read or tag it. If you don’t do that within 24 hours of saving the article, it gets deleted.

Image Credits: Burn 451 Image Credits:Burn 451

The app is currently available on the web and iOS. If you use AI tools, the app also offers a model context protocol (MCP) server to reason over reading habits.

Omphalis

Omphalis is an AI-powered consume-it-later app, as you can save articles, documents, podcasts, and videos. The app turns these media into a more comprehensible version by adding a summary, top points, and a chapter-like structure.

The free version gives you limited AI-powered comprehensions, subscribed sources, and transcription minutes. Pro plans starting from $9 per month will get users higher limits and features like key moments recaps and read-alongs.

This is not an exhaustive list, and we will keep adding more tools as we discover them.

Tech.title: Unforgetful is a new reminders app for people who can’t stop hitting snooze
Tech.content:
Marco Arment, the indie developer who created popular apps like Overcast and Instapaper, and who previously served as Tumblr’s chief technology officer, is out today with his latest creation — an alternative to Apple’s Reminders designed for procrastinators, called Unforgetful.

The new iOS and Mac app works with your current Reminders database, but it’s designed for people who find Apple’s system doesn’t work for them.

As Arment explains in his announcement on Friday, “Siri, for all of its faults, has always been very good at creating tasks in Apple’s Reminders app… The Reminders app, though, doesn’t fit me at all. I don’t like how it looks, how it works, or how it’s organized. Hell, I don’t even like its icon. There’s nothing about it I like. So I never open it.”

The developer pointed to specific issues where he felt Reminders fell short, like how its snooze feature worked, or those times when he accidentally dismissed a reminder instead of snoozing it, losing the reminder altogether. Arment also noted that if he forgot to include a time when setting a reminder, he’d miss getting a notification, so the task never got done.

Image Credits:Marco Arment/Unforgetful

Unforgetful is meant to address these issues and make it impossible to lose your tasks. For some, the solution could be overkill, but for those who are addicted to snoozing reminders or need more regular nudges, it could help keep them on track.

For starters, notifications will always repeat — even if you miss them or dismiss them — until the task is actually done and deleted. This makes it harder to lose reminders, especially if you’re guilty of dismissing them before completing the task.

Snoozing has also been revamped so that the intervals scale as you continue to snooze your tasks. However, it won’t overwhelm you with multiple tasks at the same time, which could lead you to freeze and do nothing at all.

The app keeps things fairly simple, too, as there are no tags, different views or modes, or other organization tools to learn. (For more advanced features like this, Apple’s Reminders app would still be a better choice.)

Image Credits:Marco Arment/Unforgetful

In short, Unforgetful becomes the tool that makes sure you stay on top of your reminders, no matter whether you prefer to enter them by hand or tell Siri, and no matter whether they have a deadline or not. Because the app works with your existing Apple Reminders, you can continue using reminders as you always have — you just turn off the Apple Reminders notifications and replace them with Unforgetful notifications instead.

While there are other well-designed, third-party reminders apps on the market, the best thing about Unforgetful’s setup is this Reminders integration. This means you don’t have to explicitly tell Siri to use Unforgetful when you’re adding reminders. And if you find you don’t like the app, you won’t need to export your reminders back to Apple’s database. (Because they’re already there!)

Unforgetful also ships with its own in-app microphone for voice reminders and a full suite of widgets for the Lock Screen and Control Center.

The app is $19.99 per year and works across both Mac and iOS.

Tech.title: Google will now allow users to remove visible watermark from its AI generations
Tech.content:
In Brief

Google announced on Friday that it will now allow users to remove a visible watermark from its AI generations, including images, videos, and songs. The company specified that this won’t affect the invisible SynthID watermark and C2PA standard-related metadata.

Josh Woodward, the company’s VP for Gemini, said in a post on X that this toggle will be available for Nano Banana, Omni, and Lyria models. He specified that the setting to turn the visible watermark off will be available in Gemini and Google’s video editor, Flow, with support for Search coming soon.

The change reflects an evolving approach to labeling AI-generated media, as visible watermarks can often make content less useful for professional and creative work, but the need to identify AI-generated content remains.

“We’re striking a balance here between creative control and safety: while the visible watermarks are now optional, invisible SynthID watermarks and C2PA metadata are still being used for transparency. So you can still use Gemini or Search to see if an image was AI-generated,” he wrote.

The feature is rolling out in the coming days, and once available, users will be able to go to Settings > Media Watermark to turn the visible mark on or off.

Google is also open sourcing a new library called Credentio to let developers embed a local validation mechanism in their apps.

This comes after Anthropic’s hotly debated move to include a watermark in text and files generated by Claude to comply with EU regulations.
